news.Title: 1 Reason to Buy Microsoft Stock for 10 Years
news.Content:
Microsoft (NASDAQ: MSFT) has long charged businesses for each worker using its software, a model known as seat-based pricing. The one reason to buy the stock for the next 10 years is that Copilot, its AI assistant, is moving from per-seat subscriptions to usage-based pricing. This could have a significant impact on Microsoft's growth that isn't yet priced into the stock.

The shift to usage-based pricing will allow Microsoft to sell into a bigger market and earn more per customer. The latest numbers in the earnings report show why this is a big deal.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

CEO Satya Nadella said, "The number of Copilot customers actively consuming credits through usage-based billing grew over 75% over the quarter." Customers are increasingly using Copilot to perform higher-value work, driving daily users up fivefold year over year.

Overall, Microsoft's revenue from agents and infrastructure (Azure, 365 cloud, productivity and server licensing, and industry solutions) grew 25% year over year to nearly $77 billion.

The momentum in Copilot is a positive signal for investors. It matters because investors have worried that AI would shrink the number of workers Microsoft can charge for, since it can make each worker more productive. But the recent results suggest usage-based offerings can keep revenue growing even when seat counts don't. Microsoft's 365 commercial cloud revenue grew 17% year over year on a reported basis, even though paid seats rose only 5%.

The stock trades at about 27 times forward earnings, and analysts expect earnings to grow about 16% annually over the next several years. That's a reasonable price for a business whose revenue can scale with real work being done with AI over the long term.

news.Title: Midterm Elections, Important Earnings and Other Key things to Watch this Week
news.Content:
Markets face a crowded week as midterm elections land Tuesday alongside a heavy earnings calendar. Apple (AAPL) and Palantir Technologies (PLTR) kick off results Monday. Advanced Micro Devices (AMD), Qualcomm (QCOM), Arm Holdings (ARM), and Uber Technologies (UBER) follow as the week unfolds.

Capital continues rotating out of tech and AI stocks into defensive sectors. Investors want to know if this week's results can slow that shift.

More News from Barchart

Coca-Cola Delivers Strong Growth - But is KO Stock Undervalued?

Tired of missing midday reversals? The FREE Barchart Brief newsletter keeps you in the know. Sign up now!

Monday's ISM Manufacturing data and Wednesday's services readings will gauge economic momentum.

Midterm results could also shift expectations on taxes, tariffs, and spending into 2027.

Here are 5 things to watch this week in the Market.

US Midterm Elections: Policy Uncertainty Ahead

Tuesday's midterm elections could reshape control of Congress and the policy agenda for two years. Markets dislike uncertainty, so volatility may rise until results are clear. A divided Congress would likely limit major new legislation. Some investors view gridlock as supportive for stocks, since it reduces policy surprises. Historically, the S&P 500 has tended to rally in the months following midterm elections. That pattern is not guaranteed, but it shapes positioning heading into year-end. Healthcare, energy, and defense stocks often react sharply to election headlines. Treasury yields will also be watched for any reaction to fiscal policy expectations. Close races could delay final results and extend uncertainty beyond Wednesday.

Capital Rotation Out of Tech and Into Defensives

Money has been steadily leaving richly valued technology and AI names. Consumer staples, utilities, and healthcare have attracted much of that capital. Investors are favoring earnings visibility and dividends over speculative growth stories. This week offers several tests for the defensive trade. Pfizer (PFE) and Amgen (AMGN) report Tuesday. Novo Nordisk (NVO) follows Wednesday. Keurig Dr Pepper (KDP) adds a consumer staples read Tuesday. Power producer Vistra (VST) reports Friday, bridging utilities and AI energy demand. Solid results would reinforce the rotation. A strong showing from tech, however, could slow or reverse the flow.

Big Tech and Semiconductor Earnings Test

Apple (AAPL) reports Monday, with focus on iPhone demand, services growth, and AI features. Palantir (PLTR) tests AI software adoption and government contract momentum. AMD (AMD) reports Tuesday, with investors watching data center chip demand against Nvidia. Arista Networks (ANET) and Astera Labs (ALAB) also report Tuesday. Both offer a read on AI networking spend. Qualcomm (QCOM) and Arm (ARM) report Wednesday, covering mobile and edge AI demand. Datadog (DDOG) and AppLovin (APP) add software views the same day. Cloudflare (NET) reports Thursday. Strong guidance could steady the battered chip sector. Weak outlooks would likely extend the selloff and fuel further rotation.

Story Continues

Consumer and Energy Earnings Read-Through

Booking Holdings (BKNG) reports Tuesday, offering a read on travel demand into the holidays. Shopify (SHOP) also reports Tuesday, showing e-commerce trends ahead of peak shopping season. Uber (UBER) and McDonald's (MCD) report Wednesday. Uber reflects ride-sharing and delivery spending, while McDonald's shows value-seeking behavior. ConocoPhillips (COP) and Devon Energy (DVN) report Thursday. Their results will show how volatile crude prices are affecting profits. Berkshire Hathaway (BRK.B) closes the calendar Friday with a broad view of the U.S. economy. Investors will also watch Berkshire's cash pile for signs of new buying.

Economic Data and Crude Inventories

Monday's ISM Manufacturing PMI at 10:00am opens the week's economic calendar. The ISM Manufacturing Prices component will show whether input costs are still climbing. Tuesday's JOLTS job openings offer a look at labor demand. Wednesday's ADP report at 8:15am previews private sector hiring. Services PMI and ISM Non-Manufacturing data follow Wednesday morning. Crude oil inventories at 10:30am Wednesday will show supply and demand trends. Thursday's initial jobless claims at 8:30am round out the labor picture. Weak data could revive rate cut hopes and ease bond yields. Strong readings may keep yields elevated and pressure growth stocks further.

Best of luck this week and don't forget to check out my daily options article.

news.Title: Could Apple's Latest iPhone Be Its Biggest Growth Catalyst in Years?
news.Content:
In September, Apple (NASDAQ:AAPL) announced a new lineup of products, as it always does. The company debuted the iPhone 18, but the main event was arguably the unveiling of the iPhone Duo, Apple's first attempt at a Foldable smartphone. This was hardly a surprise. Rumors that Apple would finally launch a foldable version of its famous device had been circulating for months.

Apple's decision to launch the iPhone Duo was likely driven by its perception of tangible consumer interest. But will demand for the iPhone Duo be strong enough to make this device a meaningful growth driver?

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

Image source: Getty Images.

Early signs are positive

So far, the evidence suggests that Apple was correct: Demand for the iPhone Duo has been off the charts. Pre-orders apparently sold out quickly. According to some estimates, iPhone Duo shipments through the end of 2026 could total between six million and 10 million. Here's why that's meaningful.

This is a premium device with a starting price of about $2,000 -- versions with more memory and other advanced features are even more expensive. At the lowest price, and with six million devices sold and perhaps as many as 10 million, that's between $12 billion and $20 billion.

The lower end of that range represents 22% of total iPhone revenue in the company's latest quarterly update. Of course, iPhone Duo sales will somewhat cannibalize other models' sales. But note that the iPhone 18 Pro -- the cheapest one available right now -- has a starting price of roughly $1,200, or $800 less than the cheapest iPhone Duo model.

Even assuming every base iPhone Duo sale is a foregone iPhone 18 Pro sale, that could add $4.8 billion to Apple's revenue through the end of the year.

However, there is a decent chance that Apple will successfully attract at least some users switching from other smartphone brands . That highlights the company's long-term strategy. Apple doesn't necessarily seek to be first to market. One of the tech leader's biggest strengths is releasing better versions of existing devices. That's what it did with the iPhone, changing the smartphone market forever. It did the same with several other products, including its Apple Watch and AirPods. The iPhone Duo is the company's latest attempt.

Story Continues

In recent quarters, Apple's revenue growth has been much higher than its average over the past three years.

AAPL Revenue (Quarterly YoY Growth) data by YCharts

The iPhone Duo could help the company maintain that trend. The company could also profit from a long-term opportunity in this niche. Foldable smartphones account for only 2% of the smartphone market. Apple could expand that total, and as it does, the company's revenue and earnings could grow faster than they otherwise would. The iPhone Duo could, indeed, be Apple's best growth catalyst in years. The excitement surrounding this device is arguably the most we have seen from a new iPhone launch in a very long time.

What's next for Apple?

The iPhone Duo launch wasn't a flawless success for Apple. The company is dealing with supply constraints, and there have apparently been rare instances of cracked screens. These problems should do little to slow Apple's momentum, in my view. The company will likely seek to increase capacity to meet demand for the iPhone Duo, and the tech giant will offer replacements to users whose screens cracked. Meanwhile, Apple's entire business remains healthy.

It has launched several other new devices and continues to integrate artificial intelligence (AI) capabilities into its products to improve the user experience. These efforts could lead to a growing installed base and an expanding number of paid subscriptions in the company's services segment, which will help boost profits and margins in the long run.

Apple's strategy hasn't changed, and it still looks likely to support consistent financial results over the long term. And there are other great reasons to buy the stock, including management's willingness to reward shareholders through dividends and share buybacks. The bottom line: Apple remains a great stock to buy and hold, and the brand-new iPhone Duo is just one of many reasons.

news.Title: Warren Buffett's Apple Bet Is Still Berkshire Hathaway's Biggest Stock Holding at 22% of the Portfolio
news.Content:
Warren Buffett spent the final years of his run as CEO of Berkshire Hathaway (NYSE: BRKA) (NYSE: BRKB) selling Apple (NASDAQ: AAPL) stock. Even though the conglomerate sold off hundreds of millions of shares, Berkshire still owns more Apple stock than any other holding.

At the end of June -- the period covered by the company's latest regulatory filing -- Berkshire held 227.9 million Apple shares worth about $66 billion, roughly 22% of the company's total investment portfolio. That's a long way from the roughly half of the portfolio Apple once made up.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

However, I think the current stake says more about the confidence that Buffett -- and new CEO Greg Abel -- have in Apple than the selling does.

Why Buffett fell for Apple

Buffett has long treated Apple less as a tech company and more as a consumer products business whose customers rarely leave. That loyalty shows up in the numbers. In the fiscal third quarter (ended June 27), Apple reported record revenue of $109.4 billion, up 16%, and said its installed base of active devices reached an all-time high across every major product category. Services, which include the App Store and subscriptions, generated $30.7 billion in revenue at a gross margin of about 76%.

Buffett hasn't soured on the company, either. In a March CNBC interview, he said he sold it too soon and would buy a lot more at the right price.

Trimming is how you stay diversified

Berkshire Hathaway cut its stake from about 915 million shares in mid-2023 to 227.9 million, a reduction of roughly 75%. Buffett was clear about why. He was happy to have Apple as the largest holding, but not for it to be "as large as almost everything else combined."

That's basic portfolio discipline . Even a great business becomes a problem when it's too big a share of what you own, because one rough stretch for a single stock can drag down everything else. A diversified portfolio doesn't depend on any one company being right.

Berkshire has put some of that money to work elsewhere. In the second quarter, the company bought about $17 billion of stock in Alphabet , including $10 billion directly from the company. And Berkshire hasn't sold any Apple shares since the end of 2025, which suggests the position is about where it wants it.

Story Continues

What to watch now

Apple isn't risk-free. At 22%, it's still Berkshire's biggest holding, so a stumble would hurt. Apple guided for revenue growth of 9% to 11% in the September quarter, slower than the 16% in June. And Buffett said he'd add more only at a lower price, while the stock is near a record.

Apple reports on Nov. 2, its first call under new CEO John Ternus. Berkshire's next 13F is due by Nov. 16 and will show whether it changed its Apple stake in the September quarter. If not, that's another quarter of Berkshire holding its largest stock.

news.Title: A Wall Street Firm Modeled Out an AI Crash: S&P 500 Down 30%, $20 Trillion Gone. But Here's What Happens Next
news.Content:
Tech stocks closed out October on Friday with the Nasdaq Composite's worst month since March 2025, and the strain has reached the bond market too. Intel (NASDAQ:INTC) stock plunged 29% in one day, and CoreWeave (NASDAQ:CRWV), whose bonds came under heavy selling over worries about an AI slowdown and its weak balance sheet, has seen its stock drop 35% over the month.

Those jitters are the backdrop for a recent report in which TS Lombard's Dario Perkins models what happens if the AI investment boom ends. In his scenario, U.S. stocks fall at least 30%, wiping out about $20 trillion in market value. However, the firm's advice is still calm: hold a normal amount of risk through diversified global stocks, don't bet against tech too early, and add government bonds only once strain shows. The firm's working assumption shows a reversal in early 2028, though it says that date could slip. Perkins writes that the recent market wobble may be the beginning of the end or may blow over, and the report does not claim to know which.

Image source: Getty Images.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

The one move: stay invested, stay global, wait for strain

Perkins, managing director for global macro at TS Lombard, says the firm does not know when the boom will end, so its answer is not to try to time it. In the report's words, "Investors can maintain a normal amount of risk via a diversified portfolio of global stocks." The firm argues this bubble differs from the dot-com era because it is "much more concentrated on the U.S. and the AI supply chain," so investors can hold exposure that sidesteps the most concentrated bets.

Bonds come second. TS Lombard says investors "can also add government bonds, but only once signs of fragility emerge." The reasoning comes down to timing. Shorting U.S. tech now, or adding long-dated bonds early, would risk underperforming if the investment boom runs for several more years, with stocks rising and yields drifting higher in the meantime.

The report also expects non-U.S. stocks to outperform over time and argues the dollar is ultimately headed lower.

What a crash could look like

In the scenario, the S&P 500 falls at least 30%, with tech down 40% and other sectors down 20%. That erases about $20 trillion of market value. The report's detailed estimate puts losses on AI-related debt, including private credit, at $125 billion to $190 billion. Perkins said in the report that "the AI crash scenario is now overdetermined. There is just a lot that could go wrong."

The weakest links are AI cloud providers such as CoreWeave, Oracle (NYSE:ORCL), stand-alone model developers like OpenAI and Anthropic, and construction and equipment suppliers. Hyperscalers, the giant spenders, would face revenue downgrades but are not seen as serious credit risks.

Even so, TS Lombard expects only a mild U.S. recession, comparable to 1990 or 2001. That's because the Fed has room to cut rates, private-sector balance sheets are healthy, and rate cuts would help the lower end of what the report calls America's K-shaped economy. It estimates the crash would cut about 2 percentage points from the level of U.S. GDP. It also estimates that the AI data-center construction boom has created around 500,000 jobs, which could reach 800,000 by the end of 2027.

Story Continues

The financing worry, in plain English

The report's central concern is how the buildout is paid for. AI labs sign contracts promising to pay for computing power they haven't yet used. The cloud provider or hyperscaler counts that promise as backlog and borrows against it to build the data center. TS Lombard likens the labs to the no-income borrowers of the subprime era: the data center is the collateral, and the structure holds only while the lab can keep raising money. The firm calls the subprime comparison a little stretched and says the crash would be nothing like 2008.

The numbers behind the worry are large. U.S. tech companies are investing around $1 trillion a year, and AI companies are expected to issue around $700 billion in new bonds in 2027, $400 billion of it from hyperscalers. Hidden liabilities from off-balance-sheet structures are estimated at $1.5 trillion to $2 trillion, and CoreWeave is already paying 15% interest. Revenue is still largely recycled spending, and 80% of OpenAI's and Anthropic's combined earnings come from just 1% of their customers, mostly unprofitable AI start-ups.

The long view

For investors thinking in years rather than months, the report's conclusion is more reassuring than its headline numbers. In TS Lombard's model, most of the damage lands on stock prices, not on the financial system: credit losses are real but not systemic, and the firm sees no 2008-style wave of defaults spreading across the economy. "We're not expecting major job losses and the Fed has plenty of room to cut interest rates," the report says.

Cheaper borrowing could also unlock demand that has built up in corners of the economy squeezed by tight monetary policy, housing among them. "If lower rates can unlock that potential, it should be possible to deliver a swift economic recovery," the report says. The firm expects stock markets outside the U.S. that largely missed the AI boom to outperform, perhaps significantly, and expects long-term interest rates to fall. That falling-rate outlook is the reason it wants government bonds in the mix once strain shows.

That logic sits behind the playbook. A diversified spread of global stocks should do well if the boom keeps running and should beat a concentrated bet if it breaks. And as the TS Lombard report puts it, "If something can't go on forever, it will stop" -- but even in the model, the end of the boom is a recession to sit through, with a recovery on the other side.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger

Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005.

But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout, a massive technology build-out that Google's CEO says could be more profound than fire or electricity.

While everyone watches the chip designers, one "backbone" company provides the critical technology that Nvidia and AMD literally cannot function without. We've detailed this under-the-radar player in our new AI Playbook.

Continue »

Jonathan Ponciano has no position in any of the stocks mentioned. The Motley Fool has positions in and recommends Intel and Oracle. The Motley Fool has a disclosure policy .

news.Title: 5 Huge Winners From Anthropic's IPO
news.Content:
Anthropic has released its S-1 registration document, which highlights how its business runs and gives investors a chance to understand the company before it goes public. It's slated to be the biggest IPO ever, likely debuting with a market cap of around $2 trillion. While Anthropic may be the featured company in its own S-1, there are several other stocks that could thrive based on the information in this document.

The five that I think have the most to gain are Nvidia (NASDAQ: NVDA), Broadcom (NASDAQ: AVGO), Taiwan Semiconductor (NYSE: TSM), Amazon (NASDAQ: AMZN), and Alphabet (NASDAQ: GOOG) (NASDAQ: GOOGL). There are two primary categories here, but each of them is an investable theme.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

Computing suppliers have a bullish outlook based on Anthropic's information

Two of the most notable points in Anthropic's S-1 are just how much money the AI lab has spent on compute already, and how much it plans to spend. Over the next decade, it plans to spend around $518 billion on computing infrastructure. That's a massive amount of money, but Anthropic isn't hosting all of the workloads that utilize its platform.

While the average Claude user may use the webpage or app to work, most businesses will choose to host their Claude instances on their own servers to keep the information that they enter into the platform sequestered. That requires those companies to run the workloads on servers they lease from external cloud providers, which means a substantially greater amount of infrastructure will be needed beyond the $518 billion worth that Anthropic's planning for.

As two of Anthropic's primary computing unit providers, Nvidia and Broadcom should thrive over the next decade as more AI computing power is built out to handle those growing workloads. Taiwan Semiconductor will also be a beneficiary because it manufactures the chips designed by both Nvidia and Broadcom. These three stocks are the cornerstones of my personal AI computing power basket, and each looks like a tremendous buy right now.

AVGO PE Ratio (Forward 1y) data by YCharts.

All trade for less than 20 times next year's expected earnings, which makes them great values, as Anthropic has confirmed that the AI data center build-out will last for many more years.

Story Continues

Cloud computing providers are generating solid income as well

Anthropic doesn't maintain any of its own data center infrastructure. Instead, it runs workloads on servers hosted by Amazon Web Services (AWS) and Google Cloud -- its primary cloud computing providers . This allows the cloud providers to benefit in two ways. First, they charge Anthropic for the compute used to train models. Second, they make money from Anthropic when Claude models are used because they're the ones running the workloads.

This places these two companies in a great position, as they're set to continuously profit from AI usage. They have created a powerful subscription model that generates revenue each time it's used, and the growth likely to come from AI will push these two higher.

Both Amazon and Alphabet are popular tech investments, and the market understands the continuous revenue streams they're generating. As a result, they have a premium valuation to the computing unit providers.

AMZN PE Ratio (Forward 1y) data by YCharts.

These are two dominant and mature businesses that will be no-brainer beneficiaries of a long-term AI build-out. They're also a great pair of companies to build a portfolio around because of their consistency.

Although I have no idea how Anthropic will do post-IPO, I'm confident that these five stocks -- all heavily featured in its S-1 -- will easily crush the market over the next five years, making them great stocks to consider buying now.

news.Title: Greg Abel Just Spent $330 Million on This Tech Stock. Here's What It Means for Investors.
news.Content:
Although former Berkshire Hathaway (NYSE: BRKA) (NYSE: BRKB) CEO and resident stock-picking guru Warren Buffett eventually warmed up to certain kinds of technology stocks, he still never really embraced the higher-risk, higher-priced sliver of this sector's opportunities before stepping back from both roles at the end of last year.

Current Berkshire chief executive Greg Abel, however, isn't quite as averse to the idea as his predecessor was.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

That's the top takeaway from a choice he made in July of this year, and then doubled down on in October. Already holding a major stake in technology giant Alphabet , in mid-October, Abel steered another $330 million worth of Berkshire's idle cash into a company called Bending Spoons (NASDAQ: BSP), adding to a $600 million stake Berkshire quietly scooped up as part of its IPO in the middle of this year.

This is definitely not yesteryear's Berkshire Hathaway. And yet Bending Spoons somehow seems like a perfect Berkshire holding.

What's Bending Spoons?

You've probably never heard of the $30 billion company. You're most definitely familiar with some of the digital platforms it owns, though. Ticket-sales website Eventbrite, cloud-based note-taking service Evernote, video-sharing venue Vimeo, and web portal AOL are now some of the brands owned and operated by Bending Spoons.

At first blush, it seems like the patron saint of lost causes. AOL was once one of the internet's go-to navigation options, but it was eventually displaced by Alphabet's Google. Vimeo can't really compete with Alphabet's YouTube either. And to be sure, Google and YouTube aren't in any existential danger.

Bending Spoons doesn't necessarily need to topple its competitors, though, to reward its shareholders. It only needs to identify digital platforms with more potential than is being unlocked, and then acquire those platforms and make those necessary changes.

And it's done so. Since acquiring Evernote back in 2023, it's added over 200 improvements or features, including integrations with AI platforms like Claude and ChatGPT. It's also quintupled the number of users of AI-powered photo-editing app Remini since buying it in 2021. Vimeo is getting better, too, gaining traction as a tool that increasingly caters to enterprises with specific business-oriented needs.

Story Continues

Its customer numbers confirm the company's capabilities as well. There are now over 1 billion registered users of Bending Spoons' digital products, over 400 million of which use its tech at least once per month.

The results speak for themselves

Then there are the fiscal numbers that investors -- and Greg Abel -- really care about.

Yes, as you might have guessed, the company is borrowing and issuing stock to fund its acquisitions. Long-term debt grew from nearly $2.3 billion in mid-2025 to nearly $4.1 billion as of June 2026, and the recent sale of $330 million worth of its shares to Berkshire Hathaway was a dilutive private placement of newly created stock.

It's arguably well worth it, though. Bending Spoons is not only growing like wildfire, but it's also doing so profitably. Its second-quarter top line of $704 million was up 126% year over year, pumping up per-share earnings from $0.11 in Q2 last year to $0.28 for the second quarter of this year. On an adjusted basis, profits improved from $0.17 then to $0.46, on a 150% increase in operating income.

Analysts are calling for 47% revenue growth next year, too, driving earnings growth of 37%, with bottom-line growth of 48% in the cards the year after that. Clearly, the analyst community believes the company understands how to make existing digital products more marketable.

Not Buffett's Berkshire, but that's OK

If nothing else, it's just a very cool story.

Most of the turnaround projects that Bending Spoons has taken on are platforms that have been around for a while, with many of them being well loved by a small group of loyal users. These digital services just could never figure out the right competitive chemistry. Now, with the right tweaks, they're getting their shot.

There's a much more meaningful takeaway for investors than the satisfaction of seeing some digital brands finally getting their day in the sun, though. That's the fact that Greg Abel's Berkshire Hathaway is increasingly looking different from Warren Buffett's. Instead of making a philosophical point of steering clear of technology stocks, it's making a point of seeking out the right opportunities within the sector -- the ones with real, predicable staying power -- even if it means taking on a bit more risk.

So far, however, Abel hasn't made any investment decisions that would defy Warren Buffett's basic selection standards (even if some of these names aren't picks that Buffett would have made himself). And Bending Spoons is no exception. While not a value stock by any means, priced at only 24 times next year's projected per-share profit of $1.92, there's certainly no valuation concern that would cause Buffett to balk.

If you're a current Bending Spoons shareholder or considering a stake in this stock, of course, there's certainly no greater vote of confidence than being selected to become a part of Berkshire Hathaway's equity portfolio.

news.Title: Microsoft Delivered a Beat on Both Earnings and Revenue. Here’s How to Think About MSFT Stock Now.
news.Content:
Microsoft (MSFT) gave Wall Street what it wanted, leaving investors to decide what that performance is worth. The company's latest quarterly revenue rose 18.8% to $92.28 billion, beating expectations, while adjusted earnings of $4.89 per share also came in ahead of estimates.

Still, a good quarter does not automatically make a stock a good buy. What matters next is whether Microsoft can build on those results and deliver enough growth to reward investors buying at today's price. That is where the conversation moves beyond the earnings headlines and into the expectations attached to the shares.

Why It's Time to Buy the Pullback in Alphabet Stock

SoFi Stock Is Ready for Its Next Big Move. Here's Why.

Stop Missing Market Moves: Get the FREE Barchart Brief – your midday dose of stock movers, trending sectors, and actionable trade ideas, delivered right to your inbox. Sign Up Now!

The harder question is whether there is enough opportunity left for investors who have yet to buy. Does the latest report strengthen the case for owning MSFT now, or does the price demand more patience? Let's find out.

About Microsoft Stock

Microsoft builds software, operates cloud infrastructure, and sells computing devices from its headquarters in Redmond, Washington, with a market value of approximately $3.9 trillion. Its operations include Azure, Microsoft 365, Windows, and Xbox, serving businesses and consumers through subscriptions, software licenses, hardware sales, and a global cloud platform.

Microsoft's shares closed at $530.14 on October 29, gaining 9.62% year to date but losing 2.11% over the past 52 weeks.

MSFT's forward P/E of 27.03x trails the sector median of 29.85x, but its higher PEG ratio of 1.67x versus 1.19x suggests that the discount disappears when expected growth is considered. The company returned $10.2 billion through dividends and share repurchases, while its annualized dividend of $3.64 per share offers a 0.69% yield.

What Microsoft's Latest Numbers Show

Microsoft reported fiscal Q1 2027 results on October 28, with revenue climbing 18.8% to $92.28 billion, exceeding the $90.64 billion consensus by 1.8%. Its GAAP EPS figure reached $4.92 against expectations of $4.72, a 4.3% beat, while quarterly net income totaled $36.63 billion.

This performance extends a longer expansion, with annual revenue increasing from $176.3 billion five years earlier to $346.4 billion, representing 14.5% annualized growth. MSFT generated $76.8 billion from Agents and Infra, up 25%, while Microsoft Cloud revenue advanced 30% to $63.9 billion, or 31% in constant currency.

Story Continues

Its Azure business grew 48%, while commercial remaining performance obligations increased 73% to $677 billion, expanding the company's contracted future revenue. The Microsoft 365 commercial cloud business grew 17% as reported and 18% after normalizing a prior revenue recognition benefit.

Microsoft recorded Devices and Consumer revenue of $15.5 billion, down 3%, although search and advertising revenue excluding traffic acquisition costs grew 12%.

Where Microsoft Could Improve AI Returns

Microsoft's next opportunity is to improve the economics of its AI business. Azure President Girish Bablani reportedly asked managers overseeing roughly 11,500 employees to identify cost cuts of at least 20%. However, Microsoft denied directing teams to develop those plans, so investors should not count on those savings yet.

A more concrete development is Microsoft-Decision-1, a model designed for tasks such as routing requests, classifying information, and checking outputs. It costs $0.042 per million input tokens, with responses free. Testing cited in the report showed it running 35 times faster than GPT-6 Sol. That pricing could make repeated automated decisions cheaper for business customers.

Microsoft is targeting the hardware bill through Maia 300. Deployment is planned at a multi-gigawatt scale beginning in 2027. The company expects 40% more tokens per megawatt than leading GPU-based systems, meaning more AI processing from the same electricity supply. Microsoft intends Maia to become its primary inference hardware for internal products. It reportedly seeks capacity exceeding one million chips but has not confirmed production targets.

The opportunity for Microsoft is to turn those lower costs into stronger margins as AI usage grows. But the reported Azure cuts remain disputed, and Maia 300's planned 2027 rollout means the hardware benefits will take time.

Wall Street's Outlook On Microsoft

Microsoft's earnings are expected to reach $4.84 per share for the quarter ending December 2026, up 16.91% from $4.14 a year earlier. That outlook follows bullish brokerage changes ahead of the latest earnings report. Stifel upgraded MSFT from "Hold" to "Buy" and raised its target from $530 to $575, implying approximately 8.46% upside.

Michael Burry is less comfortable with the spending behind that growth. He said companies such as Microsoft "are spending as if their lives depended on it when their lives clearly do not." He also questioned whether Microsoft uses its financial figures "as a lever to get what it wants." His broader warning concerned roughly $3 trillion in AI data center obligations kept off balance sheets across major technology companies, not Microsoft alone.

Despite those concerns, Microsoft carries a consensus "Strong Buy" rating based on 51 analysts, reflecting the group's overall recommendation rather than unanimous agreement. The average price target of $594.15 implies approximately 12.07% upside from its October 29 closing price of $530.14.

Conclusion

Microsoft looks worth buying gradually rather than chasing after the earnings beat. The business is growing, and its work on AI costs could help generate more revenue for the bottom line. A move higher looks more likely if earnings keep improving, but the spending bill remains a risk. With analyst targets suggesting roughly 12% upside, expectations should stay measured. There is a case for owning MSFT here, just not for treating one strong quarter as a reason to rush in today.

news.Title: AI Stocks Are Getting a Reality Check, But Don’t Count the Trade Out Just Yet. Here’s Why.
news.Content:
The artificial intelligence (AI) trade, which has driven markets ever since Nvidia (NVDA) posted that epic beat in its fiscal first-quarter 2024 earnings report in May 2023, is getting a reality check this earnings season. There has been across-the-board disappointment from Meta Platforms (META), Amazon (AMZN), Tesla (TSLA), and Alphabet (GOOG) (GOOGL). Microsoft (MSFT) did come up with a good set of numbers, but the pre-earnings rally captured that optimism, and the stock closed lower after what was otherwise a strong report.

Amazon and Alphabet Missed Q3 Estimates

Amazon and Alphabet were real duds this time around and missed on most metrics. The last thing markets want from these two companies that plan to spend upwards of $200 billion on capex this year is an earnings miss, and the stocks got punished accordingly. Intel (INTC) — which made its way into the AI trade — also plunged following the Q3 earnings on weak guidance, which the company blamed on the slowdown in PC sales.

More News from Barchart

SpaceX Reportedly Faces Higher Borrowing Costs on Its $40 Billion GPU Deal. What It Means for SPCX Stock.

Why It's Time to Buy the Pullback in Alphabet Stock

SoFi Stock Is Ready for Its Next Big Move. Here's Why.

Markets move fast. Keep up by reading our FREE midday Barchart Brief newsletter for exclusive charts, analysis, and headlines.

Notably, while AI plays — barring some chip and memory names — have sagged this year, the "anti-AI" trade has been in action in recent months, and names like Accenture (ACN) and Adobe (ADBE) have risen sharply from their 2026 lows.

The September quarter earnings and the resultant crash in Big Tech stocks prompt a question: is the AI trade dead for good, or are these names taking a breather and giving a good buying opportunity in the process? Let's explore.

What's Going on With AI Stocks?

The trend we're seeing this earnings season is no different from the June quarter. Markets have given an unequivocal message on AI and want more signs of monetization and are not buying into mere cloud growth, particularly as some of that growth is being proxy-funded by hyperscalers themselves through their investments in AI startups.

Markets are particularly unforgiving of slowdowns in core businesses, for instance, e-commerce for Amazon, search for Alphabet, and PC chips for Intel. Meta's core business is doing relatively well, and it finally called for peak Reality Labs losses, projecting that segment's losses to taper down from here. However, it has plenty of legal woes to address, plus its AI capex as a percentage of revenues is the highest among hyperscalers, which makes markets wary of the Mark Zuckerberg-led company.

Story Continues

On AI capex, investors are getting increasingly restive as that number has only been going up and companies have guided for further ramp-up next year. The attention has shifted to AI companies returning to generating positive free cash flows. Incidentally, apart from Microsoft, which expects to generate positive free cash flows next year, no other hyperscaler has provided a timeline, and if anything, Alphabet talked about its free cash flows remaining under "pressure" as it ramps up AI capex. Tech giants that pushed U.S. buybacks to record highs are now posting mind-boggling cash burn, with Amazon reporting negative free cash flows of $42.4 billion in the September quarter.

Is the AI Trade Dead?

Signs of exuberance in the AI trade have been visible for quite some time now. Things are getting problematic now for two main reasons. First, interest rates are on an upward trajectory, which means that there won't be any easy money to fund the AI buildout. Second, the macro environment has worsened as higher energy prices have pushed inflation and are hurting consumer spending on other goods. Some of the core-business slowdown tech companies are witnessing is also attributable to the macro slowdown, which is taking a toll on overall economic activity and is not limited to tech.

That said, I still don't buy the argument that the AI trade is dead for good, even though I believe the capex spree is getting out of control and not every company would be able to generate an attractive return on that investment. As for buying the dip in AI names, I am proceeding cautiously and making incremental purchases while keeping some dry powder for any further weakness.

news.Title: AppLovin Stock Is Struggling: 3 Things to Watch in Q3 Earnings That Could Get APP Back on Track
news.Content:
AppLovin (APP) has gone from being one of Wall Street's hottest growth stocks to one investors are suddenly questioning. After soaring 97% in 2025, the stock's dramatic 58% drop this year is enough to rattle even the most bullish AppLovin investors.

But savvy investors know stock performance doesn't always reflect what's happening with a business. Short-term volatility depends on many factors, including changing market mood, valuation concerns, analyst downgrades, competitive pressures, and broader market conditions. AppLovin is one such case. The company missed Q2 consensus estimates. Analysts have questioned whether AppLovin can consistently improve its AI advertising models and retain its market-share gains against competitors such as Meta Platforms (META), Google (GOOG), and Unity (U), which has weighed on the stock.

More News from Barchart

SpaceX Reportedly Faces Higher Borrowing Costs on Its $40 Billion GPU Deal. What It Means for SPCX Stock.

Why It's Time to Buy the Pullback in Alphabet Stock

SoFi Stock Is Ready for Its Next Big Move. Here's Why.

Our exclusive Barchart Brief newsletter is your FREE midday guide to what's moving stocks, sectors, and investor sentiment - delivered right when you need the info most. Subscribe today!

But while these concerns explain much of the selling pressure, they don't mean the company's growth story is falling apart. Its AI-powered advertising technology is still evolving, and its ambitions in consumer advertising are picking up steam. In fact, AppLovin has several opportunities to win back Wall Street.

Its Q3 earnings report on Nov. 4 could offer important clues.

1. AI Model Improvements Could Put AppLovin's Gaming Business Back on Track

AppLovin is an advertising technology company that helps businesses find customers and monetize apps using AI-powered advertising software. Its three main business segments are AI-powered advertising, app monetization, and e-commerce advertising.

AppLovin's gaming advertising business relies on AI-powered models that help advertisers reach potential customers and improve returns on ad spend. Better targeting encourages advertisers to increase budgets, making ongoing improvements to this technology essential for growth. In Q2, CEO Adam Foroughi openly admitted the company fell short of its usual pace of model improvement, causing a modest revenue dip versus guidance. However, meaningful improvement arrived shortly after the quarter ended, putting the business back on a stronger growth trajectory. He also emphasized that advertiser demand remained healthy, with MAX publisher earnings growing by double digits sequentially.

Story Continues

As the third quarter unfolds, investors will be keen to see if these recent improvements spark a spike in advertiser spending and elevate campaign results. If AppLovin continues to upgrade its models, it is poised to boost its gaming advertising business and revive the growth surge investors have been waiting for.

2. Consumer Advertising Could Be AppLovin's Next Big Growth Driver

AppLovin is setting its sights beyond mobile gaming, striving to tap into the vast advertising budgets of e-commerce and consumer businesses. This audacious move could not only diversify its revenue streams but also open up a much larger audience for its AI-powered advertising platform. During the Q2 earnings call, Foroughi revealed that consumer advertiser spending soared to 28% above Q4 2025 levels. This jump was largely driven by existing customers, who increased their investments after seeing strong results on the platform.

AppLovin has also opened its advertising platform to the public through AppLovin Ads Manager. However, management is initially focusing on mid-market businesses rather than aggressively onboarding smaller advertisers. By targeting clients with healthy advertising budgets, AppLovin aims to gather impactful campaign data and showcase just how effective its platform can be. However, consumer advertising is a relatively newer market for the company. Sustained progress would strengthen the case for consumer advertising as a meaningful second growth engine. I'd keep an eye on that.

3. AppLovin's Strong Cash Flow Leaves Plenty of Room for Further Investment

AppLovin's financial performance is still a key reason why investors shouldn't rush to sell. In Q2, revenue rose 53% year over year (YOY) to $1.92 billion. Adjusted EBITDA climbed 58% YOY to $1.61 billion. Free cash flow reached $863 million, showing its ability to generate substantial cash while funding expansion. Its balance sheet also provides financial flexibility. AppLovin wrapped up the quarter with $3.05 billion in cash and $3.7 billion in total debt. After buying and holding about $551 million in shares this quarter, it still has nearly $1.8 billion left in its share-repurchase authorization.

Yet, building smarter AI models demands more computing power, which could weigh on costs. Still, management believes these investments will unlock improved ad performance and boost monetization in the long run. For Q3, AppLovin guided revenue of $2.05 billion to $2.08 billion, representing 46% to 48% growth from the year-ago quarter. Adjusted EBITDA is expected to reach $1.71 billion to $1.74 billion with a margin of 83%. Investors should watch whether the company can meet these targets while continuing strong cash generation. Balancing technology spending with profitability will be important to supporting long-term growth.

The Bottom Line on APP Stock

Despite the stock performance, AppLovin has a strong position in gaming advertising, an expanding consumer advertising opportunity, and generates substantial cash to support further investment. AppLovin deserves a spot on any long-term investor's radar, especially if Q3 brings further proof of stronger advertising models and rising consumer spending. For those already holding shares, the company's ample cash flow and diverse growth opportunities offer compelling reasons to stay the course, even when the market gets choppy.

Wall Street still supports AppLovin stock, with an overall "Strong Buy" rating. Out of the 30 analysts who cover APP stock, 21 rate it as a "Strong Buy," while two rate it as a "Moderate Buy," and seven rate it a "Hold." The average target price of $455.97 is 78% above current levels. However, the high price estimate of $710 implies that the stock could rally by up to 178.5% over the next 12 months.

news.Title: Wall Street Braces for More Wild Days in Stocks After Tech Rout
news.Content:
(Bloomberg) -- The stock market got a long-awaited jolt of volatility late last week after disappointing earnings from technology giants added to angst around the AI-driven rally.

Most Read from Bloomberg

Ray-Ban Heir Rejects $3.9 Billion Offer for Stake in Family Firm

WSJ Wins Dismissal of Trump's $10 Billion Defamation Suit

Binance Estimates $6.3 Billion Hacked in Crypto's Biggest Heist

Apple Overtakes Nvidia to Become World's Most Valuable Company

Valero to Buy, Restart Idled Texas Refinery as Fuel Rallies

Now traders are bracing for further shocks this week from the US midterm elections and Nvidia Corp. earnings later in November.

The Cboe Volatility Index on Friday touched the highest intraday level since April as the S&P 500 dropped the most since June. The premium for puts protecting against further losses also surged, as did correlations among stocks, which can signal broader stress in the market. Still, those measures remain well below the levels in March after the US and Israel attacked Iran.

With Nvidia due to report earnings, following disappointing results from Amazon.com Inc., Alphabet Inc. and Intel Corp., investors are preparing for more episodes of volatility. Traders are also eyeing US midterm election results for the potential effect on the war in Iran and domestic economic policy.

"This looks more like a bullish rotation with a derating at its core than the beginning of a broad market deterioration.," said Florian Ielpo, head of macro research at Lombard Odier Investment Management.

So far, the latest selloff has been largely focused on the technology sector, with investors rotating away from the high-flying firms that led the gains this year. Realized 60-day volatility on the US benchmark last week touched the lowest in more than a year, with the low correlation this year and tendency of zero-day options traders to buy dips and sell rallies helping to restrain moves.

The late-week slide comes in a year that's been relatively placid. While 2025 saw a cluster of extreme market swings around the tariff tumult in April, in 2026 US stocks have largely shrugged off spikes in oil prices and interest rates.

But even as the technology-heavy Nasdaq 100 capped its worst month since 2025, some investors were betting on a recovery. There were pockets of call and call spread buying seen Friday on the benchmark indexes and some of the most beaten-down tech names such as Intel.

Options were relatively pricey before the larger gyrations late in the week, with the VIX at the higher end of the range over the past five years compared with 20-day realized swings.

Story Continues

Beyond the AI worries, traders are also eyeing the status of Iran talks, which could determine the trajectory of US military action, and oil prices, after the midterms.

Some investors appeared to be positioning for an end to the war, which has curbed supply from the region for months. Earlier in the week, call spreads were bought in Delta Air Lines Inc., United Airlines Holdings Inc. and General Electric Co., all of which would benefit from peace in the Middle East.

"The wild card is still Iran de-escalation and I think we've seen positioning for potential for that through some of the call spreads in the airlines and GE," said Christopher Jacobson, co-head of derivatives strategy, Susquehanna International Group.

The US midterm elections themselves are seen as less important than earnings and the Middle East, with the S&P 500 option market's pricing of the event risk remaining fairly constant over the past weeks at about a 0.9% move for the following session.

An analysis of midterm election years and market volatility by Brett Friedman, a contributor at Winhall Analytics/OptionMetrics, shows that higher market returns and lower volatility surround midterm elections. However, Friedman notes that in years where control of Congress shifts dramatically, returns are less consistent and more prone to be negative.

With recent inflows from retail investors into leveraged tech exchange-traded funds, moves within semiconductors may be exacerbated by ETF re-balancing flows which buy into rallies and sell into declines to maintain target fund leverage.

The selloff could offer opportunities for some traders to position for a recovery. With hedge funds running low net exposure, positive macro headlines could result in significant upside volatility as investors reposition for a year-end rally.

"With volatility low and hedge funds running limited net exposure, calls offer an attractive way to retain upside exposure into year-end," said Ielpo.

--With assistance from Bernard Goyder.

news.Title: Wall Street just got a candid look at who is winning the AI race
news.Content: The biggest names in tech spent the final week of October explaining how they plan to keep paying for AI. From Elon Musk to Andy Jassy, Magnificent Seven leaders used earnings calls and public remarks to talk about spending, cash flow and who might get left behind. The talk was less about what AI can do and more about who can afford it. Investors did not like everything they heard, and some of them made that clear in a hurry. Alphabet suffered a sharp post-earnings sell-off, falling more than 8% in after-hours trading following its October 28 earnings release. The growth is real. So is the bill. Elon Musk sees a shakeout coming for neoclouds Elon Musk set the tone on October 25 with a warning for neoclouds, the companies that rent out AI computing power. He wrote on X that more than 200 of them face "guppy-level death and consolidation," with few likely to survive. Also read: Elon Musk's latest move brings good news for Nvidia investors His argument comes down to debt. Lenders, he said, are wary of backing companies that make nearly all their money from AI data centers. SpaceX carries about $40 billion in debt to buy GPUs, but it also earns money from Starlink and rocket launches. In his view, that outside business is what makes the difference. Some traders read the remarks as a sign that Musk might go bargain hunting among beaten-down neocloud stocks. He shut that idea down quickly, saying SpaceX was not looking to buy any of them and calling it "pointless," as reported by Reuters . In other words, he expects the weaker names to fade on their own rather than be rescued. The bigger players, meanwhile, still have room to borrow. Microsoft CFO Amy Hood said the company is fortunate to have access to debt markets and has plenty of options to tap financing when conditions suit it. Leasing is one of the tools it is using, and Hood still expects Microsoft to stay free cash flow positive in fiscal 2027. Meta raises cash as Nvidia steps in Meta picked a different route to fund its AI ambitions. It priced 40 million Class A shares at $625 each on October 26, raising $25 billion, up from the $22.5 billion it planned at launch. Orders came in at roughly five times the shares on offer, according to Reuters . The spending behind the raise explains the hurry. Meta's capital expenditures hit roughly $35 billion last quarter, outpacing its approximately $33 billion in operating cash flow and pushing free cash flow to negative $2.1 billion for the first time since 2012. Nvidia is investing $3 billion in Meta's offering, and the two are expanding their partnership. Meta plans to use more Nvidia Vera Rubin systems, Vera CPUs and Spectrum-X networking for its next wave of AI agents, and the companies will work to cut the cost of training and running Meta's Muse models, as reported by TheStreet . The chipmaker is starting to look as much like a backer of its customers as a supplier. Story Continues Jensen Huang also had tougher questions to answer. On October 29, he described Nvidia's business with Singapore-based Megaspeed International as normal after U.S. authorities reportedly began investigating a former Megaspeed executive. He said Nvidia had checked that its chips were not illegally sent to China and that his talks with the former executive were typical of those with Chinese customers, as reported by Bloomberg . Alphabet and Microsoft show the cost of growth Alphabet's quarter showed both sides of the AI trade. Google Cloud revenue more than doubled from a year earlier to about $30.7 billion, yet free cash flow was negative $9.1 billion as capital spending outpaced operating cash flow. Earnings per share also missed estimates by a wide margin. Capital spending is the reason for the pressure. Alphabet spent about $51.4 billion in the quarter and guided full-year spending to $195 billion to $205 billion. More Wall Street: Nvidia and Micron are about to lord their successes all over Wall Street Nvidia, Palantir, and Alphabet send waves through Wall Street Wall Street elites will pocket windfall from record $46 billion profits Microsoft had a smoother week than most. Revenue rose 19% to $92.3 billion and Azure grew 48%, beating forecasts, while capital spending reached $39.4 billion. Satya Nadella described enterprise AI adoption as a long-term opportunity rather than a quick quarterly boost, according to Microsoft . Amazon bets demand will keep up Andy Jassy sounded the most confident of the whole group. AWS grew 39.3% in the third quarter, its fastest pace in nearly five years, and its backlog hit $578 billion. Amazon is now installing an AI accelerator about every 14 seconds, and customers are taking new capacity nearly as fast as it comes online, Amazon reported . That confidence carries a big price tag. Amazon raised its full-year 2026 capital spending forecast to about $220 billion and Jassy said spending will rise meaningfully in 2027, as reported by TheStreet . Jassy also said the AWS investment should yield a far larger revenue and free cash flow business than the company expected just a couple of years ago. Put together, the week drew a clear line. The giants can still raise money and keep growing, while smaller players without other revenue may struggle to keep up, a split Musk spelled out when he said debt markets have largely closed to them. For now, Wall Street seems willing to reward growth only when the cash story holds up. Related: Kevin Warsh sends a strong warning sign on rates to Wall Street This story was originally published by TheStreet on Nov 1, 2026, where it first appeared in the Markets section. news.Title: Microsoft and Skydance announced buyouts. What does it mean for workers in a 'low-hire' market?
news.Content: Microsoft ( MSFT ) and Skydance ( SKYD ) announced voluntary buyouts this past week, cutting payrolls amid underlying business shifts and increased investor scrutiny. Microsoft announced its largest voluntary buyout ever, offering it to about one-quarter of its staff, or 60,000 people. Eligible Microsoft employees have until early December to decide whether to accept the voluntary exit offer, with participating workers scheduled to leave by Dec. 31. Skydance is offering some employees a one-time voluntary buyout, three weeks after Paramount Skydance acquired Warner Bros. Discovery in a $111 billion deal. "As we bring our ⁠teams together, we recognize that not everyone will ​see their future here, and we respect that," Skydance ​CEO David Ellison and co-CEO Ynon Kreiz said in a memo to employees . It did not specify the number of employees targeted. Companies use buyouts as a fast way to bolster their bottom line. Buyouts can motivate employees to leave and avoid mass layoffs, though they can also be an early signal that layoffs are ahead. In most cases, buyout packages are at least worth considering. If you've been offered one, there's a real possibility that your position has already been targeted for cuts. In general, if you're part of a company-wide layoff, it's not likely to come with as generous a package. It might be only straight severance pay, often one or two weeks' pay for every year you've been on the payroll. If you're nearing 65, when Medicare kicks in and full Social Security benefit eligibility is not too far away, you might accept the offer without too much anxiety. If you've been socking away retirement savings for decades, and your 401(k) or IRA accounts are well-funded, you might be in a position to happily say yes and move on. How long will it take to find a job? If you're in the thick of your working years, the state of the job market and economy when you get your buyout offer shouldn't be ignored. The current average length of unemployment is 25.4 weeks, according to the US Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS). Roughly 3 in 10 of all unemployed individuals have been out of work for nearly half a year or longer. Would a buyout offer continue paying you if your job search took that long? This year, unemployment is low, but people are holding onto their jobs, and the labor market has been characterized as low-hire, low-fire. That doesn't make things easy for those hunting for a job. "Employees have been emotionally battered by layoffs, AI, resurgent inflation, and more," Glassdoor chief economist Daniel Zhao told Yahoo Finance. Story Continues "Anxiety has been growing for years. Sluggish hiring rates mean that many workers feel stuck in their job because career growth has stopped, it doesn't pay enough, or the culture has worsened." Financial factors for a buyout decision Scrutinize the details These packages can be complicated. The amount offered is typically based on the number of years you've worked for the company and your salary. It's often similar to a standard severance offer, but these are usually more substantial. It could include extended health insurance coverage, accrued vacation pay and bonuses, life insurance, career assistance from an outplacement firm, or financial planning help. Compute your tax bill A lump-sum buyout can drastically inflate your annual income for the year, which translates to a hefty tax bill. If your employer offers an option to break it down into periodic checks, that is worth considering. Review your health insurance coverage Some buyouts come with as much as a year of coverage, but it can depend on how long you have worked there and your level of seniority. Others provide none. Health insurance might not be a big deal for you if you're confident that you're likely to find a new position that provides an employer-provided health plan, or if you have a spouse who is still working and you can get coverage through their employer. Otherwise, you'll need to shop for Affordable Care Act options through Healthcare.gov or your state's marketplace. You can typically continue enrollment in your existing plan for up to 18 months — perhaps longer — under a federal law known as COBRA. It requires firms with at least 20 employees to offer this option. The downside: COBRA premiums are steep. On average, COBRA insurance premiums range from $400 to $700 per month per person. Insuring more people can top $1,500 per month for family coverage. Examine your income sources Knowing your monthly income, your spending, and your insurance coverage makes it easier to run the numbers for accepting a buyout. Will you need to tap your personal investments, savings, or retirement accounts to get by? Tapping into tax-deferred retirement accounts before you're 59 1/2 is rarely a smart financial move, because you pay a penalty plus taxes and make a dent in your future nest egg. And while you can start receiving Social Security retirement benefits as early as age 62 , delaying tapping into your benefit can boost your payout over time. For each year you defer taking benefits past full retirement age up to 70, you get an 8% increase in delayed-retirement credits. Hire a financial adviser If you don't have a financial adviser, this is a good time to find one to sort through your buyout offer and your situation. Look for one who is a fiduciary — which means they put your interests first. You might ask for recommendations from people you trust. It's smart to interview a few. Some databases to search for a financial planner: the nonprofit Certified Financial Planner Board of Standards, the National Association of Personal Financial Advisors, the Financial Planning Association, and Wealthramp.com. Finally, take a step back and remember that large-scale buyouts are about your employer, not you. If your position is targeted, it's rarely a critique of your performance. Kerry Hannon is a Senior Columnist at Yahoo Finance. She is a career and retirement strategist and the author of 14 books, including " Retirement Bites: A Gen X Guide to Securing Your Financial Future, " " In Control at 50+: How to Succeed in the New World of Work ," and "Never Too Old to Get Rich." news.Title: 5 Best Tech Stocks for the Next 5 Years According to Financial Media
news.Content: Big Tech just had a week investors will remember. At its low on Friday, Alphabet had lost $477 billion in market value for the week, its worst week ever and the second-biggest weekly wipeout for any US-listed stock by Yahoo Finance's calculations, Yahoo Finance reported on October 30. Most of the damage came Thursday, when the Google parent lost $475 billion in a single session after its third-quarter results. For October as a whole, Yahoo Finance calculated a loss of about $766 billion at Friday's low. That is the second-biggest monthly loss ever for a US-listed company, behind only SpaceX's roughly $822 billion drop in July. Heavy Losses Spread Beyond Alphabet Alphabet wasn't alone. SpaceX, Intel and Nvidia each lost more than $100 billion in market value this week, according to Yahoo Finance . Intel fell as much as 30% on Friday after a weak outlook, its steepest drop in decades, and Amazon shed about $70 billion after reporting results Thursday. Software stocks took some of the sharpest hits in percentage terms, with ServiceNow and Fortinet down roughly 25% to 33%. Nvidia was among the biggest losers. Our analysis of whether Nvidia can sustain its exceptional margins as it becomes more than a chipmaker looks at what keeps its profits so high. UBS Argues Against Heading for the Exits Not all the money left the market. Eli Lilly, Tesla and SK Hynix added about $370 billion in combined value over the same stretch, even as the Magnificent Seven stumbled, Yahoo Finance said. UBS's chief investment office argued against retreating. Ulrike Hoffmann-Burchardi, the bank's CIO Americas and global head of equities, wrote on Friday that further volatility does not make leaving markets an effective way to protect a portfolio from drawdowns. She said UBS still sees scope for equity gains overall and believes investors should focus on "building a resilient portfolio that includes exposure beyond tech." The selloff also left Alphabet's price-to-earnings ratio at its lowest in more than a decade, Yahoo Finance noted. You might also be interested in reading our piece on why Alphabet's low P/E is misleading even as the AI opportunity looks real . That is why a five-year view has to look past any single earnings reaction. The ten stocks below were built on very different businesses, from chip equipment to advertising, and each has been picked up on lists of the best technology stocks to hold for the long term. Here is how they rank by size. For the expanded ranking, read 10 Best Tech Stocks for the Next 5 Years . Story Continues Our Methodology To compile this list, we searched for the best tech stocks for the next five years and reviewed rankings published by financial websites over the past 12 months. From the stocks that came up, we picked the 10 with the largest market caps and ranked them in ascending order of market cap, as of October 31, 2026. These stocks are also popular among elite hedge funds that we track. Why are we interested in the stocks that hedge funds pile into? The reason is simple: our research has shown that we can outperform the market by imitating the top stock picks of the best hedge funds. Insider Monkey's quarterly newsletter strategy selects 14 small-cap and large-cap stocks every quarter and has returned 599.2% since May 2014, beating its benchmark by 372 percentage points ( see more details here ). 5. Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing (NYSE:TSM) Market Cap: $2,106.39 billion Number of Hedge Fund Holders: 249 Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing makes chips designed by other companies. In 2025 it manufactured 12,682 products for 534 customers, so it earns money when AI spending rises, whichever chip design wins. Because it builds chips for many different designers, it is less tied to any single product launch than the companies that sell the finished chips. That breadth is the heart of the case. Third-quarter revenue was $46.72 billion, up 41.2% from a year earlier in US dollars. Gross margin was 66.4%, operating margin was 58.7% and net profit margin was 51.1%. Advanced technologies, meaning 7-nanometer and more advanced, made up 79% of wafer revenue, and 2-nanometer shipments already accounted for 8%. High-performance computing, which includes AI chips, made up 68% of revenue. Chief Financial Officer Wendell Huang said TSMC expects continued strong demand for its leading-edge processes, including the steep ramp-up of 2-nanometer technology. For the fourth quarter, the company guided revenue of between $52.3 billion and $54.3 billion. Earnings per share grew 25.67% a year over the past five years. Our analysis of whether TSMC's next chip breakthrough can justify its valuation weighs that growth against the price. 4. Alphabet (NASDAQ:GOOGL) Market Cap: $3,412.31 billion Number of Hedge Fund Holders: 275 Alphabet owns Google Search, YouTube and Google Cloud, and it designs its own AI chips and models. Investors like that the cloud and AI side is now growing fast, while the shares have dropped to their lowest earnings multiple in more than a decade, according to Yahoo Finance. Third-quarter revenue rose 25% to $127.6 billion, the 13th straight quarter of double-digit growth. Google Cloud revenue climbed 103% to $30.7 billion on demand for AI infrastructure, and Chief Executive Officer Sundar Pichai pointed to strong demand for its TPU systems from a wide range of customers. The Gemini app reached one billion users, which Alphabet called the fastest growth of any product in its history, and Search query growth was the highest in five years. Together, those results show the AI business reaching beyond Search into products and customers of its own. The company backs that growth with a 33.33% operating margin over the past 12 months, and earnings per share grew 29.82% a year over the past five years. Our analysis of whether Alphabet's valuation reflects the potential of Waymo looks at one more source of upside. 3. Microsoft (NASDAQ:MSFT) Market Cap: $3,876.25 billion Number of Hedge Fund Holders: 273 Microsoft sells cloud computing through Azure, business software such as Microsoft 365, and the Copilot AI assistant built into it. Investors like it because its AI spending is turning into faster cloud growth. In its fiscal first quarter, revenue came in at $92.28 billion, ahead of the $90.63 billion Bloomberg estimates called for, and earnings per share of $4.89 beat the $4.73 forecast. Azure revenue grew 48% to $33.17 billion. Chief Financial Officer Amy Hood expects Azure growth of 49% to 50% next quarter and said better engineering efficiency helped Microsoft meet more demand with the capacity it had. That growth reflects customers buying more AI and cloud capacity from a vendor they already use. Chief Executive Officer Satya Nadella said the number of customers with 50,000 Copilot seats rose eightfold from a year earlier. The business behind that growth is highly profitable, with a 47.10% operating margin over the past 12 months. Earnings per share grew 17.38% a year over the past five years. Our analysis of whether security bundles can earn Microsoft more profit per customer looks at another way to grow from customers it already has. 2. Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA) Market Cap: $4,934.48 billion Number of Hedge Fund Holders: 285 Nvidia designs the processors that train and run most large artificial intelligence models, and it now sells them as complete data center systems. Investors like it because orders keep growing as customers expand their AI computing capacity. In its fiscal second quarter, revenue reached $96.2 billion, up 106% from a year earlier. Data Center revenue was $89.0 billion, up 117%. Data Center is the engine, accounting for nearly all of the company's revenue. Chief Executive Officer Jensen Huang said the build-out of AI computing capacity is moving at top speed. For the fiscal third quarter, Nvidia expects revenue of $108.0 billion, plus or minus 2%, and that outlook assumes no Data Center compute revenue from China. The next product cycle is already underway. Vera Rubin, its newest platform, is now in full production. Nvidia also returned about $26.0 billion to shareholders in the quarter through share repurchases and dividends, and earnings per share grew 95.27% a year over the past five years. Our look at how Nvidia is using its AI growth to expand into autonomous driving covers one place that growth could go next. 1. Apple (NASDAQ:AAPL) Market Cap: $5,032.07 billion Number of Hedge Fund Holders: 169 Apple makes the iPhone, Mac, iPad and Apple Watch, and it sells the services that run on them, such as the App Store, iCloud and Apple Pay. The appeal is a loop: every device sold adds to an installed base that keeps paying for services. Apple's fiscal third quarter showed that loop working. Revenue was $109.4 billion, up 16 percent from a year earlier, and iPhone, Mac and Services each set a June-quarter record. Services alone brought in $30,739 million. Chief Financial Officer Kevan Parekh said the installed base of active devices reached a new all-time high across every major product category and geographic segment, and Tim Cook called it Apple's strongest June quarter ever. The record rests on a long earnings climb. Over the past five years, earnings per share grew 17.91% a year, and Apple earned a 33.17% operating margin over the past 12 months. New hardware keeps the base growing, with a 14-inch MacBook Pro and a new iMac, both built on its M6 chip, introduced recently. Our analysis of whether Apple's valuation is running ahead of its growth looks at how much of that strength investors already price in. While we acknowledge the risk and potential of AAPL as an investment, we believe certain AI infrastructure stocks offer far stronger long-term potential at a much more attractive entry point.
