news.Title: 1 Reason Alphabet Stock Is Worth Buying on This Pullback
news.Content:
Shares of Alphabet (NASDAQ: GOOG) (NASDAQ: GOOGL), Google's parent company, were trading down over 10% on Oct. 29, the day after its third-quarter report. It appears decelerating growth in search revenue and heavy spending on artificial intelligence (AI) are the two main factors to blame. Capital spending on data centers and equipment topped $51 billion in the quarter, pushing free cash flow to negative $9 billion.

But that spending is funding the one reason to buy the dip: Alphabet is becoming more than a search company. Revenue from Google Search now brings in less than half of total revenue, down from 55% a year ago. Revenue outside of Search grew 40% year over year to $64 billion.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

Google Cloud is the star of the show, with revenue more than doubling, and its operating margin climbed to 36% from 24% a year ago. Its backlog reached $561 billion, which puts the cloud business on course to potentially exceed Search revenue over time if it maintains high growth.

The growing profits in the cloud segment show that AI spending is generating returns on investment. Management expects capital spending to increase "significantly" in 2027. This should enable more cloud growth by unlocking more of its backlog, as data center capacity translates into revenue almost as soon as additional compute is brought online.

At just under 19 times 2027 earnings estimates, Google stock now trades in line with the S&P 500 's average forward earnings multiple. This looks like a good opportunity to invest in one of the most dominant companies at an average valuation.

news.Title: Alphabet Gets Kicked Out of the $4 Trillion Club After Its Record $505 Billion Drop. Here's What History Says Could Come Next
news.Content:
Alphabet (NASDAQ: GOOG) (NASDAQ: GOOGL) made history for all the wrong reasons on Thursday. It shed a staggering $505 billion in market cap after falling 12.6% in the session.

The sell-off was both the largest nominal loss in Alphabet's history and its largest single-session percentage decline.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

Alphabet is now out of the $4 trillion club and was just surpassed by Microsoft for the world's third most valuable company behind Apple and Nvidia .

Here's how Alphabet fared during past sell-offs, why a historically powerful valuation metric no longer applies, and what could come next for the communication services stock.

Alphabet's FCF yield has plummeted to 0.6%

Buying Alphabet stock today is far riskier than in the past because much of its future earnings growth depends on its artificial intelligence (AI) investments paying off.

Alphabet is investing in the entire AI stack, from its in-house-built Tensor Processing Unit chips (designed by Broadcom ) to its frontier Gemini large language models powered by Google DeepMind to Google Cloud infrastructure to AI use cases at the consumer and enterprise application levels. This is a completely different company from the one that last experienced a steep, prolonged downturn.

Let's take a trip back to 2022, when the Nasdaq Composite (NASDAQINDEX: ^IXIC) fell by 33.1% -- the worst decline since the index fell 40.5% in 2008. At the worst point, on Nov. 3, 2022, Alphabet closed at a split-adjusted $83.43 per share -- marking a 44.3% drawdown from its all-time high. But the price-to-earnings ratio was just 16.6 -- a dirt cheap valuation for such a high-quality company. And even more importantly, Alphabet's free cash flow (FCF) yield was 5.6%.

Similar to how dividend yield is simply the dividend per share divided by the stock price, FCF yield is the FCF per share divided by the stock price. Like dividend yields , FCF yields increase when a stock's price falls or FCF outpaces the growth rate of the stock price. A FCF yield of 5.6% is incredibly strong -- meaning that if Alphabet wanted to, it could theoretically support a 5.6% dividend purely on FCF. Or use that cash to buy back stock, reinvest in the business, or bet big on its best ideas without harming its balance sheet.

Story Continues

GOOGL data by YCharts

During that 2022 sell-off, Alphabet's FCF yield was at its lowest level in a decade. But as Alphabet began investing heavily in AI, its FCF stagnated and eventually declined sharply. A one-two punch of Alphabet's declining FCF and its rising stock price has taken a sledgehammer to its FCF yield. Given Alphabet's cash burn rate, its FCF yield will likely turn negative in early 2027.

Alphabet is a buy for AI investors

Alphabet used to be a beautifully boring business with multiple high-margin segments and a virtually endless runway for moderate but dependable growth. Alphabet's stock buybacks regularly exceeded its stock-based compensation, bringing down the outstanding share count. And Alphabet even began paying a dividend in 2024 -- reflecting its capital-light business model.

Under that framework, if Alphabet sold off too far, the stock would simply become too cheap to ignore. Like pushing a volleyball underwater, the buoyant force rockets the ball out of the water the second you loosen your grip, which is similar to how sellers can only push an excellent stock down for so long.

The Alphabet of today isn't a submerged volleyball waiting to shoot up. It has a lot more uncertainty. And therefore requires a higher-risk appetite. That may appeal to growth investors, but the days of Alphabet being a high-margin value stock are on hold.

With Alphabet's capex expected to increase in 2027, it's hard to value the company using traditional metrics such as price-to-FCF or price-to-earnings. Therefore, investors who don't have high conviction in Alphabet, or who simply want to wait to see how AI spending pays off, may want to keep it on a watch list for now.

At the same time, investors who believe in Alphabet's ability to convert its long-term investments into future cash flows are getting a compelling opportunity to buy the stock at a much lower price.

news.Title: A big sell-off collides with more Big Tech earnings and a midterm election: What to watch this week
news.Content:
Last week, we opened the Morning Brief newsletter by saying the first week of Big Tech earnings looked promising — until Thursday. This time, we're here to say the second week of Big Tech earnings looked promising — until Tuesday.

Lackluster earnings from Alphabet ( GOOG ), Amazon ( AMZN ), Intel ( INTC ) sent the tech complex into a steep sell-off, ending a wild week that began with Anthropic's S-1 filing.

Coming into this week, all eyes will be on potential sparks to relight the fire under the tech sector. Fire, to be clear, in a bad way.

Kicking off the week on Monday are earnings from Apple ( AAPL ) and Palantir ( PLTR ), alongside Tower Semiconductor ( TSEM ) and Lattice Semiconductor ( LSCC ) in the chips sector.

On Tuesday, our focus shifts to politics, as US midterms are set to influence everything from control of Congress and the Iran war to the data center boom. On top of that, AMD ( AMD ) and Marathon Petroleum Corporation ( MPC ) both report earnings, and the US government will report JOLTS data in the first major labor market update of the week.

Wednesday and Thursday bring earnings from Toyota Motor ( TM ), ConocoPhillips ( COP ), Eaton Corporation ( ETN ), Arm Holdings ( ARM ), McDonald's ( MCD ), and a range of other corporate market heavyweights, alongside a smattering of economic data.

And all of that excitement sets up Friday's October nonfarm payrolls report, the banner data release of the week.

Big Tech's sell-off wasn't about the actual fundamentals

It was a deeply red week for the tech sector after a slew of earnings failed to give investors the signs of strength they were looking (and hoping) for.

At Alphabet, a miss on both revenue and profit sent shares falling 13% as Sundar Pichai said that while the company's search division had grown, the money wasn't keeping up as AI cuts into search monetization.

Down the street at Amazon, a double miss on both earnings and revenue triggered a sell-off that couldn't be stopped by strong cloud growth in AWS.

And we can't forget Intel, where a beat on earnings and in-line revenue were overshadowed by weakness in PC sales, attributed to heightened memory costs. That company lost a quarter of its value after the report, falling over 28%.

But there's a conundrum for investors in these earnings reports. As Barron's associate editor Al Root said to Yahoo Finance, the numbers weren't all bad; it's more like investors have gotten more demanding.

"It's not that the earnings were awful, it's just that it wasn't enough to support the market," Root said on "The 8:30." He added, "The level of nerves going into earnings season was so high, like everybody was waiting for the shoe to drop."

Story Continues

At Amazon, the company's AWS unit — effectively, its data center and AI beating heart — reported revenue of $45.9 billion, representing growth of 40% and healthily exceeding estimates. Alphabet's cloud unit brought in $30.7 billion where analysts had only seen $29.1 billion.

Intel's data center and AI segment pulled down $7.318 billion against estimates of $6.675 billion expected, marking 78% growth year on year, while Sandisk ( SNDK ) beat on both the top and bottom lines yet still got pulled into a sell-off.

To quote Evercore ISI's Mark Mahaney, writing about Amazon, "This was an expectations correction and not a fundamentals correction."

The crypto fallout from the Binance heist

Binance, the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange, was hit late Thursday by what investigators say is the biggest crypto hack in history. with $6.3 billion in digital assets affected. It might just be the biggest heist of all time.

In the immediate aftermath, Binance said it has temporarily suspended customer withdrawals. Binance added it "will cover all losses" using its Secure Asset Fund for users and company reserves. "User funds are safe," the exchange said, adding that it temporarily suspended deposits and withdrawals while security checks are completed.

But that didn't stop other major crypto assets from tumbling, led by ether ( ETH-USD ), which dropped 4% to around $2,200. Binance's native token, BNB ( BND-USD ), also plunged by more than 5%.

The question for the crypto industry writ large will be: What comes next, after a multibillion-dollar heist off the largest cryptocurrency exchange on the market?

"The industry has to wake up to the point that they have to protect the customer funds," Owen Lau, managing director at Clear Street, told Yahoo Finance on "The 8:30," adding, "They have to have a pretty good cybersecurity system to give more confidence to people."

After the news initially broke, Coinbase CEO Brian Armstrong said on X that his platform had reached out to Binance to offer assistance, and that his team would do "everything we can to support in the current situation." He added that "moments like this call for the industry to work together." (Disclosure: Yahoo Finance has a partnership with Coinbase.)

With the industry pursuing legislation in Washington that would meaningfully shift its regulatory landscape toward the banking world, how does it adapt after such an attack, and how does it earn trust?

"We need a good regulatory framework to really protect the industry and also give confidence to investors," Lau said. "Right now, we don't have it."

A wild week in Washington awaits with a pivotal midterm election

It's a busy week in Washington, to say the least.

Not only will there be 470 active elections — all 435 House seats and 35 Senate seats — for the country to pore over, but Friday will bring the Bureau of Labor Statistics' monthly nonfarm payrolls report, a key check on the labor market.

There's an argument to be made that the jobs report is downstream of the midterms in multiple ways. Two of the banner issues in these races — the cost of living and the trajectory of AI — are set to play key roles in determining how the labor market shifts over the next few years.

A particularly big focus for investors is the key races set to make big determinations on the direction of states' data center development pipelines. Races to watch include the Ohio Senate election between Democratic candidate Sherrod Brown and Republican Jon Husted, and the Texas gubernatorial election between incumbent Republican Greg Abbott and Democrat Gina Hinojosa.

Keep a close eye on California, too, as voters take to the polls to determine the fate of Proposition 40, the proposed billionaire wealth tax that saw Meta issue new shares to protect CEO Mark Zuckerberg's voting power in case he has to sell shares to pay it.

All that said, strategists caution that companies make decisions on a longer-term basis than one single election cycle.

"The historic investment hyperscalers make in artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure today is done so with the aim of growing earnings over the next decade and even longer," Seth Meyer, global head of client portfolio management at JanusHenderson Investors, wrote. "When allocating capital over such horizons, management teams factor in potential changes in the macroeconomic cycle and regulatory environment."

On the labor data front, economists are looking for Friday's nonfarm payrolls report to show 55,000 jobs added, coming after a report well below estimates that showed 29,000 jobs added last month. Zooming in, that entire +55,000 balance is expected to be made up in the private sector, and manufacturing is expected to see zero jobs added or lost even given the data center construction boom.

One of the key arguments for the Federal Reserve's ability to raise rates in September — and its potential to do so again in December — is strength in the labor market. Any perceived weakness could complicate that outlook.

news.Title: Alphabet Says Its AI Spending Will Keep Rising. 2 Data Center Stocks to Buy and Hold Through 2030.
news.Content:
Alphabet (NASDAQ:GOOGL)(NASDAQ:GOOG) spent $51.4 billion on capital projects in the third quarter of 2026 while it builds out its artificial intelligence infrastructure. That was more than double its spending a year before. And it isn't planning to slow down. With its Oct. 28 report, the Google parent kept its 2026 range of $195 billion to $205 billion and said it expects that spending to grow significantly in 2027.

To hit even the bottom of this year's range, Alphabet would have to spend around $63 billion in the fourth quarter alone. That would beat the third quarter's total by about $12 billion, after a rise of over $6 billion from the second quarter.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

Microsoft (NASDAQ:MSFT), which reported the same day, spent $45.2 billion in its fiscal first quarter (the three months ending Sept. 30). That came in below the more than $50 billion it had guided for, because some capacity from third-party providers arrived late. But management expects spending to speed up in the second half of its fiscal year, mostly on central processing units (CPUs) and graphics processing units (GPUs) .

Yet two of the firms supplying these data centers trade far below their highs. As of this writing, Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA) is around 10% below its Oct. 6 record close, and Vertiv (NYSE:VRT) is about 35% below its May record close -- even after surging 16% on Oct. 28.

Image source: Getty Images.

1. Nvidia

Of course, a big part of this spending goes to chips like Nvidia's. Around three-quarters of Microsoft's capital spending last quarter went to short-lived assets, mostly CPUs and GPUs, up from about two-thirds the quarter before. And CEO Satya Nadella said Microsoft has docked its first Nvidia Vera Rubin GPUs.

Nvidia's revenue surged 106% year over year to $96.2 billion for its fiscal 2027 second quarter, which ended July 26. Management guided for fiscal third-quarter revenue of around $108 billion, which would be about 89% above the year-ago period.

Sequential growth is slowing, though. It's come down from 22% in fiscal Q3 2026 to 20%, 20%, and 18% since, and the new outlook works out to about 12%.

In other words, Nvidia is still growing fast, just not as fast as before. But for a long-term shareholder, I think the more important trend is that customers keep upping their budgets, and Alphabet just said it plans to again in 2027.

Story Continues

Yes, Nvidia faces competition. Google Cloud's revenue climbed 103% last quarter, and Alphabet CEO Sundar Pichai pointed to strong demand for the company's own tensor processing unit (TPU) systems from a broad range of customers. But with Alphabet's spending set to rise significantly again, there's arguably room for both.

2. Vertiv

Vertiv, which provides the power and cooling gear data centers need, just reported its fastest growth this year.

Showing how sharply demand picked up, Vertiv's third-quarter net sales surged 61% year over year to $4.3 billion. Organic growth (which leaves out acquisitions and currency moves) accelerated to 55%, around triple the second quarter's 18% pace. Its non-GAAP (adjusted) operating margin has widened every quarter this year, from 20.8% to 22.6% to 25.2%. Adjusted earnings per share climbed 78% to $2.21.

Plus, organic orders more than doubled year over year, management said on the earnings call. But it also said it won't report orders data from now on, so investors will have less to go on.

Management lifted its 2026 forecast again, too. It now sees adjusted earnings per share of around $7.15 at the midpoint, up from $6.02 in February, and organic sales growth well above the market's in 2027.

Still, the stock can swing hard. Shares dropped 17% on July 29, when Vertiv posted 24% second-quarter sales growth and said temporary supply chain congestion had held sales back a bit.

Which is the better buy now?

Both companies get paid by the same build-out. The key difference is price.

Analysts, on average, expect Nvidia to earn about $15.90 a share in fiscal 2028 (the year ending January 2028). With shares near $215, that's about 14 times earnings. Vertiv, at roughly $243, trades at about 26 times what analysts expect it to earn in 2027 -- almost double Nvidia's price-to-earnings multiple, for a business that will stop reporting its orders.

In the end, I'd be glad to hold both stocks through 2030. If I could start with just one, I'd consider Nvidia first, as investors pay far less for every dollar of its expected earnings. With Vertiv, I'd likely begin with a smaller position.

news.Title: Should You Buy Sandisk Stock at About 5 Times Its Guided Earnings?
news.Content:
Sandisk (NASDAQ:SNDK) had two pieces of news in its Oct. 29 report. The flash memory specialist's revenue grew 23% sequentially, hitting $11.0 billion for the period ending Oct. 2, 2026 -- the first quarter of its fiscal 2027. And it announced an eight-for-one stock split.

A share that closed near $1,330 the day of the report comes to about $166 when the new shares arrive.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

But after a roughly 13% drop on Oct. 30, the growth stock is about 51% under its 52-week high of about $2,354, hit in June, though Sandisk's profits have kept rising since then. Should investors buy before the split?

Image source: Getty Images.

The split won't change what investors own

Shareholders of record as of Nov. 9 will get seven extra shares for every share they hold, issued after the market closes on Nov. 19. Trading on a split-adjusted basis is expected to begin on Friday, Nov. 20. Sandisk said its market value and each shareholder's ownership percentage won't change.

In other words, every per-share number just gets divided by eight. CFO Luis Visoso guided for adjusted earnings per share between $55 and $57 in fiscal Q2 on a pre-split basis, which he said comes to around $6.88 to $7.13 after the split.

Sandisk said it's splitting the stock to make shares more accessible, including to employees buying through its employee stock purchase plan. But a lower share price doesn't change what a buyer gets for the money.

Growth is coming more from volume now

Revenue leaped 378% year over year in fiscal Q1. Sandisk's non-GAAP (adjusted) gross margin ticked up to 85.1% from 84.6% in the previous quarter, and adjusted earnings per share climbed 26% sequentially to $49.51. Showing where the demand is coming from, data center revenue jumped 61% sequentially to $4.8 billion, rising to around 44% of total revenue from about one-third in fiscal Q4.

But Visoso said about 60% of the quarter's sequential revenue gain came from shipping more storage and about 40% came from higher prices. In fiscal Q4, pricing had driven around two-thirds of Sandisk's sequential growth.

In dollars, higher prices added about $2 billion to revenue from fiscal Q3 to fiscal Q4, but only about $800 million from fiscal Q4 to fiscal Q1.

Management's forecast points to even slower growth. Sandisk guided for fiscal second-quarter revenue of $12.2 billion to $12.6 billion, and the midpoint implies around 12% sequential growth. That'd be about half fiscal Q1's 23% pace, which was itself under half of fiscal Q4's 51%.

Story Continues

"[W]e expect pricing to continue to increase modestly throughout the year," Visoso said on the earnings call.

I think the steepest part of the price rise is behind Sandisk. There's even a sign of buyers pushing back on price. Consumer revenue dropped 29% sequentially to $397 million, which Visoso attributed to the market adapting to higher pricing.

How cheap is the stock?

At around $1,150, Sandisk has a market value of about $165 billion. Shares trade for under 10 times adjusted earnings over Sandisk's past four reported quarters. Around its June peak, the stock traded at more than 70 times earnings by the same measure.

But Sandisk now earns much more a quarter than that four-quarter number shows. If every quarter matched the midpoint of the fiscal Q2 guidance, Sandisk would earn around $224 per share in adjusted earnings in a year. The stock trades for about 5 times these earnings.

At a price-to-earnings multiple so low, investors seem to expect Sandisk's profits to drop, probably when memory prices do. It's a reasonable worry. A year ago, the company's adjusted gross margin was around 30%.

Much of Sandisk's output is also spoken for. CEO David Goeckeler said around half of the company's bits (its units of storage capacity) for this fiscal year are committed under its multiyear customer deals, climbing to two-thirds for next year.

The company also bought back about 3.2 million shares for $5 billion in fiscal Q1, and it closed the quarter with $5.1 billion in cash and no debt.

In the end, the split itself isn't a reason to buy. But Sandisk's earnings keep climbing, and at about 5 times its annualized guided earnings, I think the stock price already reflects much of the slowdown in pricing. Of course, memory profits can drop fast when prices fall.

I'd be comfortable starting a small position at today's price. It's a stock best suited to investors who can handle big swings. And buying before Nov. 20 instead of after won't change what an investment is worth.

news.Title: Here's Where I Think Meta Stock Will Be in 2030
news.Content:
Shares in Meta Platforms (NASDAQ:META) cost about $612 as I write. The stock has dropped around 22% from its August 2025 record close of $790, even as third-quarter revenue rose 26% year over year to $64.6 billion.

Much of the gap probably boils down to spending and new shares. Meta expects 2026 capital expenditures (counting finance-lease principal payments) of $135 billion to $145 billion. And on Oct. 26, it priced a $25 billion stock sale at $625 a share, with plans to sell up to about $60 billion more later.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

Using an earnings path based on the company's own trend and guidance, I think Meta stock could trade near $880 in late 2030. That would be about 44% above today's price, or a bit over 9% a year -- a solid return, but arguably less than Meta's sales growth alone might suggest.

Image source: The Motley Fool.

Revenue may reach about $435 billion

The social media company 's revenue growth is slowing, though just a bit at a time. It was 33% year over year in the first quarter of 2026 before cooling to 28% and then 26%. And its guidance of $73 billion to $76 billion for the fourth quarter points to around 22% to 27%.

Add the guidance to the $181.7 billion in sales Meta posted through September, and 2026 revenue totals around $255 billion to $258 billion, up about 27% to 28% over 2025.

Management said in the third-quarter earnings release that it expects to "sustain strong overall revenue growth throughout 2027." I assumed growth keeps cooling from there: 20% in 2027, 15% in 2028, 12% in 2029, and 10% in 2030. And this takes revenue to around $435 billion in 2030, about 70% over this year's level.

Margins are the tougher call

Meta's spending is now showing up in its expenses. Depreciation on its property and equipment jumped 43% year over year to $6.81 billion in the third quarter. Leaving out the $9.89 billion charge Meta took for its August deal with state attorneys general (a cost I'm counting as one-off), the operating margin was about 35%. It was down from 40% a year before and 41% for all of 2025.

True, Meta expects Reality Labs losses to fall to roughly $15 billion in 2027, from $18 billion to $19 billion in 2026. But it also plans to keep "investing aggressively" next year.

I used a 35% operating margin for 2030, or about $152 billion of operating income. After a tax rate of about 16% (in line with Meta's fourth-quarter forecast) and a few billion dollars of interest and other costs, net income is near $125 billion.

Story Continues

More shares to go around

Meta had about 2.56 billion Class A and Class B shares as of Oct. 16. The Oct. 26 sale adds 40 million by November 2027, and the mandatory convertible preferred stock sold alongside it converts to about 17 million to 20 million more in 2029.

Plus, selling $60 billion of stock at today's price would add about 98 million shares.

Meta also hasn't bought back a share in the last four quarters, and its average number of shares outstanding climbed by around 35 million over the past year. If that rate holds, I get to about 2.86 billion shares by 2030, around 12% more than now.

Split $125 billion in net income across that total, and earnings per share are about $44. Today, Meta shares cost around 18 times expected 2027 earnings. At 20 times earnings, a little above that, the 2030 number works out to about $880 a share.

All this is in today's share terms. Meta plans to pay a stock dividend of one Class C share (with no vote) per existing Class A or Class B share sometime after Jan. 19, 2027. It expects the Class A price to then reflect a 2-for-1 split, which would make $880 look more like $440.

Is Meta stock a buy at $612?

I'd say the upside hinges mainly on the margin. If Meta's operating margin got back to 40%, near where it was a year ago, the same math suggests around $1,000 a share.

Of course, legal costs might drag earnings down, too. Meta said it has some youth-related trials set for the coming months.

Still, around 9% a year is a fair return for a company likely to keep growing revenue at a double-digit rate through 2030. I'd consider buying Meta stock here, perhaps a little at a time. But at a 35% margin, the shares look fairly priced, not cheap.

news.Title: 2 Unstoppable Growth Stocks I'd Buy With $1,000 and Hold for a Decade
news.Content:
If you have $1,000 that you can put into an investment account, you have plenty of options -- index funds , thematic exchange-traded funds, or single stocks can be solid choices. But as artificial intelligence (AI) and the companies capitalizing on the technology have been one of the biggest generators of wealth in the market, I'm willing to keep my money in growth stocks playing an outsize role in the AI space.

Specifically, I'm turning to two companies that sit at the top of the food chain: ASML (NASDAQ: ASML) and Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing (NYSE: TSM).

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

Neither of these companies designs advanced AI processors that are critical to training and running AI programs. And neither of them is building data centers to provide gigawatts of computing power for AI.

But they're important in their own ways -- and they have incredible advantages that make them indispensable for the growth and operation of AI.

1. ASML

ASML doesn't design AI processors or manufacture semiconductors. Instead, the Dutch company builds the incredibly sophisticated machines that semiconductor manufacturers need to produce their most advanced chips.

Its biggest competitive advantage is extreme ultraviolet (EUV) lithography technology, which uses light to print microscopic circuit patterns onto silicon wafers.

And here's the important part: ASML is the world's only commercial supplier of EUV lithography systems.

That gives the company an extraordinary position in the semiconductor supply chain. Whether Nvidia , AMD , or another chip designer wins market share, manufacturers still need ASML's equipment to produce cutting-edge processors.

The company's latest financial results demonstrate how valuable that position has become. ASML reported record third-quarter revenue of 11.7 billion euros ($13.07 billion), with net income reaching 5 billion euros ($5.58 billion). Its gross margin climbed to 57.5%, up from 54% in the previous quarter.

But I found management's comments about future demand even more interesting. CEO Christophe Fouquet said customers are already expressing interest in ordering equipment for 2029 and 2030. In fact, ASML now expects its planned production capacity for 2027 and 2028 to fall short of customer demand.

That's remarkable visibility for a business that manufactures extremely expensive industrial equipment.

Story Continues

ASML expects full-year revenue between 44 billion and 45 billion euros, and the company is exploring ways to expand manufacturing capacity.

ASML's near-monopoly on EUV technology gives it a competitive advantage that would be extremely difficult to replicate. That's exactly the kind of business I want to own for the next decade.

2. Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing

Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing, better known as TSMC, occupies another critical position in the AI industry. Unlike Nvidia and AMD, which design their processors, TSMC actually manufactures them. It's the world's largest dedicated semiconductor foundry, producing chips for customers including Nvidia, AMD, Apple , and Broadcom .

And as those companies compete to develop increasingly powerful processors, TSMC stands to benefit from their spending.

The company's latest earnings report was outstanding . Revenue in the third quarter was $46.72 billion, up 41.2% from a year ago. Net income jumped 68.7%, and gross margins were 66.4%.

But there's another figure that really caught my attention. High-performance computing accounted for 68% of TSMC's third-quarter revenue, with sales in that category increasing 22% sequentially. That tells us how important advanced computing has become to TSMC's business.

Meanwhile, advanced manufacturing technologies accounted for 79% of wafer revenue. Its new 2-nanometer process already accounts for 8% of wafer revenue, and management expects production to ramp up substantially during the fourth quarter.

Management issued guidance for Q4 revenue in the range of $52.3 billion to $54.3 billion, suggesting that demand remains exceptionally strong.

And TSMC's manufacturing expertise, relationships with leading chip designers, and expanding technological capabilities make it difficult to replace. I believe that competitive advantage will continue to reward long-term investors.

Two stocks worth holding

ASML and TSMC aren't immune to downturns in the semiconductor industry, and neither stock is guaranteed to outperform over the next decade. But both companies have a quality I particularly value: They can benefit from AI spending without having to pick the winning chip designer.

ASML supplies the equipment. TSMC manufactures the chips. Both should have opportunities to expand their businesses as demand for increasingly powerful semiconductors continues to grow.

That's why I'd be comfortable splitting $1,000 between these two stocks -- using fractional shares, as a single share of ASML will cost you more than $1,000 on its own -- and holding them for the next 10 years.

news.Title: Prediction: This Will Be Intel's Stock Price by Year-End 2027
news.Content:
Two years ago, it seemed like nobody wanted to touch Intel (NASDAQ: INTC). The company that basically invented the modern chip industry had turned into its own cautionary tale, posting an $18.8 billion net loss for 2024 while it fell behind Nvidia in artificial intelligence (AI) and behind Taiwan's foundries in manufacturing.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

Then something strange happened. The U.S. government bought a stake in Intel. So did Nvidia. So did SoftBank . Companies and governments don't usually hand over billions to a business they think is finished, and that's the real reason I think the next 14 months matter more for this stock than almost any stretch in Intel's recent history.

The chip that actually has to work

Turnarounds aren't real until a real, working product ships, and Intel is finally shipping. In July, the company said its newest Arizona fab had entered high-volume manufacturing on a subset of its Core Ultra Series 3 chips, known as Panther Lake, the first processor built on Intel 18A, which Intel calls the most advanced semiconductor process ever developed and manufactured in the United States. Its second-quarter 2026 release adds that the next node behind it, 18A-P, had already entered risk production, meaning Intel isn't just trying to catch up on one generation, it's trying to stay on pace for the one after. On the data center side, that same release says Intel also launched Xeon 6+, its first server chip built on 18A.

Why the smartest money in the room bought in anyway

Money talks, and in 2025 three very different yet massive buyers said the same thing with their wallets. The U.S. government invested $8.9 billion in Intel common stock, structured largely out of unpaid CHIPS Act and Secure Enclave funding , in exchange for roughly 275 million shares and warrants for up to 241 million more. Nvidia added $5 billion, and SoftBank put in another $2 billion, both also in Intel common stock. None of this money really guarantees Panther Lake sells well, or that Intel's foundry business ever turns a real profit. But I think it's an odd thing to do if you think a company is circling the drain, and you don't have any faith in it.

That said, I won't pretend this is a clean story. Intel raised another $20 billion through a common stock offering this past August, priced at $95 a share. A raise that size dilutes existing shareholders even while it shores up the balance sheet. That's on top of the hundreds of millions of shares discussed above already issued to the government, Nvidia, and SoftBank, which means every dollar of future profit gets split more ways than it used to. Retail (the common investor) is getting the short end of the stick.

Story Continues

Standing up a brand-new manufacturing process at scale is also genuinely hard, and Intel has fallen behind schedule before, more than once. Betting on this stock right now means betting the company actually fixed what broke, not just that it bought itself more time with other people's money.

So, where does that leave the stock?

Here's my honest number and take: I'm bullish on this stock. If Panther Lake ramps the way Intel says it's ramping, and 18A proves it can carry more than one product line, I'd expect Intel shares to trade somewhere in the $110 to $130 range by the end of 2027, a real step up from where they sit today in the low $90s.

If the ramp stumbles, or foundry customers stay lukewarm, I'd expect something closer to the high $60s to low $80s instead. What tips me toward the higher end isn't optimism for its own sake, it's that the parties with the most information, the federal government, Nvidia, and SoftBank, all put real money in before the comeback was proven. I'd really rather follow that money than bet against it.

news.Title: I Graded Microsoft's Latest Report on 3 Things. Here's My Verdict on the Stock.
news.Content:
Microsoft (NASDAQ:MSFT) posted results for the fiscal first quarter of 2027 (the three months ending Sept. 30, 2026) on Wednesday, Oct. 28. Revenue climbed 19% year over year to $92.3 billion, and earnings per share grew 18% on a non-GAAP (adjusted) basis.

The stock hardly moved. Shares trade near $530 as I write, about 2% under the record close of $543.45 they set on Oct. 13.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

This quiet response makes sense to me. The quarter combined great growth in Microsoft 's cloud business with another big jump in spending. I graded the report on the three things I think matter most to shareholders today: Azure's growth against the company's own forecast, spending and margins, and the outlook.

Image source: The Motley Fool.

1. Azure beat Microsoft's forecast

I give Azure an A.

In early September, Microsoft narrowed what it counts as revenue from Azure, its cloud computing platform, and changed its forecast to match. The forecast was for Azure revenue growth of 44% to 45% in constant currency in the fiscal first quarter. Azure instead grew 48%. And it did that even though some third-party data center capacity Microsoft expected in the quarter was late.

Showing how high demand for the platform still is, Azure's growth has sped up sharply over the last year. Under the new definition, it grew 40% a year ago, 42% in the fiscal fourth quarter (the period that ended in June), then 48% in the September quarter. In other words, Azure is growing faster today than it was a year ago, even after passing $100 billion in revenue in fiscal 2026.

"Customer demand continues to exceed available supply," CFO Amy Hood said on the company's fiscal first-quarter earnings call.

Earlier this month, I wrote that I thought Microsoft shares needed Azure to keep growing faster than 40%. It cleared that bar easily.

2. Cash flow took a hit

I'd give spending and margins a C+.

Capital expenditures came to $45.2 billion in the fiscal first quarter. This compares to $34.9 billion a year ago (up around 30%) and $41 billion in the fiscal fourth quarter. Of course, the total could have been higher had the delayed capacity arrived on time.

The spending is hurting free cash flow. Cash flow from operations climbed 29% year over year to $58 billion. But free cash flow dropped around 27% to $18.6 billion, down from $25.7 billion a year earlier and $19.6 billion in the fiscal fourth quarter.

Story Continues

Yes, Microsoft's operating margin inched up to 50%, from 49% a year ago. But Microsoft Cloud's gross margin dipped to 66%, from 68% a year earlier, because lower-margin Azure made up a bigger part of cloud sales.

The money is going into capacity that customers already want. Still, free cash flow shrinking while profits grow isn't a trend I can grade far higher.

3. Azure should speed up again

The outlook gets a B+.

For the fiscal second quarter, management forecast revenue between $96 billion and $97.1 billion, or growth of 18% to 19%, around the same rate as the fiscal first quarter. More importantly, management expects Azure revenue to climb 49% to 50% in constant currency.

But management also expects operating margins to dip slightly year over year. And it sees Windows OEM and devices revenue dropping in the mid-30% range, partly because of lower PC demand and a year-ago quarter that got a boost from the end of Windows 10 support. Plus, capital expenditures should pass $50 billion in the fiscal second quarter, taking spending in calendar 2026 to around $170 billion.

I'd still call it a strong outlook, as Azure is arguably the figure that matters most for the stock.

Is Microsoft stock a buy now?

Overall, the report gets an A, a C+, and a B+, which is better than I thought going in.

In the past four reported quarters, Microsoft's adjusted earnings per share totaled about $18.04. With the stock around $530, shares cost about 29 times adjusted earnings. Before the report, the stock cost about 31 times adjusted earnings.

Last weekend, I wrote that I'd want to buy the stock closer to $465. The Azure grade is what moves me. With growth well above my 40% bar, I'm less worried the stock might deserve a lower price-to-earnings multiple than I used. And because my buy price is linked to adjusted earnings, a quarter like this raises it.

But the spending grade stops me from paying $530. With free cash flow shrinking, I think 29 times adjusted earnings already reflects most of the good news. I'm closer to buying than I was a week ago. But I'd still want a lower price.

news.Title: Tesla's Cybercab Reaches Dallas in November, and Nevada Just Cleared 5,000 Robotaxis in Las Vegas. Here's the Number That Makes the Bulls Right.
news.Content:
Tesla (NASDAQ: TSLA) plans to expand its Cybercab presence in Dallas in November, beyond its initial expanded deployment in Austin. Meanwhile, Nevada regulators have authorized Tesla to operate up to 5,000 fully autonomous vehicles in the Las Vegas area during its first year under the new permit.

But the bigger question isn't how many robotaxis Tesla can put on the road. It's how much money each vehicle can generate.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

The magic number is $0.30

During Tesla's Q3 earnings call, CFO Vaibhav Taneja reiterated the company's goal of reducing robotaxi operating costs to approximately $0.30 per paid mile. Tesla hasn't reached that target yet. But consider the potential economics if it does.

During Tesla's 2024 Cybercab unveiling, Elon Musk projected passenger fares of approximately $0.30 to $0.40 per mile. At $0.40 per mile, a robotaxi completing 50,000 paid miles annually would generate $20,000 in revenue. Assuming Tesla achieves its $0.30-per-mile operating cost target, each Cybercab could generate $5,000 in profits (before any additional expenses).

Now consider Tesla's longer-term ambitions . Musk's compensation plan includes a milestone requiring an average of at least 1 million robotaxis in commercial operation over three consecutive months. At that scale, assuming each vehicle completes 50,000 paid miles annually at a fare of $0.40 per mile, Tesla could theoretically generate $20 billion in annual gross passenger fares. Achieving its $0.30-per-paid-mile operating cost target would leave approximately $5 billion in annual contribution before taxes and any additional expenses.

Tesla still has plenty to prove

Those figures are just rough estimates and assume significant vehicle utilization. Tesla also has to demonstrate that its Cybercabs can operate safely, reliably, and profitably at scale.

Management expects robotaxis to begin making a noticeable financial contribution in Q2 2027. So if you're bullish on Tesla, the $0.30-per-mile target is the number to watch. If Tesla can hit that target while maintaining strong utilization and pricing, robotaxis could eventually become a substantial source of recurring profits.

news.Title: Anthropic's Frenemies Meta and Google Are Showing Cracks In the AI Trade. What That Tells Us About the Anthropic IPO.
news.Content:
Here's the thing about Anthropic's (ANT) relationship with hyperscalers like Alphabet (GOOG) (GOOGL) and Meta Platforms (META). They are collaborators, and they are competitors. So if you are confused by all of that "circular financing," you are certainly not alone.

That tangled web isn't just an academic debate for venture capitalists. It is showing up in real time on the tape. Specifically, it is starting to cause serious trouble for the Communication Services Select Sector SPDR Fund (XLC).

More News from Barchart

What to Expect From AMD's Q3 Earnings

SpaceX Reportedly Faces Higher Borrowing Costs on Its $40 Billion GPU Deal. What It Means for SPCX Stock.

How Investors Should View the Launch of Alphabet's Gemini 4 Carbon

Get exclusive insights with the FREE Barchart Brief newsletter. Subscribe now for quick, incisive midday market analysis you won't find anywhere else.

That table shows one of the modern stock market's classic issues on full display. If you want broad diversification in the communication sector, one of 11 subdivisions of the S&P 500 Index ($SPX), you can't rely on the biggest index fund with that sector tag.

The equal-weighted version for the communications sector is the Invesco S&P 500 E.W. Communication Services ETF (RSPC), and as we see here, it is a fraction of the size of the S&P 500 Communication Sector SPDR (XLC). We're talking $22 billion in assets for XLC versus only $52 million for RSPC.

XLC has performed much better over time. And its hyper-focused portfolio, topped by a pair of hyperscalers (44% in META and GOOG/GOOGL combined), trades at about a 35% trailing price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio discount to RSPC.

In the game that is predicting the success of ANT post-IPO next month, I think the sudden vulnerability in XLC could be a bearish signal.

If Google and Meta are firing on all cylinders, XLC looks like a genius growth play. But if their AI spending triggers margin compression, or if their cloud and advertising dominance faces friction, XLC drops fast.

Recently, the cracks have begun to show. Investors are no longer giving hyperscalers a blank check to spend hundreds of billions on custom silicon and server farms without showing immediate, tangible returns on invested capital.

As valuation scrutiny mounts, both META and GOOGL have started dragging on XLC. That's the type of dark cloud over the AI trade that could take some shine off the upside potential for ANT in the coming weeks and months, once it crosses the threshold to become a public company.

Story Continues

Google and Meta's Relationship With Anthropic

To understand why Meta and Google are stumbling, look at how they interact with Anthropic. Google is one of Anthropic's largest financial backers and primary cloud compute providers. Every time Anthropic trains a frontier Claude model, Google Cloud books revenue.

At the same time, Google is pouring tens of billions into its own proprietary model ecosystem, Gemini, aggressively pitching enterprise clients to bypass third-party models entirely. Google is simultaneously acting as Anthropic's landlord, its banker, and its fiercest commercial rival.

Meta took an entirely different path. Instead of locking its frontier models behind an expensive API paywall, Mark Zuckerberg open-sourced the Llama family, releasing top-tier model weights to the public for free. Meta's goal: Commoditize the model layer.

By giving away those high-grade enterprise AI capabilities, Meta is driving the market price of foundational intelligence toward zero. If businesses can run and fine-tune open-source models at a fraction of the cost, paying premium token pricing for proprietary models like Claude becomes a very hard sell in corporate IT budgets.

What All of This Means for the ANT IPO

Underwriters are floating valuation figures between $1.5 trillion and $2 trillion. A valuation of that scale requires public investors to believe that Anthropic will generate monopolistic, software-like gross margins for the next decade. Below, I've indicated where it would slot into the S&P 500 at some point, based on that valuation and accounting for the company's full value.

We don't need ANT to be a public company currently to get a preview of what might impact its stock price down the road. The cost of compute is crushing hyperscalers. If Meta and Google are experiencing valuation pushback due to unsustainable AI capex, public markets will not tolerate Anthropic's massive, non-cancelable compute liabilities. When the landlords are feeling the pinch, the tenant is in far worse shape.

Meta might just be starting to train the corporate world not to pay software margins for frontier intelligence. If enterprise buyers can substitute Claude with an open-source alternative, Anthropic's revenue projections fall flat. That's the type of thing that will likely surface in the market's eyes some time after the IPO frenzy fades. But I think it is a real threat.

And with ANT's primary partner (Google) actively developing competing software to replace it, customer acquisition costs surge. Anthropic must spend aggressively on sales and marketing just to keep enterprise clients from migrating to Google's native ecosystem.

Here's the picture that could be starting to form from all of this intertwined mega-cap business.

As I write this, Google's stock is cratering after hours on Wednesday. By 11%. One in every nine dollars invested in it a few hours earlier is gone. For now, at least.

And this is XLC. The chart is as of Wednesday's market close. But it was already breaking down and appears to be retracing its way back to around $100 a share, or around where it was in June of 2025.

What is more concerning for XLC, Meta, and Google fans, as well as the other large-cap stocks atop XLC, such as Disney (DIS), Verizon (VZ), and Netflix (NFLX), is the weekly chart below.

A daily chart that is rolling over can be rescued by a couple of stellar earnings reports. Barring some immediate change of heart by the market, that's not what is happening here.

Hey, at least you can short the future misery of these stocks through an exchange-traded fund (ETF) that bets on a decline in the communications sector? OK, just kidding. You can't. You could for a while, but all three ETFs devoted to doing that were closed by their issuers a while back. Due to lack of interest. Go figure.

Rob Isbitts is a semi-retired CIO, former fiduciary investment advisor, Barchart columnist, and straight-talker. Download his new free e-book on hedged bond investing for retirement at ETFYourself.com. His research and model portfolios are at ROAR.PiTrade.com.

news.Title: Apple is taking Wall Street's top spot back from Nvidia — for the fifth time
news.Content:
Apple ( AAPL ) has taken Wall Street's crown back from Nvidia — for the fifth time.

Apple closed ahead of Nvidia in market value on Oct. 30, its first closing lead since July. It's a move Apple has made before, and it has rarely stuck.

Apple finished Friday, Oct. 30, worth about $5.03 trillion, nearly $100 billion more than Nvidia ( NVDA ), as chip stocks in the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index ( ^SOX ) had their worst day since June.

Apple first edged past Nvidia briefly on Oct. 23, alongside a record run for its stock and the day the tech giant's $1,999 iPhone Duo hit stores , capping a battle investors had been watching all morning. Nvidia moved back ahead that day and held the lead until Friday.

For most of the past decade, this wasn't much of a contest. Apple closed as the most valuable US-listed company in about 7 of every 10 sessions since October 2015. Microsoft ( MSFT ) took the top spot in stretches, Amazon ( AMZN ) held it for 12 sessions in early 2019, and Alphabet ( GOOG , GOOGL ) got exactly one day in 2016.

Then the AI boom rewrote the leaderboard.

Nvidia first closed at No. 1 on June 18, 2024. It held the spot almost without a break from June 2025 until Friday, interrupted only by a four-session Apple run in late July.

Apple keeps knocking on the door

Apple had reclaimed the crown from Nvidia four times before Friday. Only once did it last, when the DeepSeek scare sank chip stocks in January 2025 and Apple held on into the spring.

Since the start of 2024, the No. 1 spot has changed hands 25 times, according to Yahoo Finance calculations. Apple and Nvidia alone have traded places at the close 16 times since June 2024.

This time, the two stocks are heading in opposite directions. Apple set a record close on Oct. 29 and finished Friday about 1% below it. Nvidia closed nearly 15% below its Oct. 6 record after this month's chip rout , and the roughly $900 billion lead it held that day vanished in 18 sessions.

Since that Oct. 6 close, which was also the S&P 500's ( ^GSPC ) record, Apple and Tesla ( TSLA ) are the only megacap stocks in the green. Apple is up about 3%, and its roughly $160 billion gain in market value is the biggest of the group. Over the full year, Apple is up about 27%, about 2.5 times the S&P 500's gain.

news.Title: Jim Cramer issues 'falling knife' warning on top chip stock after Intel's outlook
news.Content: One thing trading has taught me is that just because a stock has fallen sharply doesn't mean it can't fall further. I've watched prices drop to levels that looked attractive, only to see them keep falling. I have learned to be careful and not to rush into a trade simply because something looks cheap. Jim Cramer offered " Mad Money " viewers a similar warning on Oct. 29, 2026, specifically about Lam Research stock (LRCX). If you want to buy 100 shares of Lam, I don't want you to buy more than 25 right now. You buy 25, and then you wait another five days because right now the stock is in free fall, and I don't want you to get hurt. Cramer had nothing but praise for the company itself, calling Lam Research "the best in the game of capital equipment." The warning is about timing, not the business, and the trigger is Intel. Also Read: Intel CEO reveals a PC problem as Goldman cuts stock target Intel's bad night became Lam's bad day "We have some bad numbers from Intel, really bad numbers, and I'm kind of bummed out about it," Cramer said. Intel reported Q3 fiscal 2026 results on Oct. 29 and guided Q4 revenue to between $15 billion and $16 billion, well short of the roughly $17.1 billion analysts expected. Non-GAAP EPS guidance is $0.25 compared with a $0.43 consensus. Gross margin is expected to fall to 38% from 44.1%. Client PC revenue is projected to drop more than 20% from $8.1 billion as high memory prices choke PC demand. An Oct. 14 fab explosion in Israel, which killed two workers, carries an estimated $300 million hit, with a similar impact expected in Q1. Intel shares fell roughly 30% on Oct. 30 and trade at $63. More Semiconductors: Chip stocks set for $229 billion payday before Nvidia ships a GPU Bank of America makes bold chip call after AI sell-off Why Richard Ross is buying semiconductors after the AI pullback I covered Intel in early September when Mizuho reset its price target to $92, and the debate then was whether the AI server story could offset PC weakness. This quarter answered part of that. Data-center revenue is guided to about $8.4 billion, surpassing PC revenue, but the PC side dragged everything down. Intel matters to Lam because it buys Lam's etching and deposition tools. When chipmakers begin to tighten budgets, spending on new equipment is often among the first things to slow. A strong Lam Research September 2026 quarter that still carried a warning Lam's own numbers were good. In Q1 fiscal 2027 , reported Oct. 21, revenue hit a record $8.22 billion, up 54.4% year over year, beating the $8.14 billion consensus, according to ZACKS . Story Continues Non-GAAP EPS was $2.20, up 74.6%. Non-GAAP gross margin was 52.4%, and operating margin was 40.2%. Systems revenue rose 61.6% to $5.73 billion on foundry and NAND demand. The stock fell anyway. On the earnings call , CFO Doug Bettinger said the December-quarter revenue guide of $8.6 billion would have been higher without near-term supply chain constraints, with some shipments possibly slipping into March. Shares dropped more than 11% on that disclosure, according to Yahoo Finance . As a trader, I've learned that even when a company's fundamentals look strong, the market can still punish its stock over short-term concerns. That's why I try not to rush into a falling stock. A good business doesn't always mean it's a good time to buy. Why Lam is not just an Intel story Intel is a major customer, but not Lam's only one. Lam also sells to TSMC, Samsung, and SK Hynix and carries heavy exposure to NAND and DRAM, a market Intel left years ago. If TSMC takes share Intel loses, it tends to buy more Lam equipment. The wider sell-off has added pressure. Amazon 's weaker Q4 outlook stoked fresh doubts about the durability of AI-driven capital spending, the demand engine under Lam's growth. I wrote about that spending theme with Micron and SanDisk , where the thesis was memory tightness. The same logic helps Lam on the NAND side, which is why Cramer still likes the company. His advice is therefore about pace instead of direction. Buying 25 shares now, then waiting a few more days, is a great way to avoid catching a falling knife while still owning a position if the stock steadies. If Lam keeps sliding, you have cash to buy lower. If it rebounds, you are in. The next questions for you as an investor are whether supply constraints ease enough to pull shipments back into December, and whether Intel's weak guidance spreads to other equipment customers. news.Title: 5 Best High Growth Stocks Outside Big Tech
news.Content: The market's growth leadership has become abnormally concentrated in a small number of mega-cap technology stocks, leaving investors with fewer obvious opportunities to find rapid earnings growth outside of the AI trade. Ten AI-related stocks currently account for over 40% of the S&P 500's market capitalization, with NVDA, AAPL, and MSFT accounting for approximately 21.7% of the index. That concentration has made non-tech growth stocks more appealing, but also more selective: a company can generate strong revenue growth while struggling to justify its valuation if margins, debt, customer concentration, or capital intensity are all trending in the wrong direction. The opportunity comes from identifying businesses with long-term growth that can support multiples rather than merely riding the broader AI story, something we previously covered in our 10 High Growth Stocks Outside Tech Analysts Are Bullish On article. The case for looking beyond mega-cap technology is that large tech companies haven't stopped growing. Their valuations already account for much of the predicted AI-driven earnings acceleration, while a number of healthcare, industrial, consumer, finance, and energy companies are growing at rates that may surprise investors. According to Russell Investments, analysts anticipate the "Magnificent Seven" to increase third-quarter earnings by 20.3% year over year, while the other 493 companies in the S&P 500 are expected to grow by 27.7%. In other words, earnings momentum is broadening beyond the largest tech firms, potentially offering up opportunities for companies outside the AI trade. The idea is to avoid using "growth" as a single metric. A company that grows revenue at 30% per year could still be a bad investment if it burns cash, relies on a small number of customers, or funds expansion through repeated dilution. Netskope is a good example : the cybersecurity company announced second-quarter fiscal 2027 revenue of $220.5 million, up 29.2% year-over-year, but trailing EBITDA remained negative at $721 million, and the stock traded at about 9x sales. That is, investors are paying a premium for ongoing top-line momentum as they wait for more proof that growth can translate into durable profits. In contrast, a company growing earnings in the high teens or low twenties can be appealing if it has pricing power, recurring revenue, a strong balance sheet, and a clear path to margin improvement. The issue is that some companies have already been rerated as "AI adjacent," even though their underlying earnings haven't yet justified the premium. That's why the best opportunities are typically identified where growth is still undervalued, rather than where the AI label has already done the majority of the work. Story Continues The sector has expanded beyond construction, mining and machinery cycles to include companies that benefit from data-center power needs, grid modernization, automation and infrastructure spending. Caterpillar, for example, reported record second quarter sales of $20.5 billion , up 24% year-over-year, with its Power Generation division up 29% to $3.10 billion on demand for large reciprocating engines and turbines used in data centers. Despite AI taking up a lot of the news in the market, Mario Gabelli's fund has an industrial stock in its second biggest position , highlighting the idea that there can be interesting growth opportunities outside of the tech industry. Analyst estimates can help identify expectations, but they should not be used in place of company-specific evidence. A stock with a high consensus growth rate and a high valuation may be more exposed to a modest guidance miss than a cheaper company with a less exciting but more consistent growth profile. So, what are the best high growth stocks outside big tech? We listed 10 Best High Growth Stocks Outside Big Tech here . You can find the top 5 below. Our Methodology For this list, we screened for non-tech stocks with a market cap of more than $20 billion that report a 5-year EPS growth rate of at least 25%. We have also mentioned hedge fund ownership numbers for Q2 2026 to provide insight into smart money sentiments around each stock. Note : A 5-year EPS growth rate is useful for comparing how quickly earnings are expected to compound, though it is not always the most reliable metric as estimates can change sharply with commodity prices, interest rates, clinical trial results, and other macroeconomic conditions. Why are we interested in the stocks that hedge funds pile into? The reason is simple: our research has shown that we can outperform the market by imitating the top stock picks of the best hedge funds. Insider Monkey's quarterly newsletter strategy selects 14 small-cap and large-cap stocks every quarter and has returned 599.2% since May 2014, beating its benchmark by 372 percentage points ( see more details here ). 5. (NYSE: VALE ) EPS Growth Over the Next 5 Years: 46.62% Hedge Fund Holders: 39 Vale S.A. is one of the world's top iron ore producers, and is growing into copper and nickel through Vale Base Metals. In the second quarter, iron ore production reached 84.3 million tons, the highest since 2018, with copper recording its best second quarter in nine years. Base metals EBITDA increased 79% to $1.29 billion, accounting for three out of every ten dollars of segment EBITDA, while iron ore contributed $3.06 billion. Moreover, in October, Vale sought to establish a Panda bond program in China worth up to 10 billion yuan, which provided roughly half of second-quarter revenue. That dependence is also a risk. Back in August, Chinese crude steel output declined 3.7% from the previous year, and iron ore prices followed suit. Iron ore costs also rose with the stronger Brazilian real. See how Vale is strengthening its relations with China, including a potential yuan bond . 4. Phillips 66 (NYSE: PSX ) EPS Growth Over the Next 5 Years: 48.40% Hedge Fund Holders: 69 Phillips 66 operates refineries, midstream pipelines, chemicals, and marketing operations. By mid-September, its shares had risen more than 110% for the year, as the Middle East war reduced global refining capacity and increased margins. The company's third-quarter results, released on October 28, showed how powerful that backdrop had become: adjusted earnings increased to $5.6 billion, or $14.08 per share, from $3.8 billion, or $9.41 per share, in the second quarter. Revenue and cash generation also improved. Total revenues and other income reached $51.5 billion, with operating cash flow of $7.3 billion. Net debt decreased by 23% sequentially to $12.7 billion from $16.5 billion, and the company returned $2.8 billion to shareholders during the quarter. The results were driven by refinement. Refining adjusted pre-tax income increased from $3.09 billion to $6.06 billion, driven by record Central Corridor processed inputs of 848,000 barrels per day and a 41% distillate yield in the third quarter. The recent rally is still depends on unusually wide refining margins. BMO warns that even a minor decrease might cause a significant downturn, while Morgan Stanley expects fuel markets to remain tight through mid-2027 but values Phillips 66 at a premium to peers on EV/EBITDA. The shareholder-return program, which aims to return more than half of operating cash flow, will also be more difficult to maintain if crack spreads stabilize. Even so, BMO believes the stock can reach new highs due to its record refining profitability, lower net debt, and ongoing shareholder returns. Read why BMO sees new highs ahead . 3. Reddit, Inc. (NYSE: RDDT ) EPS Growth Over the Next 5 Years: 51.32% Hedge Fund Holders: 91 Reddit, Inc. runs the community platform where members debate everything from hobbies to finances, and it makes the majority of its money from advertising. The company's second-quarter revenue increased 61% to $805 million, the eighth straight quarter above 60%, with net income of $253 million and adjusted EBITDA of $343 million, representing a 43% margin. At the same time, daily active uniques rose 18% to 130.3 million, weekly actives exceeded half a billion, international revenue grew 84%, and gross margin reached 91.3%. The weaker spot is the quality of user growth. Logged-in users increased only 7%, while logged-out users, who frequently arrive via search, climbed 27%, and management reported choppy search referral volume late in the quarter. The company's third-quarter projection of $860 million to $870 million suggests a growth rate of 47% to 49%, down from 61%. Reddit currently trades at 31.32x trailing earnings and 18.87x forward earnings, with analysts forecasting fiscal 2026 EPS of $5.27 and $6.94. The lower forward multiple suggests that the market expects profitability to continue expanding rapidly, though the stock's premium is dependent on Reddit maintaining both user engagement and advertising growth. Investors will get the next update on those trends when Reddit announces Q3 results after the close on October 29. The Street expects revenue of around $874.8 million and adjusted EPS of $1.33, indicating around 50% revenue growth and 66% earnings growth year-over-year. The key risk to the bull case is user trends, especially as AI search and algorithm changes impact referral traffic. Read whether user trends are the bigger risk here . 2. The Boeing Company (NYSE: BA ) EPS Growth Over the Next 5 Years: 69.75% Hedge Fund Holders: 90 Boeing is a commercial aircraft manufacturer and a major defense contractor. The company's third-quarter report, released October 27, revealed a revenue increase of 4% to $24.2 billion, with defense revenue increasing 15% to $7.9 billion. Boeing delivered 161 commercial airplanes, the most since 2018, and its overall backlog hit a record $745 billion, including more than 6,300 commercial jets. Despite Justice Department settlement payments reaching roughly $700 million, free cash flow came in at $464 million. Management expects $2 billion in free cash flow in 2026, $3 billion in 2027, and $10 billion in 2029. Investors were less impressed. The adjusted loss of $0.34 per share exceeded the $0.21 loss projected, and shares plummeted almost 9% premarket to around $171. Boeing now believes it will not significantly raise 737 production above 47 per month until the second half of 2027, when it hopes to reach 52, and that total 737 deliveries will fall short of 500. Valuation reflects the stress. Boeing trades at 18.39x trailing earnings versus 86.75x forward earnings, indicating that the market is pricing in significant earnings collapse rather than near-term recovery. The premium forward multiple offers little space for more execution delays, especially as the commercial airplane business remains loss-making and debt-ridden. That is also why defense exposure is becoming more relevant in this story; Boeing and Lockheed Martin are both positioned to benefit as the Pentagon advances its contract calendar, as discussed in Boeing and Lockheed Martin Both Cash in on the Pentagon's Contract Calendar . 1. Alnylam Pharmaceuticals, Inc. (NASDAQ: ALNY ) EPS Growth Over the Next 5 Years: 72.24% Hedge Fund Holders: 64 Alnylam Pharmaceuticals, Inc. develops RNAi therapeutics, and in the second quarter, its medicine Amvuttra became the company's first to top $1 billion in quarterly revenue. Total net product revenue came in around $1.2 billion, a 74% increase, with TTR franchise revenue of $1.03 billion, up 89%. Non-GAAP operating income more than tripled to $318 million, and cash reached $3.3 billion. Management reported that 80% of new patient starts are now first-line, while royalties from Novartis's Leqvio increased 79% to $72 million. Management added stated that demand from patients switching from other medicines has normalized following a successful launch. Meanwhile, gross margin also fell to 75% from 79% due to higher royalties owed to Sanofi. Investors will now turn to Amvuttra's third-quarter earnings, which are due before the market opens on October 29, for indication that its expansion is sustainable. Consensus expects a revenue of around $1.43 billion, up roughly 14% to 16% year-over-year and 11% sequentially, with Amvuttra's revenue anticipated near $1.15 billion, up almost 68%. The report will also look into whether pipeline progress may mitigate concerns about declining switch-driven demand. In a different vein, positive Phase 1b results for brezosiran in Huntington's disease, released on October 23, gave investors more reason to be optimistic.
