news.Title: Amazon: 3 Key Takeaways for Long-Term Investors
news.Content:
On its third-quarter 2026 earnings call, held on Oct. 29, 2026, Amazon (NASDAQ:AMZN) projected that Amazon Web Services (AWS), its cloud computing arm, can become a trillion-dollar revenue business within the next five to 10 years. Capital expenditures, or capex, are increasing to meet massive artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure demand while retail operating margins expand.

Three key takeaways from management's call explain how these investments shape the long-term outlook for shareholders.

1. Cloud Growth Could Propel AWS to a Trillion-Dollar Business

AWS accelerated its revenue growth to 39.3% year over year in the third quarter. The segment reached an annualized revenue run rate of $184 billion as expanding cloud migrations and enterprise demand for AI compute capacity drive multiyear commitments.

With our continued pace of innovation, new core and AI functionality, enterprises wanting to run their core and AI workloads in AWS, and the amount of capacity that we're adding each year, we believe that AWS can grow north of 40% in each of 2027 and in 2028 and be a trillion-dollar revenue business in the next five to 10 years.

-- Andy Jassy, Chief Executive Officer

2. Grocery Expansion Drives Broader Retail Spending

Delivering perishable groceries through same-day fulfillment centers acts as a primary catalyst for higher customer engagement across retail categories. Customers who order fresh groceries buy significantly more nongrocery merchandise and high-frequency, household and consumable products that people use in their daily lives from Amazon's Everyday Essentials category.

Customers who shop perishables with same-day delivery buy nearly seven times more Everyday Essential units than those who don't.

3. External Hardware Sales Open a New Revenue Stream

Amazon's proprietary microchips, such as Graviton for general compute and Trainium for AI workloads, lower infrastructure costs for cloud clients. Surging external demand is prompting management to commercialize its custom chips beyond its proprietary cloud network.

Short-term capacity for prior generation Trainium instances sell at a premium compared to the first half of the year. With Trainium demand so strong, customers continue encouraging us to make it available outside of AWS. We intend to do so late in 2027.

Looking Ahead

Capital expenditures are reaching approximately $220 billion in 2026 for cloud infrastructure. Management is watching hardware cost efficiencies and logistics network density to maintain operating leverage.

Story Continues

What we're building at Amazon is unlike anything that's ever been seen before. There has never been a business with a trillion dollars of annual revenue. Amazon is on a path to have two of them in AWS and stores.

Long-term shareholder returns depend on converting infrastructure investments into sustained free cash flow across cloud and retail operations.

We continue to accelerate our capex payback and have even more conviction than we already had that the investment we're making in AWS will yield a much larger revenue and free cash flow-generating business than we would have imagined a couple of years ago, with strong return on invested capital.

news.Title: Intel Drags Down CPU Rivals. Is it a Buying Opportunity for AMD and Arm?
news.Content:
Intel's (NASDAQ:INTC) third-quarter earnings report set off a bloodbath in the semiconductor sector . The chip giant had its worst day since 1974, plunging 29% and dragging the VanEck Semiconductor ETF down 7%.

Intel's third-quarter results were solid, with revenue up 21% to $16.5 billion, and adjusted earnings per share more than doubled from $0.23 to $0.52, showing its turnaround efforts are paying off.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

However, Intel's fourth-quarter guidance sent investors fleeing, calling for a sequential decline in revenue and a 600-point decline in gross margins due to a slowdown in the PC market triggered by memory shortages. While Intel's data center and foundry businesses are growing rapidly, its client computing business, which is mostly made up of PCs, is still its biggest segment by revenue. The company forecast revenue of $15 billion-$16 billion, well below the consensus at $17.1 billion, and adjusted earnings per share of just $0.25, compared to expectations at $0.44.

Image source: Getty Images.

Why Intel's peers also fell

Intel stock has soared over the last year in part because confidence has increased in its turnaround strategy and its foundry business, but also because CPU demand is expected to soar due to agentic AI, which includes products like Meta's Muse personal AI agent.

Along with Intel, AMD (NASDAQ:AMD) and Arm (NASDAQ:ARM) have also significant exposure to the exposure market, and all three of those stocks are up big this year, as the chart below shows.

INTC data by YCharts

You can also see that AMD and Arm both fell sharply in sympathy with Intel, as AMD lost 11% and Arm finished down 10%.

However, the sell-off in those two stocks has as much to do with investor sentiment as it does with the implications of Intel's report.

AMD and Arm don't have as much PC exposure as Intel does, and also don't own their own foundry, meaning they aren't exposed to the capital expenditures and risk that come with it.

AMD hasn't reported third-quarter results, but in its second quarter, data center revenue made up $6.7 billion out of $11.5 billion of its revenue, while it got $3.1 billion from the client segment. Weakness in PCs will impact AMD as well, but not to the extent that it will with Intel. AMD also posted 107% growth in the data center segment in the second quarter, and there's a good chance that accelerated in the third quarter, given the massive capex spending by the hyperscalers.

Story Continues

Arm, whose CPU architecture differs from the x86 used by Intel and AMD, has limited exposure to the PC market but holds dominant market share in smartphones, which are experiencing the same challenges with rising memory prices.

Arm doesn't break out revenue by segment like its peers do, but it did say that data center royalties doubled year-over-year in its most recent quarter, indicating it is experiencing similarly strong growth to AMD in that category.

Should you buy the dip on AMD and Arm?

AMD and Arm have soared this year on expectations related to AI, so as the AI rally fades, it makes sense that these stocks would pull back as well. While a double-digit sell-off in tandem with Intel's weak earnings seems extreme, the stocks have been moving on sentiment for much of the year.

Arm launched its new AGI CPU, staking its claim to agentic AI, while AMD is finally being seen as a winner from the data center boom as it's signed contracts with many of the top hyperscalers. Both stocks have benefited from the increasing potential for CPUs in agentic AI.

That potential is still very much there, but high expectations are already baked into these stocks. We'll learn more when these stocks report earnings next week, but given the rough earnings season for AI stocks thus far, investors may want to wait for sentiment to stabilize before buying these CPU stocks.

news.Title: What WEC Energy Group (WEC) Said on Its Q3 Earnings Call
news.Content:
Key Points

Interested in WEC Energy Group, Inc.? Here are five stocks we like better.

WEC Energy raised its 2026 earnings guidance to $5.60–$5.64 per diluted share after third-quarter earnings rose to $1.18 per share from $0.83 a year earlier, supported by weather, rate-base growth and operating efficiency.

The company unveiled a significantly larger $47.5 billion 2027–2031 capital plan , targeting 7%–9% or more annual EPS growth. Investment will focus on natural-gas generation, transmission, distribution, renewables and battery storage.

Data-center demand is driving much of the expansion , with forecast electricity demand growth increasing to 4.9 gigawatts through 2031, particularly from Microsoft and Oracle-related developments in Wisconsin. WEC expects large customers to cover their energy and infrastructure costs while supporting grid investments.

3 Utility Stocks With Strong Dividends and Room to Run Higher

WEC Energy Group (NYSE:WEC) reported third-quarter 2026 earnings of $1.18 per diluted share, up from $0.83 per share a year earlier, as warmer-than-normal weather, capital-plan execution and operating efficiency supported results.

Chairman, President and Chief Executive Officer Scott Lauber said the company raised and narrowed its full-year 2026 earnings guidance to $5.60 to $5.64 per share, assuming normal weather for the rest of the year. The prior range was $5.51 to $5.61 per share. The updated outlook represents 7.7% earnings-per-share growth from the midpoint of the company's 2025 adjusted guidance, Lauber said.

→ GE Vernova's Reservations Are Turning Into Real Orders—But the Market Still Wants More.

3 Utility Stocks That Will Benefit from Less Regulation

The company also unveiled a $47.5 billion capital plan for 2027 through 2031, an increase of $10 billion, or more than 26%, from its previous five-year plan. WEC expects the investment program to support asset-base growth at a 13.4% compound annual rate and earnings-per-share growth of 7% to 9% or more through 2031, measured from the midpoint of its original 2026 guidance.

Data-center demand drives expanded investment plan

Lauber said WEC now forecasts electric demand growth of 4.9 gigawatts between 2026 and 2031, 1 gigawatt more than in its prior plan. The increase is tied largely to demand from very large customers, including data-center development in Wisconsin.

→ Phillips 66 Posts Strong Earnings But the Stock Doesn't Care

3 undervalued stocks: Is now the right time to buy?

Microsoft is continuing to expand its data-center complex in Mount Pleasant, Wisconsin, where its first facility is operating and additional facilities are under construction. WEC is preparing to serve 3.2 gigawatts of forecasted demand in the I-94 corridor south of Milwaukee through 2031, an increase of 600 megawatts from the prior plan. The plan also includes an additional 400 megawatts associated with another customer, although Lauber said details were still forthcoming.

Story Continues

North of Milwaukee, Vantage Data Centers is building facilities for Oracle on about 1,900 acres. WEC currently forecasts 1.3 gigawatts of demand for the Vantage site through 2031, with the potential to reach 3.5 gigawatts over time. Lauber said Oracle had met financial-security obligations under Wisconsin's very large customer tariff.

→ FTC Puts A Wrinkle In the Cintas and UniFirst Merger

WEC's American Transmission Company has refiled a proposal with the Public Service Commission of Wisconsin to support the Vantage project. The filing includes a transmission line and an eSTATCOM system intended to help maintain grid reliability. Lauber said he did not expect the filing process to delay Oracle's project timeline and estimated construction of the line could take about 12 to 15 months after approval.

The company said its very large customer tariff is designed to ensure large customers pay their full share of energy and infrastructure costs, while protecting other customers from subsidizing those investments. Lauber also said Oracle agreed to subscribe to a portion of the energy purchased from the Point Beach Nuclear Power Plant, a step WEC expects will save customers an estimated $300 million in fuel costs. Full details are expected to be submitted to Wisconsin regulators in coming months.

Generation, transmission and distribution spending increases

The expanded capital plan is weighted toward regulated electric generation and transmission projects. WEC plans to invest an incremental $6.8 billion in modern natural-gas generation compared with its prior plan, including a combined-cycle turbine project expected online by the end of the forecast period, combustion turbines and upgrades to existing facilities.

The company increased planned renewable generation and battery-storage investments by $1.1 billion. Planned battery-storage investment increased by $3 billion, while planned solar and wind investment declined by $1.9 billion, partly because some work was completed in 2026.

WEC also reached an agreement with NextEra, subject to regulatory approval, to extend for 20 years its purchase-power agreement for about 1,000 megawatts of carbon-free baseload capacity from the Point Beach nuclear plant.

American Transmission Company is expected to invest about $5.3 billion between 2027 and 2031, up $1.2 billion from the prior plan. The broader plan includes an additional $1 billion for electric and natural-gas distribution infrastructure, including continued investment in the pipe-retirement program in Chicago. Lauber said WEC expects Illinois pipe-retirement spending to ramp to roughly $500 million annually beginning around 2028.

Quarterly drivers and financing outlook

Chief Financial Officer Xia Liu said utility operations contributed $0.28 of the year-over-year quarterly earnings increase. Weather contributed about $0.05, while rate-base growth added $0.19, including $0.15 from incremental allowance for funds used during construction equity and cash returns from projects under construction. About 80% of those incremental returns came from projects for very large customers, Liu said.

Favorable day-to-day operations and maintenance expense contributed $0.08, primarily due to the company's stock-based plan, which Liu said could reflect timing. Those gains were partly offset by higher depreciation and amortization, interest expense, taxes and other items.

Weather-normal retail electric sales increased 4.1% from a year earlier, driven by very large customers. Excluding those customers and an iron ore mine, sales rose 0.4%. WEC continues to expect weather-normalized electric sales for the full year to be relatively flat with 2025.

For the five-year plan, WEC expects to generate $26 billion to $27 billion in cash from operations, raise $19 billion through incremental debt including hybrid instruments, and issue $5 billion to $5.5 billion of common equity. Liu said common-equity needs are expected to remain relatively flat despite the larger capital plan because projects entering service and current cash returns from large customers should increase operating cash flow.

WEC raised approximately $1.16 billion of common equity during the first nine months of 2026, including $1.1 billion through its at-the-market program. The company expects equity issuance to be somewhat front-loaded as projects remain under construction early in the planning period.

Lauber said WEC expects to provide its 2027 earnings guidance and dividend plan in December. The company anticipates dividend growth of 6.5% to 7%, with a projected payout ratio of 60% to 70% as earnings grow faster.

About WEC Energy Group (NYSE:WEC)

WEC Energy Group, Inc is an energy holding company headquartered in Milwaukee, Wisconsin. Through its operating companies, the company generates and delivers electricity and provides natural gas distribution, storage and related energy services to residential, commercial and industrial customers.

WEC Energy's principal utility businesses include We Energies and Wisconsin Public Service in Wisconsin, Michigan Gas Utilities, Minnesota Energy Resources, Upper Michigan Energy Resources and North Dakota utility operations.

news.Title: Why Intel Stock Crashed on Friday
news.Content:
Shares of Intel (NASDAQ:INTC) plunged more than 28% on Friday after the chipmaker's fourth-quarter revenue and earnings guidance drove traders to the exits.

Image source: The Motley Fool.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

PC weakness offsets AI gains

Intel's third-quarter revenue rose 21% year over year to $16.5 billion.

The semiconductor giant's data center and artificial intelligence ( AI )-related sales grew at a blistering pace, rising 78% to $7.3 billion.

Yet its client computing segment suffered a 5% decline in revenue to $8.1 billion. During a conference call with analysts, CEO Lip-Bu Tan said the soaring prices of memory chips were straining corporate IT budgets and denting customer demand for personal computer (PC) processors.

Still, Intel's data center gains drove its adjusted net income up by 169% to $2.8 billion, while its adjusted earnings per share increased 126% to $0.52.

The PC market could take years to recover

Investors, however, appeared to be more concerned with Intel's guidance. Management forecast fourth-quarter revenue of $15 billion to $16 billion and adjusted earnings per share of $0.25. That was well below Wall Street's estimates, which had called for revenue of $17.1 billion and per-share profits of $0.43.

Tan said an accident at Intel's factory in Israel led to an extended shutdown that will reduce the company's server chip shipments.

Analysts are also concerned that memory chip shortages will persist for years, which could make it hard for Intel's PC business to rebound. Earlier this month, South Korean chipmaker SK Hynix said it expects memory chip demand to exceed supply through the end of the decade.

"We see the PC slowdown continuing at least through the first half of next year," chief financial officer David Zinsner said.

news.Title: ‘Big Short’ trader says Anthropic slowdown tests AI boom
news.Content: Even though you may never purchase a share in Anthropic, there's a high possibility that money in your portfolio is already riding on the success of businesses like it. Nvidia (NVDA) sells the chips powering artificial intelligence. Amazon (AMZN), Alphabet (GOOGL), Microsoft (MSFT), and other technology giants are spending enormous sums building the cloud and data-center infrastructure that AI developers need. Near the opposite end of that chain are Anthropic and OpenAI. They must transform all of that processing power into something that consumers will pay for. Investor Steve Eisman, well-known for his involvement in the subprime mortgage trade detailed in "The Big Short," interprets Anthropic's most recent figures as a warning. Eisman said on CNBC that Anthropic's sequential revenue growth slowed from 147% in the second quarter to 45% in the third quarter. He also said revenue generated relative to compute and infrastructure spending deteriorated. That does not mean Anthropic is shrinking. Third-quarter revenue reached $16.8 billion, up from $11.6 billion in the second quarter, Anthropic said in a filing. However, Eisman's worries extend beyond Anthropic's first public offering. Investors may ultimately have to reevaluate how much infrastructure the whole AI boom needs if the firms using massive quantities of processing power are unable to continue converting that expenditure into quickly increasing income. Eisman sees a change in Anthropic's growth story For almost any corporation, Anthropic's first half 2026 results would seem exceptional. Revenue reached $16.3 billion during the six months ended June 30, up from $1.2 billion a year earlier, according to Anthropic's IPO filing . It also had a very good second quarter, bringing in $11.6 billion. Revenue was somewhat more than double its compute expenditure, with compute and infrastructure costs totaling more than $5.6 billion. Anthropic highlighted that improving efficiency in its prospectus, noting that second-quarter revenue jumped 1,368% from a year earlier, while compute and infrastructure expenses increased 300%. Eisman is examining the subsequent events. Earlier in October, Anthropic informed potential investors that its third-quarter sales reached $16.8 billion, a 45% sequential rise. That growth is still really quick. According to Eisman, the contrast with the prior quarter, when sales rose by almost 147% from the first quarter, is the issue. Additionally, he determined that Anthropic made around $1.70 in revenue for every dollar spent on computing and infrastructure in the third quarter, compared to roughly $2.08 in the second. Story Continues Eisman said Anthropic's ability to turn compute into revenue decreased throughout the quarter as a result of those numbers. "The whole chain depends upon the health of Anthropic and OpenAI." Eisman attributes the shift in part to the termination of "token maxing." When users give prompts and get responses, AI models analyze the text fragments known as tokens. Businesses use more tokens and often spend more money when they deploy AI models more extensively. Eisman uses the term "token maxing" to characterize the time when companies urged employees to use AI extensively, with no regard for the expense. He contends that businesses are now becoming more mindful of what those AI tokens really do. The second half of 2026 may therefore be a more significant test of sustained demand than the previous spending boom. Why Anthropic matters to Nvidia and the rest of the AI trade This is when an obscure efficiency ratio becomes considerably more significant for the typical investor. A vast amount of computational infrastructure is required for Anthropic. Compute is its biggest operational expenditure, according to its prospectus, and it has significant obligations. Crucially, regardless of Anthropic's final income or usage, many of those obligations often have to be fulfilled. Reuters estimates Anthropic has committed more than $600 billion to computing and infrastructure partners over the coming decade. This expenditure supports a much wider ecology. Anthropic says Claude operates across Amazon Web Services Trainium chips, Google Tensor Processing Units (TPUs), Nvidia graphics processing units, and AMD (AMD) GPUs. Additionally, it distributes Claude via Google Cloud, Microsoft Azure, and AWS. This implies that Anthropic serves as a source of demand, a collaborator, and a consumer for some of the largest firms driving the AI investment surge. Therefore, whether Claude is a decent chatbot is not the only issue for someone who buys Nvidia stock. Another factor is whether businesses like Anthropic can generate enough revenue from AI services to support their ongoing use of additional processors, data centers, power, and cloud capacity. The same reasoning applies to Amazon and Alphabet, two major suppliers of Anthropic's infrastructure and distribution as well as investors in the company. Eisman's argument may be significant to a typical tech investor because of this. The expenditure cycle becomes simpler to explain if Anthropic can continue to generate much more income from each additional dollar of computer capability. The math gets uncomfortable if infrastructure needs continue to rise and GDP continues to decline. Anthropic has plenty of evidence against the bearish case Treating a quarter of reduced growth as evidence that the AI boom is ending is another serious flaw. Anthropic continues to develop at a very rapid rate. Its third-quarter revenue of $16.8 billion was more than 3.5 times the $4.7 billion it generated in the first quarter, according to Reuters . The company also told prospective investors that it was profitable on an adjusted basis during the quarter. Additionally, its clientele offers a compelling refutation of the notion that Claude demand is declining. Anthropic had more than 11,900 customers generating at least $100,000 of trailing-12-month revenue as of Sept. 30. A year earlier, it had more than 950. Approximately 250 clients made $10 million or more, while more than 1,900 generated at least $1 million. Additionally, Anthropic reported a net revenue retention of almost 900%, indicating a significant increase in the spending of current clients throughout the studied time. Over half of Fortune 500 organizations generated at least $100,000 in trailing-12-month sales. These figures don't indicate that a company is abruptly losing clients. Additionally, Anthropic advises investors to anticipate a gradual slowdown and quarterly fluctuations in its revenue growth rate. That is typical math for a business growing significantly. Growing $4.7 billion of quarterly revenue by 147% is very different from growing $16.8 billion at the same rate. When CNBC questioned whether Eisman's theory implied a sharp decline in the whole market, he likewise refrained from forecasting an impending collapse in technology stocks. "I'm not willing to make that bet just yet," he said. That difference is important. No one claims that the AI trade has already failed. Investors now have a new figure to watch. Anthropic's next numbers could test the entire AI spending story With Anthropic's IPO, public-market investors will get regular financial results from one of the firms closest to the core of the generative-AI expenditure surge, something they haven't received before. Because of this, its future revenue growth and compute efficiency are significant factors that go well beyond the final price of ANT shares. Anthropic's quarterly growth of 147% is not necessary for an investment in Nvidia. However, a future in which AI engineers always want more processing power and can afford to pay for it helps Nvidia and other infrastructure suppliers. Anthropic's own prospectus explains that link in detail. According to the corporation, in order to keep access to financing, it must show that it can make profitable investments, transform computing investment into improved models, and then translate those advancements into consumer acceptance. On the other hand, when revenue declines, its computational duties do not instantly decrease. Investors should monitor that cycle. Increased income is a result of increased client utilization. Greater computing is supported by higher income. Demand for semiconductors, cloud infrastructure, and data centers rises as computing increases. What worries Eisman is what would happen if that circle began to slow down at the first step. Anthropic's 45% quarterly sales increase seems significant. The warning comes from the direction of the numbers: Growth slowed sharply from the previous quarter, while Eisman's measure of compute efficiency also fell. A trend cannot be established in a single quarter. Still, Anthropic's next quarters may reveal far more to investors than whether its initial public offering (IPO) was priced appropriately, given the hundreds of billions of dollars invested in AI infrastructure and the fact that some of the world's biggest IT businesses are betting on that continued demand. They might help determine whether the economics behind the AI boom are keeping pace with the money being invested in it. news.Title: Amazon Just Lost $42 Billion in Free Cash Flow. Is It a Red Flag for Investors?
news.Content:
Amazon (NASDAQ:AMZN) delivered another quarter of strong growth Thursday night, but investors were unimpressed.

The stock tumbled 7% in after-hours trading following the report, and closed the regular session down 1.4%.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

Growth on the top and bottom lines was strong, as revenue rose 17% to $201.9 billion after adjusting for foreign exchange and the shift in Prime Day, and operating income jumped 61% to $28.1 billion.

Amazon's revenue was slightly below the analyst consensus at $202.3 billion, but the biggest reason for the stock's slide is that investors are skeptical of its massive capital expenditures for AI.

The company plans to spend $220 billion on capital expenditures this year, and its finances are already feeling the weight of that decision.

In just the third quarter, Amazon reported a free cash flow loss of $33.4 billion as it spent $77.3 billion on property and equipment. That may be the largest capex outlay for any company in a single quarter, as well as the biggest FCF loss.

Over the last four quarters, it's burned $42 billion in free cash flow, an enormous sum, even for a company the size of Amazon.

For perspective, its trailing twelve-month free cash flow peaked in 2024 at $50 billion, so it's basically losing as much money as it's ever gained.

So is this a red flag for Amazon ? Let's take a look at what the company's history tells us.

Image source: Getty Images.

Amazon's big spending

Amazon is the biggest company in the world by revenue, so it can more easily afford this kind of expense than a smaller company. Based on its trailing revenue of $795 billion, its free cash flow loss amounted to 5.4% of its revenue, which is comparable to the peaks of past cycles.

For example, in 2022, its trailing twelve-month free cash flow loss fell to $23.5 billion as the company ramped up spending on e-commerce fulfillment centers and cloud infrastructure as demand for both e-commerce and cloud computing spiked during the pandemic. At the time, that made up 4.8% of Amazon's revenue, or a similar percentage to where it is now.

After the ramp in spending, Amazon's capex leveled off, and revenue began to climb, quickly bringing the company back to cash flow profitability.

AMZN Free Cash Flow data by YCharts

Similarly, Amazon's capex spiked during the dot-com boom, dragging its free cash flow into the red. At that time, its free cash flow bottomed out at a loss of $560 million in Q2 2000, and just $2.2 billion in revenue, meaning the free cash flow loss made up more than a quarter of the company's revenue.

Story Continues

Amazon survived that crisis, but it did so with aggressive cost-cutting, reeling in capital expenditures from $134.8 million in 200 to $50.3 million, and it reported its first year of positive free cash flow in 2002.

What it means for investors

Investors aren't looking for a repeat of the dot-com era, and that's not going to happen. Amazon is a much different company and has grown its revenue by more than 100 times, and its core businesses are stable and profitable.

However, the experience with the pandemic-era capex boom should give investors confidence in the company's ability to manage investment cycles, and the company is on track to deliver the growth to absorb that spending. It forecast 40% growth in Amazon Web Services over the next two years, and its e-commerce business continues to deliver steady growth.

Amazon is spending even more than its peers on capex, but the company also looks better-prepared for this moment given its history with capex ramps. The company is spending a reasonable amount for its size, and it could monetize that spending through AWS. Over the long run, it should pay off.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger

Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005.

But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout, a massive technology build-out that Google's CEO says could be more profound than fire or electricity.

While everyone watches the chip designers, one "backbone" company provides the critical technology that Nvidia and AMD literally cannot function without. We've detailed this under-the-radar player in our new AI Playbook.

Continue »

news.Title: Why Arm Holdings Stock Plummeted by Nearly 10% Today
news.Content:
If Friday's stock trading session goes down in history, it will be due to the heavy sell-off of semiconductor stocks. One company caught in the downpour was U.K.-based Arm Holdings , which fell by almost 10% on that gloomy day for its industry.

The big rout

The chip stock rout can be traced to one major factor -- Intel 's (NASDAQ:INTC) third-quarter earnings release , published just after market close on Thursday. It wasn't that this was chock-full of bad news, as the company reported double-digit revenue growth and substantial gains in its data center and artificial intelligence (AI) reporting unit.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

Image source: Getty Images.

Rather, it was the unexpectedly weak guidance it proffered for its current (fourth) quarter. Not only is the bellwether semiconductor company predicting sequential and substantial declines in revenue, gross margin, and non-GAAP (adjusted) earnings per share, but its projections came in well under analyst estimates.

The following day, investor panic was palpable, with a wide range of chip stocks taking heavy losses, including Arm. Although Intel isn't quite the leading benchmark in the semiconductor industry it once was, such weak guidance is being seen as a canary in the coal mine for the sector.

Sinking as a group

When developments like this happen, markets tend to overreact by overselling. I feel that's the case for most of the chip stocks suffering collateral damage from Intel's guidance.

That said, like Intel, Arm is vulnerable to the current contraction in PC shipments, not to mention rising component costs. The factors impacting the chip giant will also affect Arm.

I've always found the company's asset-light business model appealing -- it licenses its advanced chip technology and isn't a manufacturer, so it might be less exposed than Intel. But I'd hold off on snapping up its beaten-down shares until we get the company's update in the form of its fiscal second-quarter 2027 results, slated for publication next Wednesday, Nov. 4, after market close.

news.Title: Is Intel Stock a Buy After Its Post-Earnings Plunge?
news.Content:
Intel (NASDAQ:INTC) stock dropped about 23% in after-hours trading on Thursday, Oct. 29, after the company released its third-quarter numbers. Shares that closed the regular session at $92.07 traded around $71 by the end of the evening.

The quarter itself was strong. Revenue grew 21% year over year to $16.5 billion. And non-GAAP (adjusted) earnings per share of $0.52 came in far above the $0.38 management had guided for in July, more than doubling from $0.23 a year before.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

The outlook was a different story. Intel forecast fourth-quarter revenue at $15.0 billion to $16.0 billion and adjusted earnings per share at $0.25 -- under half what it just earned.

Is the drop a chance to buy Intel stock at a lower price? I think the answer has less to do with Intel's server business, which is booming, than with how long a slump in PC sales lasts.

Image source: Intel.

Data center demand keeps rising

Showing the strength on the server side, revenue in Intel's data center and AI segment leapt 78% year over year to $7.3 billion in the third quarter. Management said it was the segment's fastest revenue growth in 15 years.

And it keeps picking up. In the first quarter of 2026, segment revenue rose 22%. By the second quarter, growth had hit 59%.

Intel still couldn't make enough chips.

"Despite our progress to increase capacity, demand for [data center and AI] products continues to meaningfully exceed available supply," CFO David Zinsner said in his prepared remarks for the earnings call.

Intel expects segment revenue to grow by a mid-teens percentage in the fourth quarter over the third. Zinsner also said Intel expects the industry to stay short of supply through 2027 and into 2028.

Why did the stock fall?

The problem is on the PC side. Revenue in Intel's client computing and physical AI group, which sells chips for PCs, fell 5% year over year to $8.1 billion. It dropped 9% from the second quarter.

Management blamed higher memory prices, which have made new PCs pricier, and tight IT budgets. Unfortunately, the next quarter might be even worse. Intel expects revenue in the PC segment to drop over 20% from the third quarter as PC makers draw down their inventory. It now expects PC unit sales industrywide to shrink around 12% in 2026 and about 10% in 2027. Intel's outlook also reflects an accident earlier this month that shut its Fab 28 plant in Israel for an extended period. The company expects that to lower fourth-quarter revenue by around $300 million and gross margin by about 2 percentage points.

Story Continues

The slump also hits profits. After climbing from 41.8% in the second quarter, Intel's adjusted gross margin reached 44.1% in the third. For the fourth quarter, though, management is guiding for 38%, mainly because less revenue is being spread across the same fixed plant costs.

The $15.5 billion midpoint of Intel's revenue outlook would be around 6% under the third quarter's total. It'd still beat the $13.7 billion Intel posted in the fourth quarter of 2025 by around 13%. But that'd be a sharp slowdown. Year-over-year revenue growth reached 25% in the second quarter, then cooled to 21% in the third.

Intel stock still isn't cheap after the sell-off

At roughly $71 as of this writing, shares trade at about 33 times the 2027 earnings analysts had expected before Thursday's results. The price-to-earnings ratio is down from about 43 at Thursday's close. Of course, the 2027 estimates might fall after a forecast like this.

Meanwhile, Intel sees 2026 gross capital expenditures of $20 billion, and it said 2027 spending should climb steeply.

And the firm sold $23 billion of new stock in August. Intel now expects about 5.44 billion diluted shares in the fourth quarter, about 20% more than in the third quarter of 2025. Put another way, every dollar of future profit is split more ways.

Yes, the PC slump will likely pass eventually. And if both forecasts hold, Intel's data center and AI segment may take in more revenue than its PC segment in the fourth quarter. But management said it doesn't expect a lasting PC recovery until memory supply improves and prices normalize, and it's already planning for another down year for PC units.

Is Intel stock a buy after the plunge? Not yet, I think.

Sure, the server business is delivering. But around 33 times earnings estimates that could still drop is a high price for a company whose PC sales are set to shrink by over a fifth in one quarter.

news.Title: Nvidia has a stake in SpaceX that came from an unexpected place
news.Content:
Nvidia doesn't usually make headlines for what it owns. It makes them for what it sells. But one line in its latest stock filing has investors paying attention: the chipmaker now holds a stake in Elon Musk's SpaceX worth roughly $18 billion.

On the surface, a chip company holding shares in a rocket maker looks odd. Look closer and it starts to make a lot of sense, because Nvidia is now part supplier and part shareholder. SpaceX has turned into an AI business, and it happens to be one of Nvidia's biggest customers.

The 13F disclosure and how an xAI stake became SpaceX shares

The stake came to light in August. Nvidia's 13F filing , submitted on August 14, showed it held about 122.8 million SpaceX shares, making SpaceX its second-largest disclosed holding behind Intel, as reported by TheStreet . At the June 30 close, those shares were worth about $21 billion. The Intel position is a separate bet, built from 214.7 million shares Nvidia bought late last year.

Also read: Bank of America sends SpaceX stock investors strong signal

Nvidia never bought SpaceX stock on the open market. It participated in xAI's $20 billion Series E funding round in January as one of several backers. When SpaceX bought xAI in an all-stock deal in February, the stake was converted into SpaceX shares.

The value has moved around since then. SpaceX shares were trading near $147 on October 23, which puts Nvidia's stake at roughly $18 billion. The stock was priced at $135 in its June IPO and opened at $150 on its Nasdaq debut, before hitting a record high above $225 just weeks later.

This fits a pattern for Nvidia. The company tends to invest in AI-focused businesses that are also its customers or partners. In the filing, SpaceX ranked ahead of the cloud provider CoreWeave and sat behind only Intel.

SpaceX has become an AI company, and that has driven its growth

SpaceX's latest numbers show why the bet looks less strange today. Revenue jumped 161% to $14.6 billion in the third quarter, beating analyst estimates, and the company swung to a $4.4 billion profit from a loss a year earlier.

The AI unit did most of the heavy lifting. Now called Super Intelligence, it brought in $7.56 billion, more than nine times its revenue a year ago and more than half of SpaceX's total sales. Most of that comes from renting data centre computing power to companies like Anthropic and Google, though the unit also includes the Grok chatbot, X and the coding tool Cursor, SpaceX's Q3 filing showed . Musk called it an "inflection moment" for the company.

Story Continues

Starlink and rockets still matter, but they're no longer the main event. The connectivity segment, mostly Starlink, posted $5.25 billion in sales, while the space segment added $1.77 billion. SpaceX also guided for first-quarter 2027 revenue of $33 billion to $37 billion.

Its customer deals are huge. Anthropic agreed to pay SpaceX $1.25 billion a month through May 2029 for computing power, and Google committed to $920 million a month for access to roughly 110,000 Nvidia GPUs, TheStreet reported . Those contracts depend on Nvidia hardware. Musk has even told investors SpaceX's annual recurring revenue could reach $500 billion to $1 trillion by the end of 2027, far above the roughly $110 billion in full-year 2027 revenue that analysts project.

Musk is going all in on Nvidia chips

That's the part Jensen Huang can see clearly. On SpaceX's first earnings call in August, Musk said the company would build its AI services exclusively on Nvidia systems. "We think the Vera Rubin architecture is the best architecture," he said. "So we're exclusive to Nvidia," according to The Motley Fool . Nvidia shares rose more than 4% that day.

He doubled down on the third-quarter call. Musk said SpaceX's new computing capacity next year will be mostly Nvidia's Vera Rubin, as the company pushes deeper into AI infrastructure.

Then came the money. On October 25, Musk said SpaceX had closed $40 billion in debt financing to purchase GPUs. "This is primarily callable debt for GPU purchases that will arrive in Q1 and Q2," he said. He credited SpaceX's investment-grade rating and its Starlink and launch revenue for keeping credit flowing. Given his exclusivity pledge, much of that spending looks headed Nvidia's way.

More SpaceX:

Goldman Sachs revamps SpaceX stock estimates before crucial earnings test

Musk called Anthropic 'evil'; SpaceX's deal with it nearly doubled

Morgan Stanley doubles down on SpaceX stock verdict for investors

Musk also took a swipe at smaller players. He predicted "guppy-level death and consolidation" among the more than 200 so-called neoclouds, while saying SpaceX could "rent out our compute several times over," as reported by TheStreet . He added that SpaceX plans to use about half its computing power itself and rent out the rest, and that it isn't interested in buying any of those struggling rivals.

What Huang sees, and what could go wrong

Nvidia is positioned to win on both ends. It sells SpaceX the chips that power its AI push, and it owns a stake in the company that profits from it. Few investors get that kind of view into a customer's plans.

The bet isn't risk-free. SpaceX spent $19.6 billion on capital projects in the third quarter, mostly on AI and data centres, and expects to spend $35 billion to $40 billion in the fourth, according to SpaceX's Q3 filing . That's a lot of borrowed and earned cash riding on demand for computing power staying strong. SpaceX's finance chief said new capacity pays for itself in under a year at current prices, but that math only holds if rental rates do.

Musk's ambitions stretch even further. He has said SpaceX plans to launch Vera Rubin systems into space next year. If those plans pay off, Nvidia's stake could be worth far more than $18 billion. If they stall, Huang's biggest customer could also become one of his biggest headaches.

news.Title: Strong Growth Momentum and Rising Revisions Fuel Bright Earnings Outlook
news.Content:
The Q3 results we have already seen from 60% of S&P 500 members through Friday, October 30th, reconfirm the broad-based growth momentum we have become used to in the last few reporting cycles. While the growth pace remains strong, it does not compare favorably with other recent periods, particularly when some of the outlier results are excluded. Most importantly, the revisions trend remains positive, with estimates for 2026 Q4 and full-year 2027 continuing to rise.

We remain in the heart of the Q3 reporting season, with this week bringing in results from more than 1400 companies, including 142 S&P 500 members. news.Title: Intel CEO reveals a PC problem as Goldman cuts stock target
news.Content:
I remember buying a new laptop back in 2020, and it was more or less a predictable and straightforward exercise.

You picked a brand, decided how much storage you need, and, for me, hoped the machine would last long enough to justify the price tag.

Lately, though, from what I'm hearing from my friends, that calculation has become frustrating. Memory has become remarkably expensive due to the AI boom, and some affordable configurations are harder to find; upgrading to a model with enough RAM for everyday multitasking can stretch an already tight budget.

What's happening at Intel ( INTC ) helps explain why.

During its Oct. 29 earnings call , CEO Lip-Bu Tan warned of an "unprecedented memory crunch" that's weighing on PC demand.

The irony is hard to miss.

Demand for chips powering the AI boom is soaring, while the cost of building ordinary computers is making buyers hesitate. Wall Street noticed. Goldman Sachs cut its Intel price target post-earnings by 33.3% after the company delivered disappointing guidance.

The question now isn't just what happens to Intel stock. It's what Americans will pay for their next PC.

Intel CEO sees a prolonged problem for PC buyers

Lip-Bu Tan says the company's PC customers are pulling back, not because computers have become less useful, but because building them has become a lot more expensive.

"In recent weeks, our customers began signaling a PC slowdown based on the memory prices and availability," Tan told analysts on Oct. 29 .

He added that rising system prices were putting further pressure on already limited corporate IT budgets.

The weakness has gathered speed.

"The pace of this PC correction has accelerated over the last two months as our OEM partners are aggressively managing inventory to match the softer sell-through," Tan said.

When fewer PCs sell, manufacturers might reduce chip orders even faster as they clear existing inventories. Intel's client computing sales fell 9% from the preceding quarter to $8.1 billion.

The company expects the worldwide PC market to shrink about 12% in units in 2026, with the second half down more than 20%. Management is planning for another 10% contraction in 2027, instead of a quick rebound.

CFO Dave Zinsner told analysts the inventory correction could run through early next year. More troubling, he said, Intel does not expect memory supply conditions to improve during 2027, leaving 2028 as a possible turning point.

The squeeze is reaching shoppers, too. IDC's June research, as reported by TechRepublic , projected a 17% increase in average PC selling prices in 2026, making it harder for families and businesses already watching their budgets to justify replacing computers.

Story Continues

For Intel, the frustration is that demand remains strong elsewhere, especially for server processors. But its traditional PC customers are facing a problem that better chips alone cannot fix.

AI spending creates an unexpected PC affordability problem

The shortage squeezing PC buyers starts far from the laptop aisle, in the data centers being built to power AI.

Memory makers have been directing more production capacity toward higher-margin server chips, particularly the high-bandwidth memory used alongside AI processors. That leaves less room for the conventional memory and storage components used in everyday computers, even as consumers become more price-sensitive.

More Intel:

Top analyst sets outrageous Intel stock target ahead of earnings

Intel stock jumps as SK Hynix weighs U.S. memory-chip deal

Intel stock surges 9% as surprising turnaround takes shape

In fact, on Micron's Sept. 30 earnings call , CEO Sanjay Mehrotra said that "HBM continues to grow faster than conventional DRAM through 2028."

In addition, at the KeyBanc Technology Leadership Forum in August , Sumit Sadana, Micron's executive vice president and chief business officer, explained how producing AI memory reduces the capacity available for conventional memory.

"To produce 100 bits of HBM, we have to reduce 300 bits of DDR supply."

TrendForce expects conventional DRAM contract prices to rise another 10% to 15% in Q4, with NAND flash prices climbing 15% to 20%.

Even though those are wholesale component forecasts, manufacturers must still absorb the costs, pass them to buyers, or change what goes into their machines.

That could mean more expensive upgrades, fewer configurations with generous amounts of RAM, or fewer choices at lower price points.

Intel's own sales offer a revealing contrast. CFO Dave Zinsner said shipments of its cost-optimized Wildcat Lake processors increased about 70% from the previous quarter, and that the product was sold out.

That's the conundrum facing investors: AI can accelerate one part of Intel's business while making the computers that power its longstanding PC franchise harder for customers to afford.

Goldman Sachs slashes Intel target after weak outlook

Intel's latest results give investors two different pictures of the company.

Q3 sales jumped to $16.5 billion, adjusted earnings reached $0.52 a share, and Data Center and AI sales surged 78%. Yet its client computing and physical AI business shrank 5%, showing how the PC slump is offsetting AI momentum.

The problem became harder to dismiss when Intel projected $15 billion to $16 billion in fourth-quarter revenue, against Wall Street's expectation of roughly $17.1 billion.

Goldman Sachs responded on Oct. 30 by cutting its Intel price target from $150 to $100, while maintaining a Neutral rating. Analyst James Schneider expects PC manufacturers' inventory reductions to continue into the first half of 2027, potentially prompting Wall Street to lower earnings estimates, even as AI server demand remains strong.

Jefferies also cut its target to $85, while Bank of America downgraded Intel to Neutral.

For Intel stockholders, the question is whether that growth can offset weak PC orders and higher capital spending until memory supply improves and Intel's turnaround generates sustainable cash flow.

Related: BofA sees 80% upside for Seagate stock, but Micron shares look cheaper

news.Title: IBM vs. ServiceNow: Which Technology Stock Is a Better Buy in 2026?
news.Content:
Investors seeking stability often look toward established tech giants, while those chasing growth prefer cloud-native leaders. Choosing between International Business Machines (NYSE:IBM) and ServiceNow Inc. (NYSE:NOW) requires weighing legacy strength against modern expansion.

International Business Machines focuses on hybrid cloud and AI consulting, making it a cornerstone for large enterprise modernization. Conversely, ServiceNow specializes in digital workflow automation, helping companies streamline complex internal processes. Comparing these two reveals how different software models approach the digital transformation market in 2026.

The case for International Business Machines

International Business Machines provides enterprise technology through its hybrid cloud and AI platforms. The company maintains a broad ecosystem of partners to deliver these solutions, including Adobe Inc. (NASDAQ:ADBE), Amazon.com Inc. (NASDAQ:AMZN), Microsoft Corp. (NASDAQ:MSFT), Oracle Corp. (NYSE:ORCL), Palo Alto Networks (NASDAQ:PANW), Salesforce.com Inc. (NYSE:CRM), Samsung Electronics (OTC:SSNLF), and SAP Inc. (NYSE:SAP). In October 2026, it launched 'IBM Ready for SAP Solutions' to assist midsize businesses with ERP modernization.

In FY 2025, revenue reached about $67.5 billion, marking a 7.6% increase from the prior year. Net income grew to approximately $10.6 billion, representing a net margin of 15.7%. This improvement suggests that the strategic shift toward high-value software and consulting is yielding financial results. As disclosed in its latest annual report, the company services thousands of organizations across more than 175 countries.

As of its December 2025 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio is 2.1x. This ratio compares total debt to shareholder equity, indicating the extent to which a company relies on borrowing to fund operations. The current ratio, which measures the ability to cover short-term debts with short-term assets, is roughly 0.9x. Free cash flow reached approximately $12.1 billion, which represents cash from operations minus capital expenditures.

The case for ServiceNow

ServiceNow provides an AI platform designed for business transformation by connecting people, data, and devices through cloud-based workflow software. The company serves approximately 8,700 enterprise customers, with a growing segment of business generated from the public sector. Strategic partners include Amazon, Alphabet Inc. (NASDAQ:GOOGL), Microsoft, and Nvidia Corp. (NASDAQ:NVDA). The rapid adoption of tech stocks across regulated industries has helped fuel its expansion.

Story Continues

In FY 2025, revenue reached approximately $13.3 billion, reflecting growth of roughly 20.9% over the previous period. Net income for the period was about $1.7 billion, resulting in a net margin of 13.2%. This high double-digit revenue growth highlights the strong demand for its automation platform. The company continues to invest heavily in innovation to maintain its competitive edge in the workflow management space.

As of its December 2025 balance sheet, ServiceNow maintains a debt-to-equity ratio of nearly 0.2x and a current ratio of roughly 1.0x. Free cash flow for the period reached around $4.6 billion. Note that stock-based compensation represented roughly 35.9% of operating cash flow, which inflates reported cash generation since SBC is a non-cash expense added back in the cash flow statement. This practice is common among high-growth software firms but remains a factor for investors to monitor.

Risk profile comparison

International Business Machines faces intense competition in software and consulting markets from both large enterprises and niche providers. The company also deals with the challenges of successfully integrating acquired companies, such as its September 2026 purchase of Logiq Consulting Ltd. Additionally, risks related to cybersecurity and AI governance remain critical as new global regulatory requirements emerge. Volatility in financial results may occur due to long sales cycles and reliance on complex global supply chains.

ServiceNow must continuously innovate its AI-powered platform to remain relevant in an intensely competitive software market. The company also manages operational and ethical challenges associated with incorporating AI into its core products. Furthermore, its heavy reliance on government procurement processes and regulation can lead to lengthy sales cycles or potential contract terminations. Managing an increasingly complex acquisition strategy, such as the $7.75 billion purchase of Armis, also poses integration risks.

Valuation comparison

International Business Machines offers a significantly lower valuation multiple compared to the high-growth premium currently assigned to ServiceNow by the market.

Valuation metrics include those sourced from Financial Modeling Prep (FMP) and may differ from those of other data providers.

Which stock would I buy in 2026?

ServiceNow shares have experienced a volatile 2026 because of fears that generative AI will replace Software-as-a-Service (SaaS) businesses. That's a vague worry right now and probably overstated in the long run.

Management sees a unique opportunity to leverage its core information technology strength in operations applications through rolling out new GenAI tools, especially its new agentic AI services. ServiceNow expects GenAI to be an accelerator for business, increasing its total available market and boosting average selling prices.

For the current fiscal year, consensus estimates project the business to grow sales 22% to $16.2 billion, although with a drop in net income of about $300 million to $1.4 billion.

IBM, meanwhile, had a stumble when it announced price increases to its mainframe customers, leading customers to switch to other providers, crimping revenue in the current fiscal year's second quarter.

Still, demand for generative AI and cloud solutions is helping IBM. In particular, AI is instrumental to IBM's future. The belief is that much of the company's extensive roster of enterprise clients in technology is seeking to upgrade IT infrastructures with a trusted partner—IBM.

For the current fiscal year, revenue will grow a little sluggishly, from $68 billion to about $71 billion, although net income will tick down by $ 1 billion to around $9 billion, according to consensus estimates.

So which stock is the better buy? With its lower forward P/E ratio and P/S ratio compared to ServiceNow, IBM is the choice for long-term investors.

news.Title: Apple's $1,999 iPhone Duo is already rewarding buyers who wait
news.Content:
Apple (AAPL) spent launch week proving people would line up for a $1,999 foldable iPhone. It's possible that some of them who waited will now get a better offer.

Resellers in China started lowering the premiums they were asking above Apple's official pricing only days after the iPhone Duo went on sale.

At Shenzhen's Huaqiangbei electronics market, one vendor cut the premium on a black 1-terabyte iPhone Duo by 2,800 yuan, or about $420, according to the South China Morning Post .

The asking price fell to 24,300 yuan from more than 25,000 yuan when the phone first reached stores.

This does not imply that Apple has lowered the Duo's pricing. It implies that consumers who are prepared to pay more only to have one right away are already spending less.

For consumers, the lesson is simple: Scarcity can be expensive, and patience can be valuable.

Apple's iPhone Duo scarcity premium is fading

Apple launched the iPhone Duo on Oct. 23 after preorders sold out within minutes. The company starts the device at $1,999 in the U.S.

Apple offers the foldable in four storage configurations ranging from 256 gigabytes to 2 terabytes.

There was a scarcity at the beginning.

Shortly after preorders started, Apple's projected delivery dates were pushed back to late January. Additionally, the firm restricted walk-in availability in several regions and limited preorders to two phones per consumer.

Some buyers and resellers queued up in an attempt to get limited launch supplies, according to Reuters .

One reseller in Hong Kong told Reuters that he intended to flip a 256GB Duo for around HK$4,000.

That is the well-known economics of launching a popular product.

Resellers might charge more only for possessing something when official supply is limited and purchasers need it right now. However, such premiums are only sustainable as long as enough individuals are willing to pay them.

China's first indications point to a possible decline in willingness.

Mixed reviews are giving buyers another reason to wait

The change coincides with a more nuanced response to Apple's first foldable.

Early evaluations praised the Duo's hinge and design.

However, critics also highlighted shortcomings, such as the absence of a telephoto camera and software that hasn't been completely updated for the bigger display. Several well-known critics questioned if the foldable design is worth $1,999 for the average iPhone user.

Reuters reported that longtime Apple commentator John Gruber described the device as feeling more like a highly polished prototype than something he would want to carry every day.

Story Continues

More Apple:

Apple's biggest AI advantage may face new privacy challenge

Apple secret new device is a challenge to Amazon

Bank of America warns Apple investors because of Meta's Muse

For the resale market, it is important. If fewer consumers are ready to pay more to avoid the queue, a product may continue to be sold out via official channels while secondary-market prices decline.

The South China Morning Post reported that social media discussion about durability and compatibility issues was contributing to softer reseller demand.

This puts purchasers in an odd predicament.

On the day of the Duo's introduction, someone who really wanted it might pay Apple $1,999, wait months for delivery, or pay a reseller considerably more. The premium can already be lower for someone who is prepared to wait a few days.

Apple's first demand signal is getting more complicated

I previously reported that as Duo delivery dates pushed into 2027, Apple's $1,999 iPhone wager drew an instant response.

However, there was a crucial disclaimer.

Tight supply made it difficult to know how much of the apparent demand reflected enormous consumer enthusiasm and how much reflected limited launch inventory.

The declining resale premiums make that topic more intriguing. They don't demonstrate a lack of demand.

In many areas, the Duo remains hard to get, and official Apple inventory remains limited.

IDC expects Apple to lead the global foldable-phone market in value and units in 2026 and 2027, according to Reuters .

Resale prices, however, provide investors with an additional means of monitoring demand. Long after introduction, if customers are still paying high premiums, it indicates that demand is still greater than Apple's supply.

The situation becomes more complicated if such premiums vanish quickly while official waiting lists remain lengthy.

Waiting could be the cheapest iPhone Duo strategy

The fact that the Duo suddenly became affordable is hardly the most crucial lesson for consumers.

It didn't.

It is still one of the priciest phones Apple has ever sold, costing $1,999 before accessories, taxes, or extra storage.

The more practical lesson is that after the launch enthusiasm subsides, it could be more difficult to justify paying more for instant access.

The official pricing of Apple in the United States has not altered. The secondary market is where the discounts are taking place.

Additionally, these discounts are occurring quickly enough to demonstrate the financial impact of early scarcity on the initial price of possessing a popular technology.

The next question for Apple investors is whether the Duo will continue to sell well after the novelty and reseller activity have subsided.

The test is simpler for customers. Keep an eye on resale pricing and availability.

Waiting could be the most affordable option to purchase Apple's priciest iPhone if the gap continues to close.

news.Content:

Apple ( NASDAQ:AAPL ) heads into fiscal fourth-quarter earnings with Wall Street focused less on the quarter that just ended and more on what management says about the crucial holiday period.

The company is scheduled to report after the market closes on Monday, Nov. 2 , with Wall Street expecting about $113.32 billion in revenue and $1.98 in EPS .

The bigger issue is guidance.

Investors will be looking for evidence that Apple can sustain iPhone momentum into the December quarter, particularly after the launch of its new foldable iPhone Duo this month.

The Duo did not contribute to the September quarter because it launched after the reporting period, making the holiday outlook the first meaningful indicator of how much the new product could add to sales. Wall Street is looking for roughly $153.5 billion in holiday-quarter revenue .

Supply could complicate the picture.

Early demand for the $1,999 Duo has reportedly been strong enough to push some delivery dates into late January, which could support pricing but also shift some potential December-quarter revenue into 2027.

The staggered iPhone rollout creates another forecasting challenge.

Apple launched the Pro, Pro Max and Duo in September, while the base-model iPhone and Air are expected in March. Analysts have warned that this could distort quarterly revenue and gross-margin comparisons even if full-year demand remains healthy.

Cost pressure is another major watchpoint.

Higher memory and component costs could weigh on hardware margins, making Services increasingly important. Investors will also be watching whether Apple can protect profitability through pricing and product mix.

Investor Takeaway

I think Apple's quarter could be a case where meeting estimates is not enough .

The stock is already trading at a premium valuation, while investors are expecting the Duo, stronger iPhone pricing and Services growth to carry momentum into the holiday period.

That makes guidance the real catalyst.

If Apple can show that Duo demand remains strong, supply improves and margins hold up despite higher component costs, the market may look past some of the quarterly noise created by the staggered launch schedule.

If guidance disappoints, however, investors may become much less forgiving given how much optimism is already reflected in the stock.

For investors, the key things to watch are holiday-quarter revenue guidance, iPhone demand, Duo supply, gross margins, Services growth and commentary on component costs .

Apple's Q4 numbers matter.

But the December quarter may matter much more.

news.Title: Big Tech Holds $3 Trillion in Spending Commitments for AI Boom
news.Content:
(Bloomberg) -- The five largest players in the data center race have committed more than $3 trillion in spending over the coming years, pointing to massive ongoing investment in AI infrastructure.

Most Read from Bloomberg

Binance Estimates $6.3 Billion Hacked in Crypto's Biggest Heist

Nasdaq 100 Slumps 10% From Peak on AI Wake-Up Call: Markets Wrap

Google Erases a Record $500 Billion as AI Eats Into Sales

Kushner's Thrive Holdings to Buy ADT for $7.6 Billion in Cash

Intel Suffers Worst Stock Thrashing in Decades on Weak Forecast

Alphabet Inc., Meta Platforms Inc., Microsoft Corp., Amazon.com Inc. and Oracle Corp. have each disclosed ballooning commitments on leases, buildings, energy and other equipment as they've rushed to build fleets of data centers. This is a mix of short-term spending and some pledges that are as long as decades away.

The largest chunk of these commitments comes from Google, which reported more than $1 trillion of commitments, including technical equipment, energy and leases. That figure is nearly eight times higher than it was a year earlier and includes agreements for technical equipment, energy and leases, according to the company's regulatory filing.

Meta has reported a similarly sharp ramp-up, disclosing more than $800 billion in future spending. A bit less than half of that is for data center leases that haven't yet started, and will be paid off over periods as long as 30 years. "We expect to continue investing aggressively to support both our core business and emerging AI initiatives," Chief Financial Officer Susan Li said during a call with analysts last week.

One of the biggest debates in business this year has been whether the hundreds of billions being spent on server farms for artificial intelligence work will really pay off. Some of the most profitable businesses in history like Alphabet and Meta have dipped into negative free cash flow, citing the need to invest in a transformative new business line.

Not all of the spending is strictly tied to data centers, and each company discloses commitments in slightly different ways, making it difficult to compare them directly. For example, Meta notes that some of its planned spending is related to consumer hardware products in the Reality Labs division. Alphabet and Amazon each note planned spending on content licenses. There are also major pools of spending — such as current leases and debt — that aren't captured by this analysis.

In all, the future lease commitments total $1.3 trillion, while other purchase commitments amount to $1.9 trillion. All of the figures come from the company's most recent financial reports, save for Microsoft, which most recently disclosed its purchase and construction orders as part of its annual report for the end of June.

Story Continues

Oracle was the first major company to dip into negative free cash flow due to its AI data center investments. During an investor presentation earlier this week, it charted a return to free cash flow in 2028. In part, it will achieve this by using vendor financing and customer prepayments to reduce its up-front costs.

news.Title: Apple Is Near a Record. Netflix Is Down More Than Half. I'd Buy Only 1 of Them.
news.Content:
Apple (NASDAQ:AAPL) shares are roughly $350 as I write, close to their all-time high and up about 29% so far in 2026.

Netflix (NASDAQ:NFLX) shares, meanwhile, reached their one-year low on Oct. 29. Near $62 today, the stock is about 54% below the record close it set in June 2025 (adjusted for the company's 10-for-1 stock split last November).

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

On valuation, Netflix wins easily. Using analysts' forecasts for 2027, Netflix's price-to-earnings ratio is around 17. Apple's, based on expected earnings for its fiscal 2027 (the year ending next September), is about 37. And Apple's own guidance suggests slower growth for the quarter it reports on Nov. 2.

But I don't think the cheaper stock is automatically the better buy. What each company may earn several years from now counts more than its price today.

Image source: Getty Images.

Netflix: cheaper, and still slowing

Netflix's growth has eased all year. Revenue rose 17.6% year over year in the fourth quarter of 2025, then slipped to 16.2% in the first quarter of 2026 and to 13.4% and 11.8% in the next two quarters. And management's guidance points to 11.5% in the fourth quarter.

Granted, earnings are still climbing. Management sees the company's operating margin rising to 31.5% this year from 29.5% in 2025. And the streamer spent a record $4.8 billion on buybacks in the third quarter.

Still, margin gains can get tougher to find when sales growth keeps slowing. Investors arguably pay less for every dollar of Netflix's earnings because it isn't clear yet where its growth will settle.

A cheap price-to-earnings ratio for a slowing business isn't the same as a bargain.

Apple's staying power

Apple has been growing fast. Revenue climbed 16% year over year in the fiscal first quarter of 2026 (the period ended Dec. 27, 2025), then accelerated to 17% in fiscal Q2 before landing at 16% in fiscal Q3.

But a slowdown is coming. For fiscal Q4, management forecast growth of just 9% to 11%, citing currency and tight supply of the advanced chips in its devices.

For that premium, though, Apple investors get things Netflix can't offer.

Showing how sticky the business is, Apple's installed base now tops 2.5 billion active devices. Its services business, which sells subscriptions and more to these users, hit record June-quarter revenue of $30.7 billion in fiscal Q3, up 12% year over year.

Story Continues

Services have far higher margins than hardware, too -- they made up about 28% of Apple's fiscal Q3 revenue but about 42% of its gross profit.

Also, Apple keeps handing cash back to shareholders. In the first three quarters of fiscal 2026, it spent around $62 billion on buybacks and about $12 billion on dividends. Operating cash flow in that time grew 43% to about $117 billion.

Apple has much more to sell

Apple has hardly started charging for artificial intelligence (AI). Its new Siri AI assistant began rolling out in beta on Sept. 14, and management has hinted at how it could earn money from heavy users.

"We will have some kind of upgrade possibilities on iCloud+ where people can buy up the stack on iCloud+," then-CEO Tim Cook said on the company's fiscal third-quarter earnings call.

With over 2.5 billion devices in use, even a small share of owners paying for extra AI features might add up.

AI could also give Apple new devices to sell. HomeView, a 7-inch home device built around Siri AI, starts shipping Nov. 13. And Apple reportedly plans to ship its first smart glasses in late 2027.

There's also the iPhone Duo. Apple's first foldable went on sale Oct. 23 starting at $1,999, or $700 more than the iPhone 18 Pro Max. This adds a pricier tier to Apple's most important product line, which pulled in $54.3 billion of revenue in fiscal Q3, up 22%.

Which one would I buy?

Netflix might still work out fine. At a price-to-earnings ratio around 17, Netflix doesn't need much to go right. And Apple's Nov. 2 report could disappoint, given management's cautious guidance.

But I'd rather pay up for Apple. Its installed base and services business make it the more durable of the two. I also think most of AI's payoff for Apple is still ahead, both in features people might pay for and in new devices like HomeView. The iPhone Duo, meanwhile, gives the iPhone a pricier top end.

Apple is the one I'd buy. At a price-to-earnings ratio around 37, though, I'd probably build a position gradually.

news.Title: BofA Spots Rare Opportunity Hidden in Stock Market Selloff
news.Content:
This article first appeared on GuruFocus .

Bank of America strategist Michael Hartnett says the massive AI borrowing boom may have created an overlooked opportunity in beaten-down technology bonds.

U.S. investment-grade tech bonds are down about 9% year to date , pushing their relative performance versus the broader investment-grade bond market to roughly 30-year lows .

Is GOOG fairly valued? Test your thesis with our free DCF calculator.

The main reason is supply.

Alphabet ( NASDAQ:GOOG ) ( NASDAQ:GOOGL ), Meta ( NASDAQ:META ), Amazon ( NASDAQ:AMZN ), Microsoft ( NASDAQ:MSFT ) and Oracle ( NYSE:ORCL ) have issued around $182 billion of bonds in 2026 , compared with just $17 billion in 2024.

That flood of new debt has pushed yields much higher.

Across investment-grade technology names, yields now sit in the 6% to 8% range for some long-dated issues. Oracles 2066 bonds yield about 8.43%, Metas 2066 paper around 7.40%, and Amazons 2076 notes roughly 6.81%.

Even stronger balance-sheet names such as Nvidia, Alphabet, Microsoft and Apple are offering yields above 6% on some long-dated bonds.

The picture is even more extreme in speculative-grade AI-linked debt.

CoreWeaves 2031 notes yield about 14.26% , while Galaxys 2031 debt yields 11.44% and SoftBanks 2034 issue roughly 9.58%.

Hartnett believes this selloff may be creating diamonds in the rough as investors increasingly demand more compensation for financing AI infrastructure.

The borrowing boom is also changing how Big Tech allocates capital.

Hyperscalers have paired their debt issuance with roughly $89 billion of equity issuance , bringing combined debt and equity issuance to $271 billion year to date.

At the same time, annualized share repurchases have collapsed to about $14 billion , down from roughly $105 billion in 2024.

Investor takeaway

I think the most important part of Hartnetts call is that the AI boom is beginning to look very different depending on whether you are a stockholder or a bondholder .

For years, mega-cap tech companies generated enormous cash and returned much of it through buybacks.

Now they are raising huge amounts of outside capital to fund data centers, chips and power infrastructure.

That has hurt bond prices, but it is also pushing yields to levels rarely associated with some of the strongest technology companies.

For investors, the key question is whether the extra yield adequately compensates for longer maturities, heavy future capex and potential deterioration in credit metrics.

The key things to watch are new bond issuance, hyperscaler capex, leverage, buyback activity and whether AI infrastructure spending continues to accelerate .

Tech bonds have been punished.

Hartnett thinks that punishment may finally be creating opportunity.
