Wallace Kou: Okay, you asked a very good question, Daniel. I think that we really want the balance between China and also the rest of world. China has YMTC, NAND maker, they are very strong. They grow very fast. We also support and collaborate with the YMTC directly or indirectly with the module maker. I think the enterprise portion, we see they will become stronger in 2027. I think we definitely work closely for China CSP for hyperscaler. Believe us, and I think that is why we try to grow China local R&D. Eventually, we want China, our local R&D can support China customer. In Taiwan, we support the rest of world, especially for U.S. customers.

Secondly, I think the China, they are growing enterprise controller company, but in the past, they also like to make enterprise C drive. In the past, as you know, NAND pricing is cyclical. They have a downside, they have upside. So some enterprise controller company, they buy the NAND in the downside, they are selling the drive in the upside. But nowadays, there is no longer the cyclical price going up or stable, right? So very hard for enterprise controller company, you use it converting to selling the whole solution if you do not win hyperscaler or even NAND maker of the CSP customer. So I think our strategy is very simple. We winning NAND maker business and designing directly.

We win hyperscaler customer in both U.S. and China. We also win CSP directly. But we do not make enterprise solution. We only sell controller and our firmware. We enable the module maker and the NAND maker. They sell and utilize our controller and the firmware, make enterprise solution, and selling to the customer. So this is where we are. That is why building Silicon Motion ecosystem, working together and supporting the growing opportunity in both China and U.S.

Daniel Yen: I see. Very clear. Wallace, if I may follow up, how should we think about the overall competitive landscape on a controller in China right now? Just want to get your opinion.

Wallace Kou: For enterprise, we really do not even. There is one or two basic company move to the IPO, but we do not see they are strong enough to compete in the long term, not just one technology or business model, right? I do not really see any threat from them. Even some also want to go overseas. Today, we feel pretty comfortable for our position and with our technology, and we have a very strong developing pipeline for both our PCIe Gen 5 as well as Gen 6.

Daniel Yen: I see. Yes. Thanks for this. The second question from me is that since right now I think you are issuing the convertible bond, I want to ask if there is any change on your dividend policy potentially in the future? Also I think just overall, how should we think about your capital structure going forward? Do you have a target, any ratio you are looking at? I think this question is actually coming from some of the investors who subscribe your convertible bond. Thank you.

Jason Tsai: Yeah. Dividend and capital allocation certainly continues to be a priority. We increased our dividend a couple of weeks ago from $2-$2.30 per ADS per year. We have had a history of increasing our dividend over the last 10 years or so, and our expectation is that we can continue to look at that strategically over time and continue to look at opportunities to raise that. The three priorities for us on capital return is dividend, share buybacks opportunistically, and then M&A as it makes sense, and that is unchanged. But certainly right now, working capital needs continue to increase as well.

The CB raise puts us in a much better position to drive growth in our business with better working capital as well.

Daniel Yen: Thank you, Jason. That is all my questions. Thank you.

Operator: Thank you. We have now reached the end of the question and answer session. I will now turn the conference back to Mr. Wallace Kou for closing comments.

Wallace Kou: Thank you everyone for joining us today and for your continuing interest in Silicon Motion. We will be attending several investor conferences over the next few months. The schedule of these events will be posted on the investor relationship section of our corporate website, and we look forward to speaking with you at these events. Goodbye for now.

Operator: Thank you for your participation in today's conference. This does conclude the program. You may now disconnect your lines.

news.Title: Why Marvell Stock Is Down Today
news.Content:
Marvell Technology (NASDAQ:MRVL) stock is sinking, down 13.9% as of 2:44 p.m. ET on Thursday, Oct. 29, after a report said the chipmaker is close to buying a big optics supplier.

The S&P 500 and the Nasdaq Composite were down 0.7% and 1.7%, respectively.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

Image source: Getty Images.

Marvell has its eye on Lumentum

Bloomberg reported after Wednesday's close that Marvell is in advanced talks to acquire Lumentum , a company that builds key optical components for AI data centers. An announcement could land as early as next week according to the report, but nothing has been finalized.

Marvell can't just write a check

Marvell has about $3.93 billion in cash and equivalents, and given Lumentum's $83 billion market cap, Bloomberg has reported it is likely to be all stock. That means dilution for existing shareholders. The company actually acquired a smaller optics company last year, in a $3.5 billion deal that included $1 billion in cash. This would be substantially larger.

The price tag is the real question

Marvell's overall business is humming, with Q2 revenue up 37% to a record $2.74 billion. I think optics is a smart place for Marvell to grow, but this is a massive deal relative to its size, and whether it pays off is a question we can't really answer until more details come to light.

news.Title: MRVL Stock Sinks as Marvell Technology Reportedly Considers Acquiring Lumentum
news.Content:
Marvell Technology (MRVL) shares opened notably lower on Thursday following reports that the chipmaker is in advanced talks to acquire optical-components specialist Lumentum (LITE). An agreement could emerge as soon as next week, with the transaction set to meaningfully expand MRVL's exposure to the technology connecting artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure.

Despite today's dip, however, Marvell stock is trading at more than 1.5x its price at the start of this year.

More News from Barchart

Dear AMD Stock Fans, Mark Your Calendar for November 3

Dear Chevron Stock Fans, Mark Your Calendars for October 30

Elon Musk Invests $1 Billion in Skydance Stock. He Could Be Setting the Stage for a Major Starlink Deal.

Stop Missing Market Moves: Get the FREE Barchart Brief – your midday dose of stock movers, trending sectors, and actionable trade ideas, delivered right to your inbox. Sign Up Now!

What Triggered the Selloff in Marvell Stock Today

One explanation for today's decline in MRVL shares is the financing burden. Heading into Oct. 29, Lumentum had a market cap of roughly $83 billion, compared with less than $4 billion in cash at the end of its latest reported quarter.

This means the custom AI chips specialist will likely have to issue new stock or tap the debt market to fund this transaction; the former will dilute existing investors and the latter will introduce interest costs. And it's fair to assume that successfully acquiring Lumentum will require Marvell to pay a meaningful premium, which would further raise the financial burden.

In short, strategic benefits alone are insufficient to establish that acquiring Lumentum would create value. Without a disclosed purchase price, funding structure, and synergy targets, shareholders can't yet determine whether the potential rewards justify the commitment.

Piper Sandler Recommends Buying MRVL Shares

Piper Sandler analysts nonetheless reiterated their "Overweight" rating on Marvell shares today, with a $400 price target indicating significant upside potential. The investment firm highlighted optical networking's growing importance in accelerating AI data transfers while reducing power consumption, identifying Lumentum's high-powered lasers as an enabling technology.

The strategic opportunity is to address more of the connectivity demands created by increasingly powerful AI systems, analysts told clients, adding that the two companies already showcased complementary optical technologies earlier this year, targeting faster, more energy-efficient networks.

Story Continues

Barchart also currently holds a "40% BUY" average opinion on MRVL, indicating technical momentum is also in its favor for the near term.

Wall Street Remains Bullish on Marvell Technology

Other Wall Street firms seem to agree with Piper Sandler's bullish view on Marvell Technology as well. The consensus rating on MRVL stock sits at "Strong Buy," with the mean price target of about $337 indicating potential upside of more than 50% from here.

news.Title: Entegris (ENTG) Q3 2026 Earnings Call Transcript
news.Content:
Image source: The Motley Fool.

DATE

Thu, Oct. 29, 2026

CALL PARTICIPANTS

Vice President, Investor Relations - Jeffrey Schnell

President and Chief Executive Officer - David Reeder

Chief Financial Officer - Sukhi Nagesh

Full Conference Call Transcript

Operator: Welcome to the Entegris Third Quarter 2026 Earnings Conference Call. [Operator Instructions] I would now like to turn the call over to Jeffrey Schnell, VP of Investor Relations.

Jeffrey Schnell: Good morning, everyone. Earlier today, we announced the financial results for the third quarter of 2026. Before we begin, I would like to remind listeners that our comments today will include some forward-looking statements. These statements involve a number of risks and uncertainties, and actual results could differ materially from those projected in the forward-looking statements. Additional information regarding these risks and uncertainties is contained in our most recent annual report and subsequent quarterly reports that we have filed with the SEC. Please refer to the information on the disclaimer slide in the presentation. On this call, we will also refer to non-GAAP financial measures as defined by the SEC in Regulation G.

You can find reconciliation tables in today's news release as well as on the IR page of our website at entegris.com. Joining me on the call today are Dave Reeder, our CEO; and Sukhi Nagesh, our CFO. With that, I'll hand the call over to Dave.

David Reeder: Thanks, Jeff, and good morning. Entegris had a strong third quarter. Revenue increased approximately 25% year-over-year to a record of slightly more than $1 billion, and adjusted gross margin improved materially more than expected, almost reaching 49%. Demand remains strong across advanced logic, advanced memory and throughout the semiconductor ecosystem, supported by continued investment in AI infrastructure. As customers ramp increasingly complex technologies, they are relying more on Entegris for technical performance, quality and reliability. Our ability to deliver on those commitments is strengthening our customer partnerships and creating new opportunities across the portfolio. Commercial engagement across Entegris has never been stronger.

We are engaging earlier in our customers' technology road maps and seeing a clear progression from co-development to qualifications and plan of record wins. That is increasing our content opportunities and strengthening our leadership position in the industry's most important technology transitions. While the demand environment remains constructive, the quarter also reflects the progress we are making operationally. We have focused on increasing manufacturing output, improving productivity and yield, strengthening and centralizing procurement and generating a higher return from our installed capacity. Our teams are identifying and resolving emerging constraints, and we're improving our ability to convert strong customer demand into revenue. Growth continued to broaden in the quarter with both APS and MS delivering strong double-digit growth.

Story Continues

Regionally, growth was strongest in the markets investing at the leading edge. Taiwan remained our largest growth contributor, but we also had strong momentum across Korea and Southeast Asia. Additionally, double-digit growth in North America highlights the breadth of the growth we are seeing across the semiconductor ecosystem. Unit-driven revenue accelerated from approximately 6% in the first quarter to 20% in the third quarter, that is roughly twice the rate of underlying wafer start growth we expect for the year. This revenue growth reflects both higher industry volumes and increasing Entegris content as semiconductor processes become more complex, require new materials and new plans of record move into production. And that is only one side of our portfolio.

Across our CapEx-related businesses, revenue increased from a modest decline at the beginning of the year to more than 35% growth in the third quarter, particularly with respect to WFE. We anticipated some of the strengthening and have been working for several quarters to unlock the significant embedded capacity across our manufacturing network by adding headcount, improving productivity and increasing inventory to better support customer demand and manage lead times. Those efforts delivered in the third quarter. Our teams increased production exceeding our expectations and converted more backlog into revenue, resulting in growth above expectation. Our commercial activity is also translating into tangible wins across the portfolio. Let me give you a few examples.

In APS, we recently won a significant EUV filtration application at 2-nanometer. In MS, we earned an advanced materials plan record with a major smartphone and technology provider. And additionally, we won multiple CMP plans of record in the quarter with leading memory providers. These new plans of record are important proof points. They span both of our segments and multiple technology applications demonstrating the breadth of opportunities we can address as semiconductor technologies become more complex. As these design wins move into production, they expand Entegris' content opportunity and support future growth. Reflecting the strong demand, book-to-bill remains significantly above 1, with backlog up more than 35% sequentially and more than doubling compared to last year.

Customers are also providing longer planning horizons, giving us greater visibility into their capacity ramps and the Entegris content required to support those ramps. Turning to profitability. We delivered another quarter of adjusted gross margin improvement, reaching 48.9%, while adjusted EBITDA margin exceeded 30%. Adjusted gross margin has expanded more than 500 basis points from a year ago and reached the highest level in more than 25 years. This improvement reflects higher volumes, improved yields and our continued focus on productivity. They were also achieved despite continued investment to support future incremental customer demand and higher performance-based compensation and these strong results are independent of any material pricing benefit.

The operational improvements we are making are strengthening the underlying earnings power of the business and reinforcing our confidence in additional margin expansion over time. Stronger earnings are also translating to the stronger cash generation and faster deleveraging. During the quarter, we fully repaid the 2029 term loan, another important step in strengthening the balance sheet and increasing our financial flexibility. Sukhi will provide more detail in the financial section. Turning to the outlook. The industry backdrop remains supportive of continued growth and is consistent with the framework we've discussed throughout the year. We expect approximately 8% wafer starts growth in 2026, leading-edge logic and memory have experienced the strongest growth this year with utilization at advanced nodes remaining high.

We are also seeing gradual improvement in mainstream utilization, although that part of the market remains the most underutilized. Industry CapEx trends continue to strengthen. Projects are progressing from construction to equipment installation and ultimately to production. The breadth of our portfolio allows us to create value across multiple phases of the investment cycle as customers build and equip new capacity and as those fabs move into production. The areas attracting the greatest investment, particularly advanced-logic and advanced memory are also among the most materials and purity intensive areas of semiconductor manufacturing. As technology complexity increases, so do the opportunities for greater Entegris content reinforcing the value of our full portfolio.

We are encouraged by what we are seeing across the 2 drivers of Entegris' business. Healthy wafer demand and significant investment in the capacity that will then subsequently support future wafer growth. In summary, the third quarter was another strong step forward for Entegris. Growth is accelerating and broadening across the business. Customer engagement is translating into new positions of record and improved execution is translating to stronger financial performance. The progress we are making is tangible. We are winning with technology and solutions, increasing the output and productivity of our manufacturing network and strengthening our financial position.

There is more work ahead, but the team is delivering against our priorities, and I am encouraged by the progress we've made over the last 62 weeks. I want to thank our employees around the world for their hard work, dedication and commitment to our customers. And before I close, I want to remind you that we will be hosting our Capital Markets Day on November 9, and we look forward to seeing many of you there. We have focused today on our third quarter performance and the progress we are making across the business.

At our Capital Markets Day, we will discuss what we believe Entegris is uniquely positioned to capitalize on the next phase of semiconductor growth, our AI native strategy and our road map for long-term value creation. We look forward to seeing you there. And if you have any questions regarding the event, please reach out to Jeff. With that, let me turn the call over to Sukhi to discuss the financials.

Sukhi Nagesh: Thanks, Dave, and good morning, everyone. Q3 results provide strong evidence of the operating leverage and earnings power we see in the business. We delivered record sales of $1.006 billion in Q3, an increase of 25% year-over-year and 14% sequentially. The strong revenue performance was broad-based with APS up 31% and MS up 16% year-over-year. GAAP net income was $158 million and non-GAAP net income was $190 million, an increase of 73% from a year ago. Both our top and bottom line results exceeded our guidance. GAAP gross margin was 49.7% and adjusted gross margin was 48.9%, an improvement of 130 basis points sequentially and 530 basis points year-over-year.

Sequentially, adjusted gross profit increased approximately 17%, outpacing our revenue growth of 14%. The sequential underlying margin improvement reflects higher volumes, fixed cost absorption, improved yield and productivity. This gross margin improvement also offset a 30% year-over-year increase in direct factory head count as well as higher performance-based compensation and other investments to support customer demand. Operating expenses on a GAAP basis were approximately $270 million and approximately $223 million on a non-GAAP basis or 22.1% of sales. The year-over-year increase primarily reflects higher performance-based compensation associated with our stronger results.

Adjusted EBITDA was $303 million or 30.2% of sales compared with 27.3% a year ago and 28.4% in the second quarter, that represents approximately 290 basis points of year-over-year margin expansion. The GAAP tax rate in Q3 was 15%, and the non-GAAP tax rate was 16%. GAAP diluted EPS was $1.03 per share and non-GAAP EPS was $1.23 per share, an increase of 71% year-over-year. The combination of approximately 25% revenue growth, 530 basis points of adjusted gross margin expansion and 71% growth in non-GAAP EPS demonstrates the earnings leverage we are generating as improved execution translates higher volumes into stronger profitability. Now switching to our segments.

Materials Solutions delivered third quarter sales of $404 million, up 16% year-over-year and 9% sequentially. Growth accelerated meaningfully from the second quarter, and the segment delivered its highest quarterly revenue since the third quarter of 2023. This growth was broad-based and for all major product categories and regions, reflecting stronger production volumes at advanced nodes and increasing demand for our materials used to manufacture at the leading edge. The strength was evident across CMP consumables, advanced deposition materials, specialty gases and coatings. MS adjusted segment margin was approximately 20.4%. Higher volume and improved productivity drove the margin expansion, offset by continued investments in capacity and resources needed to support customer demand.

APS delivered Q3 sales of $605 million, up 31% year-over-year and 18% sequentially, reaching a new quarterly record. Growth was broad across most products and geographies, reflecting the dual exposure of the APS portfolio. Higher production, advanced node transitions and the incremental contamination control requirements increased demand for our filtration and purification products, while accelerating capital investments primarily centered around leading-edge capacity drove demand for our micro environments, fluid management and CapEx-related products. Adjusted operating margins for our APS segment was 34.4% for the quarter expanding both year-over-year and sequentially. The improvement was driven by higher production volumes, driving operating leverage, along with productivity improvements and favorable mix.

These benefits more than offset higher performance-based compensation and the additional resources we are adding to support customer demand. Switching next to cash flow and balance sheet. We delivered record operating cash flow and record free cash flow of $224 million in the third quarter or 22.2% of sales. This reflects higher earnings, lower capital spending and continued working capital improvements. The strength of our cash flow generation enabled us to fully retire our term loan in Q3 ahead of schedule. As a result, net leverage improved to 2.9x at the end of Q3. We now expect to end the year at approximately 2.7x, reflecting more than a turn of improvement from where we began the year.

The combination of stronger earnings, improved cash generation and debt repayment is increasing our financial flexibility and positioning us to invest in future growth opportunities, while maintaining a disciplined approach to capital allocation. Moving on to the details of our fourth quarter outlook. We expect Q4 sales to range between $1.025 billion and $1.055 billion. At the midpoint, this represents a year-over-year increase of approximately 26%, building on the strong performance we delivered in Q3. Gross margin is expected to be between 49.2% and 49.7% both on a GAAP and non-GAAP basis. At the midpoint, this represents approximately 50 basis points of improvement sequentially and approximately 550 basis points of improvement year-over-year.

At the midpoint, we expect GAAP operating expenses of approximately $272 million and non-GAAP operating expenses of approximately $227 million, reflecting higher variable compensation and investments to support the growth we are seeing across our portfolio. At the midpoint, we expect Q4 adjusted EBITDA margin to be approximately 31%, which represents more than 40% growth in adjusted EBITDA year-over-year, significantly outpacing revenue growth and providing further evidence of the operating leverage in our model. Additionally, we expect net interest expense to be approximately $40 million, a non-GAAP tax rate of approximately 15% and depreciation at approximately $34 million.

Based on these assumptions, and approximately 154 million shares, we expect GAAP EPS between $1.09 and $1.17 per share and non-GAAP EPS between $1.32 and $1.40 per share. Finally, we expect our CapEx to be approximately $200 million for 2026 or about 1/3 lower than last year. Looking ahead to our first quarter revenue expectations, we expect the momentum to continue. Based on our current visibility, fewer days in Q1 versus Q4 and typical industry seasonality, we expect revenue to decline by a mid-single-digit percentage compared to Q4 but an increase of more than 20% year-over-year. Stepping back, the financial progression of the business is clear and increasingly visible in our results.

We are translating strong revenue growth into even stronger earnings and cash flow growth while continuing to strengthen our balance sheet. Our fourth quarter outlook reflects continued operating progress and a strong close to the year that we expect to build on in 2027. We look forward to sharing more with you at our Capital Markets Day on November 9. With that, operator, let's open the line for questions.

Operator: [Operator Instructions] Our first question is coming from Melissa Weathers with Deutsche Bank.

Melissa Weathers: Congrats on the $1 billion mark. It's very exciting. So I guess if we could just unpack the upside in the quarter versus what you had guided to. I just want to understand how much of this was incremental supply coming on, how much is demand strengthening. Yes, just any other help on the supply side that you can give us?

David Reeder: Melissa. Look, the revenue beat for the third quarter really just came down to execution. Demand was strong. The team's increased production and throughput really beyond our expectations which allowed us to convert more demand to backlog into revenue. From a strength perspective, we saw strength across the portfolio, particularly in our CapEx-related businesses, as you would expect. Internally, we're continuing to strengthen our ability to serve that demand and that backlog that we see both today as well as in the future. Our commercial engagements remain very strong. Customers are providing longer planning horizons, longer lead times. We're continuing to win new plans of record across both segments of the business.

And we're unlocking the capacity that we talked about essentially this time last year in 2025. We're improving productivity. We're increasing ultimately our output, and we're being a stronger, more responsive, more reliable partner. Sukhi, anything you'd add to that?

Sukhi Nagesh: Yes, sure. Melissa, look, in addition to the revenue growth, it really translate into gross margin expansion about 130 basis points sequentially. And that improvement was mainly due to the higher sales volume that Dave just mentioned here, which generated also a meaningful operating leverage for the company. So really, I mean, the strong production output, factory absorption, all of the yield initiatives that we're doing, lower inventories, scrap, rework, all of those things added benefit to the margin. This despite we had higher incentive compensation, labor and overhead investment to support the ramp. So if taken this altogether, I think we're pretty pleased with how we landed on the gross margin for the quarter.

David Reeder: Melissa, did you have a follow-up?

Melissa Weathers: I did. So I guess, I appreciate the help you're giving us on the first quarter of next year. It sounds like that might be -- I don't know if it's a seasonal down or if there's anything else to unpack there. But if I could get greedy. Any initial outlook for how you're thinking about 2027? Any way that we should be thinking about MSI and CapEx growth relative to WFE?

David Reeder: Sure. Look, for 2027, obviously, we're not going to provide that guidance today, but we think the industry setup is incredibly constructive really across all of our major demand drivers. The demand that we're seeing today gives us increasing confidence that the momentum that we're exiting 2026 with will carry over and extend well into 2027. On the unit side, industry forecasts are calling for MSI growth to broadly be consistent with what we saw this year. And ultimately, all of that CapEx that we're adding will eventually turn into wafer starts. So I think that bodes very well for MSI, both from '26 migrating into '27 as well as '27 migrating into '28 and beyond.

Next year, on the CapEx side, all of our indications certainly seem to point to another strong double-digit growth year for both WFE as well as for fab construction. So really, based on everything we see today and the momentum that we have in the business, we think it's a good setup for us and the industry exiting 2026 with momentum and carrying us into '27, and we'll talk a little bit more about all of at Capital Markets Day.

Operator: We'll take our next question from Elizabeth Sun with Citi.

Yiling Sun: Congrats on the good result and good execution. So I guess my first question is you are looking at -- you had like 25% year-over-year growth in Q3, and you are looking at more than 20% growth in Q4 and Q1 as well. I'm just curious, given your strong backlog, growing backlog, is there any reason for us to think this kind of strength is not going to continue into next year? And also, given your strong backlog, are you seeing any -- are your suppliers ready for that? Any emerging constraints on that front?

David Reeder: Thanks, Elizabeth. Look, we're really, really happy with the momentum in the business. As you mentioned, Q3 plus 25% year-over-year growth at midpoint of guidance, kind of a similar number for fourth quarter and then also a somewhat similar number that we've kind of indicated for first quarter of next year even with kind of seasonally down moving from Q4 to Q1. So there's just an incredible amount of momentum in the business in the second half of the year. Some of the -- a little bit of that is market-driven. The lion's share of that is really our performance.

And so we're pleased with the demand environment and I would say even more pleased with the way the team has responded to the initiatives that we put in place in the latter half of 2025. And those initiatives are starting to bear fruit for us here in 2026 and I think bode well for '27. From a supplier perspective, if I was to broaden that out just a little bit, when you think about this time last year, I said that we had significantly greater than $1 billion of incremental capacity in our network. I chose those words fairly carefully to indicate that we had well over [Technical Difficulty] to support 2027 demand and even beyond.

Obviously, we'll have to spend a little bit to kind of bundle some of those pinch points that you inevitably get, but we feel quite good about our ability to be able to satisfy the demand. From a supplier perspective, we have really been working with our customers closely to, one, understand their demand, test their demand and then take that internally, compare that to our capacity, and then even further take that down into our supply chain to make sure that our supply chain is also ready to be able to support the demand that we see in front of us. We feel good about that. There will inevitably be some pinch points.

We've already proactively identified some, and we've been able to work some of those. There will be more in the future, I'm sure. But I think what we all feel good about is how we've been able to kind of ramp to where we are today, identify the ramp that we need for Q4 and Q1, and now we're working on those additional pinch points. Did you have any follow-up Elizabeth?

Yiling Sun: Yes. And then for my follow-up, it would be a high-level question. So Lam recently highlighted that AI is driving demand for different tiers of NAND. They're talking about QLC, TLC and most -- especially they are talking about SLC emerging as a new tier for AI storage in the agentic AI area. So I'm just curious for Entegris, obviously, it is good for -- they did talk about every point of demand shifting towards SLC. It is roughly 2 points more wafer capacity, so that is good on the wafer start side. Just curious on the content side, how does the -- how does Entegris content barriers across these kind of different technologies?

David Reeder: So as you know and as we've long talked about, at Entegris, we welcome technology transitions. We are fairly ubiquitous across as a provider or as a supplier to all the memory providers as well as both mainstream and advanced logic for that matter. As the technology becomes more complex, that really gives us the opportunity to outperform with more content, more layers, as you mentioned, more wafer growth in addition to that. So we're excited to see the technology transitions that are being driven by the complexity and the performance that's required to satisfy AI, and we think that, that bodes well for Entegris.

Operator: We'll take our next question now from Brian Chin with Stifel.

Brian Chin: Congratulations on the strong results. Maybe for the first question. There was some third-party reporting on MSI recently that pointed to 2026 growth, possibly being in the low teens this year, which is an acceleration from that kind of prior high single-digit forecast that I think you've also cited. Do you feel this provided any tailwind to the unit-driven business segments in the second half? Or to your point, Dave, about the execution and conversion being bigger near-term factors, could this tick up and MSI in the back half of this year actually provide more tailwind to you in the earlier phases of next year?

David Reeder: Yes, we probably subscribe to many of the same MSI third-party reports that you do. We tend to take those reports as content and as context. MSI measures really the wafer shipments and not the actual wafer starts and then shipments out. So there typically is a little bit of a mismatch between shipments in and then ultimately, those wafers moving into production. Because of that, we believe that MSI for the year is probably going to be in kind of the mid- to high single digits, call it 7%, 8%, maybe even 9%. But somewhere in that type of ZIP code is kind of our expectations for the year.

We do expect it to be a little bit more weighted to the second half, probably 52% in the second half, 48% in the first half, something to that effect from an annual MSI perspective. So slightly more weighted to the second half. We are encouraged by the trends in wafer growth. And we did see a slight pickup in mainstream. As you know, advanced logic is pretty fully utilized. As you know, memory is pretty fully utilized. So we did see a little bit of pickup in mainstream, which is probably where the most available capacity resides today, and we're encouraged by that. As you know, our MS business has been accelerating.

So in the third quarter, it grew about 16% on a year-over-year basis, and it's kind of continued to accelerate as we've progressed through the year. So I do think it provides some tailwinds to us, particularly, I think, the CapEx that's going into place as that CapEx goes from kind of construction to fab build-out and kit up for tools to fab production, I think that bodes well for longer-term MSI as well. So we feel like we're well positioned. The team is performing and customer engagement has never been stronger. Brian, did you have a follow-up?

Brian Chin: Yes, I appreciate that. That's a great color, Dave. Maybe going back to something you mentioned and maybe also in the prepared remarks. In terms of mainstream, obviously, comprising a lot of wafers in terms of unit-driven volume. I think you made -- mentioned that geographies like Korea, maybe Southeast Asia, that might not have been specific to unit driven, it might have been more broader. But we have heard that some sincere pickup in wafer or utilization rates, I would say, actually in China, where obviously, they've had a lot of investment in capacity over the years. Is that something that you can corroborate?

Is that something that maybe gives you some encouragement in terms of what mainstream could kind of look like moving into next year?

David Reeder: Mainstream, we did see, let's talk broadly first. Mainstream, we did see a little bit of a pickup in mainstream demand, particularly the portions of mainstream that are most tied to AI. So kind of power management, we did see some good performance in kind of industrial automotive. So I do think that there was a little bit of pickup in those portions of the market for mainstream. Again, I'm speaking very broadly at this point. I think for mainstream, we have talked about this kind of all year is that a lot of those mainstream applications or maybe end markets, they require memory. And as you know, memory is incredibly tight.

So if the end market requires memory, I think you ultimately have to look and say, well, how much total memory is available and where is it going to go and be allocated. And so I do think that it kind of creates kind of an upper ceiling perhaps on maybe what we can expect from mainstream over the near term until more capacity comes online for memory. Specifically to China. China, we were flat in the quarter. I think we were up 6% sequentially if memory serves. We're now flat for the year in China, which I think is good momentum because remember, we had some tough comps to Liberation Day from a year ago.

And so we've kind of picked up momentum as we kind of went through the year with China. So obviously, the rest of the world that's more tied to the most advanced manufacturing has grown the fastest. I do think that China has kind of picked up a little bit throughout the year, and I think that's probably true broadly as well as for us specifically. Thank you for the question, Brian.

Operator: We'll go next now to Aleksey Yefremov at Barclays.

Aleksey Yefremov: Congrats on a great quarter. I wanted to ask you first question about the incremental margins. They were quite strong. Is it something we should expect near term given potential need for investments to support this growth. And also if you could address the differences in incremental margins between the 2 segments?

Sukhi Nagesh: Yes. Aleksey, thank you for the question. Look, I mean, as you pointed out, our incremental gross margin of close to 60% and our incremental EBITDA margin of greater than 40% is in line with our targets. I think we mentioned this before. That's how we want to run our operations. And so I think it was a bunch of little execution items that we did. A lot of this is self-help, right? We talked a little bit about productivity and yield initiatives, how we were able to even control inventory and scrap. So there was a lot of folks who -- our manufacturing people did a fantastic job in actually producing more out of our factories in the quarter.

And we think this trend is likely going to continue as we head into next year. Did you have a follow-up, Aleksey?

Aleksey Yefremov: I think, Dave, you mentioned that some of the pickup in the sales sequentially was due to being able to unlock some manufacturing capacity or just productivity. So to what extent was the sequential increase sort of market pull versus your internal ability to serve that market demand that maybe already was there?

David Reeder: I think the vast majority of it was our ability to be able to satisfy some demand that was already in front of us, but we were unsure if we were going to be able to complete it in the quarter. We made a couple of comments about how the book-to-bill has been quite robust. And so if you look at where we significantly outperformed, yes, we outperformed on the CapEx side of the business, but we also outperformed on units as well.

So I would say that CapEx was kind of the biggest contributor or the CapEx-related revenue, I should say, is the biggest contributor to the outperformance, but then as we kind of progress through the quarter, we did have more unit pull than we originally expected as well. So both demand that was in front of us as well as kind of, let's call it, quarterly consumption, both of those performed well, but probably slightly higher towards the -- weighted towards the CapEx business versus the unit-driven business for Q3.

Operator: We'll go next now to Timothy Arcuri with UBS.

Timothy Arcuri: Dave, I know you're probably going to talk about this. I mean you're definitely going to talk about this at the Analyst Day, but can you maybe give us a little bit of a sneak peek on what the rubric is for growth versus the market? I know you used to say 4 to 6 points of outgrowth, but it's been kind of all over the map lately. You were mostly undergoing, you undergrew in '25 and during the first half of this year. But in this most recent quarter, you were like 8 points above the market. So sort of like can you give us some breadcrumbs in terms of how to think about this rubric?

Is it like still 4 to 6 points? Is it like less than that?

David Reeder: Thanks for the question, Tim. I'm going to give you an unsatisfying answer, but I won't make you wait completely for Capital Markets Day. For the more complete answer, please show up November 9 at Capital Markets Day. For the short answer, just to help you out a little bit in the interim. Look, it will be somewhat consistent to what we've articulated in the past, and we'll give you much more color around that at Capital Markets Day.

Timothy Arcuri: Okay. And then, Sukhi, can you just speak to the impact from Colorado and KSP on the margins? I know -- I mean, you're doing great. And I think KSP is still dilutive this year and probably still next year. And then Colorado is still in qual, and I think it's supposed to be breakeven maybe in late '27, early '28. So can you talk to the impact from those? I guess I'm trying to get like what a clean gross margin would be if those weren't dilutive?

Sukhi Nagesh: Yes. Well, so good question, Tim. So let me just say on KSP side, we are actually in Q3, we reached breakeven. Big accomplishment for the team here. We actually reached breakeven in Q3, and as we look into next year, this quarter and Q4 and next year, we're pretty excited about the ramp we're going to be seeing in KSP South. And I think we mentioned about Colorado we are currently focused on customer qualifications. The facility is actually operational. It's producing samples right now, and we expect revenue to begin in next year. So it's about a 12-month lag time between Rockrimmon and KSP South.

But KSP South is now breakeven on a gross profit standpoint, and it will continue to improve as we head into next year.

David Reeder: And if I could just build on that briefly. So KSP specifically to enterprise gross margins dilutive now through most of 2027, as we exit '27, it should be somewhat neutral with respect to enterprise gross margin, and then Colorado is going to run about a year behind kind of what we see happening in KSP. So the numbers that we're delivering today are with that both of those -- fully burdened with both of those facilities in the P&L. We will give you more color on where we think long-term gross margins could reside at Capital Markets Day.

Operator: We'll go next now to Jim Schneider with Goldman Sachs.

James Schneider: Just to follow up on the prior question. Maybe could you just give us your overall view on if we continue to get increases on the revenue side for the next couple of years as the industry seems to think we can? Do you have enough capacity with what you're ramping in Colorado, KSP, et cetera? And are you at all rethinking any of the sort of shutdowns or optimization on the existing manufacturing base at all?

David Reeder: Jim. Look, we -- as you mentioned, we do have strong demand. We have strong momentum. We have run that demand profile essentially against our internal capacity models. We feel quite good about our positioning. For '27 we feel pretty good about what we think '28 could be. And so we feel good about our 4-wall capacity. We think we have a lot of capacity left in the network to optimize and deliver through really the 4 main points that I've always kind of spoken about, it's network optimization, the centralization of procurement with all of our suppliers yield and then, of course, the productivity initiatives, both through labor as well as equipment.

So we feel quite good about that capacity. We're going to constantly evaluate that. And we also recognize that there will be areas where we do get pinch points. We'll work to relieve those and we'll selectively spend CapEx to be able to unlock those. Did you have a follow-up, Jim?

James Schneider: Yes, please. And I realize this may be something you tackle at the Investor Day, but I'm curious a little over a year ago when you came into the company. I think you talked about potentially expanding the aperture of customer focus and expanding the sort of like the catch-on of sales and the kind of customers Entegris?pursues. Can you give us any kind of update on how that valuation is going?

David Reeder: Sure. The summarized update, and we'll go into more detail at Capital Markets Day. But the summarized update is we have never had more customer engagements and engineering engagements than we have today. We feel like we are communicating with our customers and engaging with our customers earlier in the process than ever. That's enabling us to then engage in the road maps earlier than ever. And then we think that's turning into a plan of record wins, both for the long-term road map as well as quick spends and derivative product that you inevitably release based upon new and kind of half node manufacturing that occurs in the fab. So we're incredibly happy with those efforts.

I think you're seeing some early signs of those efforts bearing fruit, and we'll talk more about it at Capital Markets Day.

Operator: We'll go next now to Chris Parkinson with Wolfe Research.

Christopher Parkinson: I'll do my best not to ask Capital Markets Day spoiler. Real quick. To drill into MS and CMP, there's been a lot of debate over the last couple of weeks and months on share gains momentum and kind of your position in both slurries and, to a lesser extent, pads. I'd love to hear your updated thoughts on where those businesses are trending relative to expectations, whether or not there are any differences based on the competitive environments in various geographies. I would just love to hear your kind of broader thoughts as we progress towards the end of the year.

David Reeder: Sure. And I'll -- maybe we'll just talk geographies really quickly, and I'll speak broadly and then maybe directly kind of target your question. I mean for the third quarter on a year-over-year basis, North America was up 22%; Taiwan 41%, Southeast Asia 51%, Japan 29%. I could go on. But we performed well across the geographies. We performed well in the areas where the most advanced manufacturing occurs, that's both logic and memory. And then moving that conversation specifically to the MS division and CMP, MS has picked up momentum as we've gone through this year.

And so you saw us kind of in the early part of the year, we were growing kind of in the low single digits. We moved into the mid- to high single digits, and now we're in squarely into the teens, if not migrating into the upper teens. That business is anchored by CMP and the CMP process. So we feel very good about our position in slurries. If there's an area where I wish we had a bit more capacity, it is pads. So that's an area where we have a small pinch point, and we're unlocking that as quickly as we can.

But we feel quite good about that business, and we'll talk about it more on Capital Markets Day. Do you have a follow-up, Chris?

Christopher Parkinson: Yes. I'd love to also hear your quick thoughts. I mean part of the -- you've consistently been speaking about this incremental $1 billion that you can unlock over the next several years. You gave us some helpful color on KSP as well as Colorado. I'd love to just hear your kind of broader thoughts on -- now you've been in the role for just over a year on your overall asset base utilization, perhaps how you're doing things a little bit differently just given the growth trajectory and how that continues to evolve. Just 1.5 year in or so, just a preliminary assessment would be particularly helpful.

David Reeder: Sure. Thanks, Chris. Look, I'll try to be brief on this one. We can certainly go into it in more depth at Capital Markets Day. But the way I think about it, there's no more -- there's no more attractive dollar than investing in CapEx at a brownfield site, so at a site that already exists. And the reason why that is -- because that's where you get the most fixed cost absorption, you get to leverage the existing team, the existing infrastructure. And so each incremental dollar at existing sites to drive additional scale is a dollar that returns incredibly quickly.

And so what you're actually seeing us do is you're seeing us invest dollars and we are investing to expand capacity today. We're investing at the current sites where we're already located and have critical mass. And so we are not standing path on exactly the capacity that we entered the year with, even though we've closed 3 dilutive facilities, we actually have more capacity right now than we did when we entered the year. And so we're optimizing the network. We're investing in the places where we have the most scale. Those are the dollars with the highest return and those are the dollars that unlock the most capacity for us.

That's what we're going to continue to do, is drive scale, efficiency and critical mass at those brownfield sites that exist. And then ultimately, we'll also continue to optimize the network. Thank you for your question, Chris.

Operator: We'll go next now to Charles Shi with Needham.

Yu Shi: Maybe the first one, Dave, I know this is going to be your second guidance to Q1. You guided a mid-single digit. But I look back the financial history of Entegris, minus 5%, sequential down in Q1, that's not norm. Your normal seasonality is way less than that, and we would love to thank maybe very big up cycle like this year, maybe going into next year seasonality should be thrown out of the window. But why you think Q1 would be down minus -- will be down 5% based on what you're seeing right now?

David Reeder: Charles, I'll start, and then I'll turn it over to Sukhi for the details. Look, as you know, we really only guide 1 quarter at a time, and that's fourth quarter that we guided up at midpoint about 25%. We were trying to give you some early indications of color for Q1. And Sukhi, maybe do you want to build on that?

Sukhi Nagesh: Yes. Look, I mean, like you said, we do guide 1 quarter at a time. But based on our visibility, Charles, that we have today, and we continue to see very healthy demand and strong momentum, right? And so -- but if you look at our Q1, it really reflects normal seasonality and fewer selling days for us. Nothing more than that, especially given that 75% of our business is unit driven. And so that's what -- that's why I think we wanted to give you some extra color on how Q1 is going to trend. But the underlying momentum, the orders, what we're hearing from our customers are pretty strong.

David Reeder: Did you have a follow-up, Charles?

Yu Shi: Yes. Maybe not trying to ask you more forward-looking, but maybe looking back 2026, 8% MSI, let's say CapEx is 30% year-on-year. The blended market growth is somewhere about 14%. If the math is right, you did have 300 bps of outperformance relative to the market this year. Last year, I don't think you had outperformance. So want to ask you, if you look back at 2026 based on your current guidance, out of that 300 bps outperformance, what you see as sustaining, will you see maybe a little bit of a transitory at this point?

David Reeder: Sure. I guess the first comment I would make is 30%, roughly 30% of our revenue is driven by CapEx, but the majority of that is actually driven by fab starts and fab construction, which doesn't really fall in period for us for 2026. So I would characterize our outperformance is probably a little bit higher than the number referenced but that's neither here or there. I think looking back at 2026, I think CapEx remains strong as we roll into 2027, certainly all the third-party forecasts seem to indicate that, that direction. I think fab construction that didn't fall into period for us for 2026 would probably fall in the period for 2027.

So I think that bodes well for us. And then I think MSI. MSI, it's improving and it's improving because of the CapEx that's being put online. But it's also improving because the mainstream picked up just a little bit. So I think we all kind of know like which fabs are under construction, which fabs are moving into the tooling and production and qualification stage. I think we can take those and we can kind of map those out over time and make assumptions on how they ramp, all of which I think bodes well. I think the wildcard is MSI, 55% of MSI is driven by mainstream logic.

I think the wildcard is where does utilization go for mainstream logic improved slightly. I think that helps in the second half of this year. Does that improvement continue in '27. And if so, then I think that's kind of another plus in the positive column. Thank you for your question, Charles.

Operator: We'll go next now to Edward Yang with Oppenheimer.

Edward Yang: Dave, Sukhi. Just a final question on this first quarter revenue moderation you're seeing chalking up to seasonality. Could you split that between MS and APS, I would think it would be weighted more on the CapEx side of the business?

Sukhi Nagesh: Actually, it will be both. I think we are -- what we do see will be a double-digit growth for both MS and APS division, Q4 and Q1. So I think overall, just -- I think if you think about our normal seasonality and a number of -- it's lesser selling days, right? And so that's why we're going to see a slight dip there, but the momentum, the underlying momentum from customers, the orders are pretty strong. Do you have a follow-up?

Edward Yang: Maybe a question for Dave. In the past, again, you've described the multi-wave demand cycle, fab construction followed by WFE, ultimately higher wafer starts. Just wanted to get a sense with revenue now accelerating beyond your prior expectations, which inning are we in each of those 3 ways? And are they starting to overlap?

David Reeder: I really -- I mean each individual fab is kind of its own wave. But I really think that we're probably in the earlier part of the innings. Staying with the World Series theme, I think we're in the earlier part of the innings here, just simply because of the fab construction that we've seen and how much has been broken ground, how much has been completed with Shell, how much has been being facilitized in tools. I think we're in the earlier part of these innings and not the latter part.

So I think this CapEx that I think everyone is anticipating to occur in '27, I think probably the biggest part of units are more like '28, '29, not '27. So I think we're still in the CapEx portion of the cycle, and perhaps that inflects maybe at the end of '27 perhaps middle of '28, something like that would be my expectation. But we'll see how it goes. As you know, semi is very dynamic. Thank you for the question.

Operator: We'll go next now to John Roberts with Mizuho.

Unknown Analyst: This is [ Saurabh ] on behalf of John Roberts. Can you provide some insights from your conversations from your customers that would suggest that they're open to give some pricing?

Sukhi Nagesh: Yes. Look, on pricing, our approach hasn't really changed much on pricing. We have really deep, long-standing relationships with our customers, and our priority is right now to support them as the demand accelerates and while being appropriately compensated for the value we provide. So it's really important to note that our conversations with the customers are around -- right now around the commercial engagements and how to get the product to them faster. But we always like -- we always evaluate pricing at the product and customer level. But we -- as we said, as Dave mentioned in his prepared remarks, we have not included any material pricing actions in the quarter for Q3 or Q4.

To the extent there is any pricing actions, it will be on new orders, but not on existing backlog.

David Reeder: And if there's something that I'm incredibly excited about is on a year-over-year basis, I mean we've improved adjusted gross margin by 530 bps year-over-year, independent of any pricing action. So the self-help initiatives that we talked about in the latter part of 2025 are starting to bear fruit. And as Sukhi mentioned, we'll have ongoing conversations with customers with respect to making sure that we can deliver product and receive value for that product. Did you have a follow-up?

Unknown Analyst: Yes. So -- and are you expecting to receive more tax refunds in Q4? And what would be the magnitude for that?

Sukhi Nagesh: No, we're not.

Operator: We'll go next now to Pete Osterland at Truist.

Peter Osterland: Just wanted to dig into the segment margins a bit. So just starting with the significant step-up that you saw from margins in APS. At the revenue levels you're expecting in the near term, are 34% plus segment margin sustainable? Were there any unusually favorable margin dynamics around mix or anything else in the third quarter?

David Reeder: No. Look, from an APS perspective, we don't talk a lot about individual. We don't optimize for the segments at Entegris. But the APS business is performing incredibly well. There were really no unusual one-time items that flow through the APS segment. The team performed well. My expectation is the team will continue to perform well. And I think what you're seeing on the MS side of the business just for completeness is you are seeing leverage in the MS side of the business. In fact, I think gross margins were up, I don't know, around 350 bps on a year-over-year basis. I think it's 60 bps sequentially in MS. But we just see tremendous opportunity in that business.

And we're increasingly convinced that it's our right to win in the MS business. And so we're making some significant investments there to capture those opportunities. Did you have a follow-up, Pete?

Peter Osterland: Yes, very helpful. I also wanted to just ask on cash flow expectations. Do you expect to deliver higher free cash flow in fourth quarter versus third quarter. I guess any working capital considerations to call out? And just wondering, overall, what is a reasonable normalized free cash flow conversion rate that you're expecting going forward?

Sukhi Nagesh: Yes. Look, we'll provide more information on our free cash flow targets at the Capital Markets Day, but more near term for Q4, we are -- we do have some CapEx spending and working capital requirements to support the growth that we're seeing from our customers, and that's what's embedded in our guidance that we provided to you.

Operator: We'll go next now to Mike Harrison with Seaport Research Partners.

Michael Harrison: Congrats on a nice quarter. You mentioned in APS that you were seeing good growth in micro environment. But then you also said you were benefiting from better mix. I guess my question is, is that microenvironment business, a better margin business than it used to be? Or should we still think of that as being kind of a below segment average margin?

Sukhi Nagesh: Yes. We don't talk about margins on a specific product line, honestly. But I think when we ask for -- when we sell our products, we expect to get the value for our products, and most of our products are pretty good margin structure. Dave, you want to add anything to that?

David Reeder: Yes. I think just talking briefly about the microenvironments business. When you think about new fab construction and you think about those fabs that need overhead transport for wafers for the protection, security, and the contamination control environment of those wafers. We invented the FOUPs 30-plus years ago as a company. That's an area where we have a very significant market share in that market. It is a market that is growing meaningfully and that's an area where we're participating, as you would expect as the market leader in that space.

So quite happy with that business and the way that it's growing, and the way the team is executing, and we look forward to ramping that Colorado facility where we're going to get a lot of those new units for the Americas. So happy with how that business is performing. Do you have a follow-up, Mike?

Michael Harrison: Yes. Just another one on APS in the filtration and purification opportunity, you guys in the past have projected that advanced nodes would be kind of multiples of prior nodes in terms of the purity requirements and the revenue associated with that. As you're seeing some of these new nodes actually move into production and starting to move into higher volume manufacturing. Just curious how the filtration and purification revenue is comparing to your projections. Is it tracking expectations? Or is it maybe even a little bit better than you anticipated?

David Reeder: I think when you think about migrating down to 2 nanometers and even below, I mean, 2 nanometers is 20 angstroms in a molecule, a large molecule is about 5 angstroms. So I mean you're essentially down at the atomic scale. I know we've talked about it in a while, but we're truly down to the atomic scale. I think contamination requirements have increased something like 3 orders of magnitude over the last 25 years. It's incredible how tight the controls are for contamination for the latest generation of semiconductor manufacturing. And so as the leader in filtration and purification we think that bodes well for us.

We've talked about this for a long time about how advanced manufacturing drives higher requirements both on the material side so that you can enable performance and on the purity side so that you can protect yield. And I think both divisions you're starting to see them really come together from a company perspective where you can no longer just worry about one, increasingly, you need both of those divisions to have a successful process. And so the promise of the business looks like it's finally coming to fruition.

I think you're seeing that on the contamination control side as you referenced, and we're very happy with the performance and trajectory of the business, and we certainly look forward to talking more about that at Capital Markets Day. Thank you.

Operator: Thank you. Gentlemen, it appears we have no further questions this morning, so that will bring us to the conclusion of Entegris' Third Quarter 2026 Conference Call. We'd like to thank you all so much for joining us today and wish you all a wonderful day. Goodbye.

news.Title: KLA Stocks Rise 7.2% With Cash Covering Its Capital Returns
news.Content:
This article first appeared on GuruFocus .

KLA ( NASDAQ:KLAC ) is turning chip inspection demand into cashand investors are paying up. Shares climbed to $170.19, up approximately 7.19% in October 29 regular trading, following a 7.2% gain at 10.10 a.m. ET. The semiconductor inspection and process-control supplier's quarterly performance puts cash generation at the center of the investment case: how much of that demand reaches shareholders?

Warning! GuruFocus has detected 4 Warning Signs with SSNLF.

Is KLAC fairly valued? Test your thesis with our free DCF calculator.

Revenue reached approximately $4.14 billion, while free cash flow totaled $1.34 billion. KLA reported capital returns of $1.24 billion for the quarter, consuming roughly 92.5% of free cash flow and leaving about $100 million after distributions. The payout had cash behind it, although that narrow cushion offers limited room if cash generation weakens.

The valuation adds another hurdle. At $170.19, shares sit 46.88% above the displayed GF Value estimate of $115.87, suggesting investors are paying a substantial premium to that benchmark. That estimate alone does not establish where shares should trade, but it sharpens the execution test. Management's December-quarter revenue midpoint of $4.7 billion points to further growth; investors should watch whether margins and cash collections can support both that expansion and continued shareholder returns.
